teile.einleitung: A pictogram is a simple picture symbol that gives information without words. You find pictograms at railway stations, on road signs, at emergency exits and on mobile phones. Because they need no language, people all over the world understand them.
wichtigste: A pictogram is a simple picture symbol.
People from many countries understand pictograms because they manage without words.
The sign for the emergency exit shows a running figure on a green background.
A crossed-out cigarette means “No smoking”.
For every Olympic Games, special pictograms are designed for all the sports.
A knife and fork on the motorway point to a restaurant.
On a mobile phone, a telephone receiver usually stands for “Call”.

abschnitte.text: The word **pictogram** is made up of the Latin “pictum” for painted and the Greek “gramma” for something written. A pictogram shows a thing or an instruction with a greatly simplified picture. It leaves out details and uses clear shapes and few colours. This means you can recognise its meaning at a glance, even from a long way off.

Because pictograms manage without words, people from many countries understand them. This is especially important at airports, railway stations and sports events with visitors from all over the world. In a multilingual country like **Switzerland**, they also mean that signs do not have to be written in four languages. However, you still have to learn some symbols, for example what a particular colour means.

The sign with the running figure on a **green** background shows the way to the emergency exit. A crossed-out cigarette means no smoking, and a wheelchair shows a place for wheelchair users. On the motorway, a knife and fork point to a restaurant. The care symbols on clothes, which show the washing temperature for example, are also pictograms.

For every **Olympic Games**, designers create their own pictograms for all the sports. The 1964 Games in Tokyo were the first to introduce a complete system of such sports symbols. The pictograms by the German designer **Otl Aicher** for the 1972 Olympic Games in Munich became famous. His geometric stick figures influenced the design of picture symbols worldwide.

On computers and mobile phones, such picture symbols are usually called **icons**. A telephone receiver stands for calling, a cogwheel for settings and a magnifying glass for searching. Some icons even show things that many children no longer know today, such as the floppy disk as a symbol for saving. **Emojis** are also a modern, colourful form of picture symbol.

Even the oldest writing systems in the world began with picture symbols, for example Egyptian **hieroglyphs**. In the 20th century the Viennese Otto Neurath developed a picture system with which statistics could be shown without words. Later many safety signs were standardised internationally so that they look the same everywhere. Today, for example, an ISO standard sets out how warning and escape signs must be designed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A simple picture symbol that communicates something without words.
A small picture symbol on the screen, for example for a program.
The picture writing of the ancient Egyptians.
A rule that sets out how something is designed in a uniform way.

gewusst: The green emergency exit figure was designed in Japan and later adopted internationally.
Many people no longer know what a real floppy disk looks like, but they know the save symbol.
Otl Aicher designed his Olympic figures on a fixed grid with only a few permitted angles.

teile.einleitung: A parity bit is an extra bit that is added to a sequence of zeros and ones. It helps to detect whether an error has happened when data is transmitted. It is one of the simplest methods of error detection in computer science.
wichtigste: A parity bit is used to detect transmission errors.
With even parity, the parity bit is chosen so that the number of ones is even.
With odd parity, the total number of ones must be odd.
With even parity, a 0 is added to 1011001 and a 1 to 1101000.
If two bits flip at the same time, a single parity bit does not notice the error.
A simple parity bit cannot correct errors, because it does not show which bit is wrong.
The parity bit is classically used on the serial port.

abschnitte.text: Computers store and send all data as **bits**, that is, as zeros and ones. When data is transmitted by cable or radio, interference can turn a 0 into a 1 or the other way round. The **parity bit** is an extra check bit that is added to the data. With it, the recipient can check whether the data has probably arrived correctly.

With **even parity**, you count the ones in the data. If their number is odd, you add a 1, otherwise a 0, so that there is an even number of ones altogether. With **odd parity** it is exactly the other way round: the total number of ones must be odd. Sender and recipient must agree beforehand which kind they are using.

The sequence 1011001 contains four ones, so with even parity the parity bit is **0**. The sequence 1101000 contains three ones, so a **1** is added. With odd parity, 1100110 with its four ones gets a 1 as its parity bit. If, with even parity, you receive the sequence 10110110 with five ones, you know straight away: an error has occurred.

A single parity bit only detects when an **odd number** of bits have flipped. If two bits flip at the same time, the parity is correct again and the error goes unnoticed. In addition, it does not show which bit is wrong, so it cannot **correct** errors. The recipient can only ask for the data to be sent again.

The parity bit is classically used on the **serial port**, through which modems, mice and printers used to be connected. Old punched tape also often had a separate track just for parity holes. The idea of parity is also found in some memory chips and in groups of hard drives, so-called RAID systems. Modern networks mostly use stronger checking methods such as checksums.

To not only detect errors but also fix them, several check bits are used. Around 1950 the American mathematician **Richard Hamming** developed the **Hamming code** named after him. It can find a single wrong bit and correct it automatically. Today such methods protect data, for example, on memory cards and on space probes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest unit of information; it is either 0 or 1.
The property of a number of being even or odd.
A bit is changed on the way by interference.
An extra bit with which data can be checked.

gewusst: The word parity comes from the Latin “par”, which means “equal”.
QR codes also contain error correction, which is why they can often still be read when a piece is missing.
With a card trick based on parity, you can find out which card in a grid has been secretly turned over.

teile.einleitung: A greedy algorithm simply chooses, at each step, the option that looks best at that moment. It does not think far ahead and never changes a decision. This is fast and often surprisingly good, but it can sometimes lead you astray.
wichtigste: A greedy algorithm makes the locally best choice at each step.
It never takes back a decision once made.
When giving change with Swiss coins, it gives the smallest number of coins: for 3.70 francs it is 4 coins.
With awkward coin values such as 1, 3 and 4, it does not always find the best solution.
The algorithms of Kruskal and Prim greedily find a minimum spanning tree.
Huffman coding builds a code tree by always combining the two rarest characters.
In the fractional knapsack problem, the greedy choice by value per weight always finds the optimum.

abschnitte.text: A **greedy algorithm** solves a problem step by step and always takes whatever brings the most at that moment. It does not compare all the possible solutions, but decides quickly and for good. That is why it is usually very fast and simple to program. Whether the result really is the best, however, depends on the problem. In German it is called a “gieriger Algorithmus”, which means the same.

A classic example is **giving change**. With Swiss coins of 5, 2 and 1 francs and 50, 20, 10 and 5 centimes, you always take the biggest coin that still fits. For 3.70 francs that is 2 francs, 1 franc, 50 centimes and 20 centimes, so 4 coins. With Swiss coin values this always gives the smallest number of coins. But if there were only coins of 1, 3 and 4, the greedy algorithm would choose the coins 4, 1 and 1 for 6, although two 3s with only 2 coins would be better.

Greedy methods are very useful in **graphs**, that is networks of points and connections. **Kruskal’s algorithm** finds a minimum spanning tree by always taking the cheapest connection that does not form a cycle. **Prim’s algorithm** builds the spanning tree from a starting point, edge by edge. In this way you can plan, for example, how to connect villages with as little cable as possible. Dijkstra’s algorithm for shortest paths also works on a greedy principle.

In the **knapsack problem** you are meant to pack the most valuable things possible without the rucksack becoming too heavy. If you are allowed to split things, such as sand or flour, the greedy choice by value per kilogram always gives the best solution. If you have to take things whole or not at all, this does not always work. In scheduling there is a proven greedy rule: always choose the appointment that ends earliest, and the most appointments will then fit in without overlapping.

In the **travelling salesman problem**, you have to visit many cities on the shortest round trip. The **nearest neighbour heuristic** greedily always goes to the nearest city not yet visited. This is quick, but the route is often much longer than the best one. That is why greedy algorithms are often used as a fast approximation. **Huffman coding**, on the other hand, is a greedy method that provably works optimally and is used to compress data, for example in ZIP files and JPEG pictures.

begriffe.erklaerung: Exact step-by-step instructions for solving a problem.
The decision that looks best at that moment.
The best possible solution.
A rule of thumb that quickly gives a good, but not always the best, solution.
A network of connections that links all the points without cycles.

gewusst: David Huffman invented Huffman coding in 1952 as a student, because it let him get out of a final exam.
Cashiers usually use a greedy algorithm quite automatically when giving change.
Whether a coin system always works optimally with the greedy method depends only on the coin values chosen.

teile.einleitung: The running time of an algorithm describes how many steps or how much time it needs to solve a task. Above all, it shows how strongly the effort grows when the input gets bigger. This lets you find out whether a program is still fast enough even with huge amounts of data.
wichtigste: The running time tells you how many steps or how much time an algorithm needs.
People often count calculation steps instead of seconds, because computers run at different speeds.
If a list becomes twice as long, the number of comparisons in linear search doubles in the worst case.
Two nested loops with 20 passes each run the inner part 400 times.
The case with the most steps is called the worst case.
Big O notation shows how fast the running time grows with the size of the input.
Cracking a 4-digit number code by trial and error takes at most 10,000 attempts.

abschnitte.text: The **running time** says how much work an algorithm needs for a task. It is usually not measured in seconds; instead you count the **calculation steps**, for example comparisons or additions. A new computer is faster than an old one, but the algorithm stays the same. What matters most is how the number of steps changes when the input grows. The size of the input is usually called n, for example the number of names in a list.

In **linear search** you look at one entry after another. With 100 names you need 100 comparisons in the worst case, with 200 names 200 comparisons. So the running time grows at the same rate as the list. If the list is sorted, it is much faster with **binary search**. You keep halving the search area and so find a name among 1,000 entries with about 10 comparisons.

If a loop runs n times and inside it a second loop also runs n times, the inner part is carried out n times n times. With n equal to 20, that is 400 passes. If, in a class of 30 people, everyone is to be compared with everyone else exactly once, that is 30 times 29 divided by 2, so 435 comparisons. Such algorithms have a **quadratic** running time. If the class becomes twice as big, there are about four times as many comparisons.

The running time often depends on exactly what the input looks like. If the name you are looking for is right at the front, linear search is finished after one step; that is the **best case**. If it is right at the back or missing, you need the most steps; that is the **worst case**. In between there is the average case. Computer scientists usually look at the worst case, because then they know for sure the longest it can take.

Some tasks have a huge running time. A 4-digit number code has 10,000 possibilities, from 0000 to 9999. Every extra digit makes trying them out ten times more work. That is why long **passwords** are much more secure than short ones. **Big O notation** sums up how fast the effort grows, for example O(n) for linear search and O(n²) for two nested loops.

Search engines, satnavs and social networks work with billions of pieces of data. An algorithm with a poor running time would be far too slow there. That is why computer scientists are always looking for **efficient** solutions. A better idea can achieve more than a faster computer. In computer science, the word running time also refers to the period during which a program is actually being run.

begriffe.erklaerung: Exact step-by-step instructions for solving a task.
The input for which an algorithm needs the most steps.
A way of writing that shows how fast the effort grows with the size of the input.
Using little time or memory.

gewusst: With binary search you can find a name among a million sorted entries with at most about 20 comparisons.
A good algorithm on an old computer can be faster than a bad algorithm on a supercomputer.
Whether fast algorithms exist at all for certain difficult tasks is one of the biggest open questions in computer science.

teile.einleitung: Insertion sort, in German “Sortieren durch Einfügen”, is a simple method for putting a list in order. You take one element after another and insert it in the right place in the part that is already sorted. This is exactly how many people sort the cards in their hand when playing cards.
wichtigste: Insertion sort inserts each new element in the right place in a sorted part.
The front part of the list is always already sorted.
With almost sorted lists, insertion sort works especially quickly.
With lists sorted in reverse order, it has to do the most work.
Insertion sort is stable: equal values keep their order.
It sorts directly in the existing list and needs no second list.
For very large lists it is slower than methods such as merge sort or quicksort.

abschnitte.text: Imagine you are dealt playing cards one at a time. You put each new card straight into the right place among the cards you are already holding. That way your hand is always in order. This is exactly what **insertion sort** does with a list of numbers: the front part is **sorted**, the back part is still waiting.

Take the list 4, 3, 1, 2. First the 4 on its own counts as sorted, then the 3 is inserted in front of it, giving 3, 4, 1, 2. Next the 1 moves right to the front, and finally the 2 slides in between 1 and 3. At the end you have 1, 2, 3, 4, and each time the numbers were only **compared** and **moved**.

If the list is already sorted, insertion sort needs very little work: with 6 numbers only 5 comparisons. If, on the other hand, it is **sorted in reverse**, every new element has to move all the way to the front. Then the effort grows roughly with the square of the number of elements, which computer scientists write as **O(n²)**. With 1,000 numbers that is already about half a million comparisons.

Insertion sort is a **stable** sorting method. This means that two equal values stay in the same order as before, which is important when sorting by several features. It also sorts **in-place**, that is, directly in the existing list. It does not need a second list of the same size as temporary storage.

Insertion sort is very well suited to small or almost sorted lists. That is why many fast sorting programs, for example in Python or Java, use it for short sections. For huge, unordered lists people prefer methods such as **merge sort** or **quicksort**. Insertion sort is popular in school because you can easily try it out by hand.

begriffe.erklaerung: Exact instructions on how to put data into an order.
Step-by-step instructions for solving a task.
Equal values keep their original order when sorted.
The sorting happens directly in the existing list without a large second list.

gewusst: Many people sort their playing cards quite automatically using the principle of insertion sort.
The sorting method Timsort, which is built into Python, uses insertion sort for small sections.
An already sorted list is the best case for insertion sort and a bad case for some other methods.

teile.einleitung: A cash machine is a device where you can take out cash from your bank account around the clock. In Switzerland many people call it a Bancomat, and inside it there is a small computer that is connected to the bank.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the cash machine is often called a Bancomat.
You get cash at the Bancomat.
You need a bank card and the PIN code for it.
The money comes from your own bank account.
You never tell anyone your PIN and cover it with your hand when typing it in.
If you type the PIN in wrongly several times, you risk your card being blocked.
A Bancomat usually gives back the card first and then the money.

abschnitte.text: A **cash machine** is a machine that gives out banknotes. You find them at bank branches, railway stations, shopping centres and airports. In Switzerland people usually say **Bancomat**, which was originally the name of a particular system. The world’s first cash machine was put into service in London in 1967. Today there are millions of such devices around the world.

You put the **bank card** into the slot and type in the secret **PIN code**. Then you choose the amount, for example 50 or 100 francs. The machine usually gives back the card first, so that you do not forget it, and only then the money. If you want, it also prints a receipt. The amount is immediately taken from your own **bank account**.

Inside a cash machine there is a computer with a screen, a keypad and a card reader. Over a secure **data connection** it asks the bank whether the card is valid and whether there is enough money in the account. The data is **encrypted** so that nobody can read it. Only when the bank agrees does a mechanism count out the banknotes. An armoured safe protects the money inside the machine.

You must not tell anyone your PIN code, not even friends or people claiming to work for the bank. When typing it in, you cover the keypad with your hand so that nobody can watch. If you type the PIN in wrongly several times, the card is **blocked** or kept by the machine. This stops a thief from simply guessing the code. If you notice something strange at the machine, such as a loose attachment on the card slot, you should not use it.

In Switzerland there are banknotes of 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 1000 francs. Most machines mainly give out 20, 50, 100 and 200 franc notes. Many Bancomats also offer euros, especially near the border. Although people today often pay by card or **mobile phone**, many people in Switzerland still like to use cash. For children there are youth accounts with their own card, often from about the age of 12.

begriffe.erklaerung: The usual word in Switzerland for a cash machine.
A secret number with which you prove that the card belongs to you.
An account at a bank in which money is kept.
Turning data into a secret code so that strangers cannot read it.

gewusst: The world’s first cash machine stood outside a bank branch in London in 1967.
PIN is short for “personal identification number”.
The Swiss 1000 franc note is one of the banknotes with the highest value in the world.

teile.einleitung: A pipeline in a processor works much like an assembly line in a factory. An instruction is broken down into several steps, and each step is done by its own stage. This means several instructions can be worked on at the same time in different phases, and the processor becomes much faster.
wichtigste: With a pipeline, several instructions are worked on at the same time in different phases.
The classic RISC pipeline has 5 stages.
In the first stage the instruction is fetched from memory.
If an instruction needs a result that is not yet ready, this is called a data hazard.
With forwarding, results are passed directly to the next stage.
Branch prediction helps against waiting times with conditional jumps.
An ideal 5-stage pipeline needs 104 clock cycles for 100 instructions.

abschnitte.text: Imagine a laundry: washing, drying and folding each take an hour. If you finish each load completely before starting the next, three loads take nine hours. If you are already washing the next load while the first is in the dryer, you finish much more quickly. This is exactly how the **pipeline** in a **processor** works.

The classic **RISC pipeline** has five stages. First the instruction is fetched, then it is decoded, and then the calculation is done. In the fourth stage the instruction accesses memory, and in the fifth the result is written back into a register. Each stage needs one **clock cycle**, and in each cycle every instruction moves on one stage.

Without a pipeline an instruction takes five clock cycles, so 100 instructions take 500 cycles. With an ideal 5-stage pipeline, the first instruction is finished after five cycles, and after that another one follows in every cycle. So 100 instructions need only **104 cycles**. The pipeline does not make a single instruction faster, but it increases the **throughput**, the number of finished instructions per unit of time.

Sometimes an instruction needs the result of the previous instruction, which is not ready yet. This is called a **data hazard**. Then the processor has to wait and inserts an empty cycle, a so-called **pipeline bubble**. Conditional jumps also cause problems, because the processor only knows later which instruction comes next.

With **forwarding**, a result is passed directly to the next stage without waiting for it to be written back. **Branch prediction** helps against waiting times with jumps: the processor guesses which way will be taken and carries on working in the meantime. If it guesses wrong, it throws away the instructions it has started. Modern processors guess right very often.

Almost all of today's processors in computers, mobile phones and games consoles use pipelines. Some processors even had pipelines with far more than 20 stages in order to reach very high clock speeds. However, long pipelines have the disadvantage that a wrong branch prediction costs more time. That is why developers always look for a good middle way.

begriffe.erklaerung: The calculating centre of the computer that carries out instructions.
The steady heartbeat of the processor that controls all the steps.
A tiny, very fast storage place directly in the processor.
How many tasks are finished per unit of time.

gewusst: A modern processor can carry out several billion clock cycles per second.
The idea of the pipeline was already used in large computers around 1960.
Many processors have several pipelines side by side and can therefore finish several instructions per clock cycle.

teile.einleitung: Open source means that the “source” is open. It refers to software whose source code is open and may be read, changed and passed on by everyone. Many programs that you use every day are based on such open software.
wichtigste: With open-source software, the source code can be viewed by everyone.
The source code is the human-readable instructions in a programming language.
In 1991 Linus Torvalds started developing the operating system kernel Linux.
The web browser Firefox is developed by Mozilla as open source.
The GNU General Public License (GPL) requires changed versions to be released under the same licence again.
Software with secret source code that belongs to a company is called proprietary software.
Since 2024 the Swiss federal administration has in principle had to publish software it has developed itself openly.

abschnitte.text: A computer runs programs as machine code, which people can hardly read. But programmers first write **source code** in a programming language such as Python or C. With open source, exactly this source code is published. That way anyone can look at how the program works, find errors and suggest improvements.

What you may do with open software is stated in a **licence**. The best known is the **GNU General Public License (GPL)**, which appeared in 1989 and goes back to Richard Stallman. It requires changed versions to be under the GPL again and so to remain open. Other licences such as the MIT licence are less strict and also allow the code to be built into closed programs.

Richard Stallman founded the GNU project in 1983 because he wanted a free operating system. In 1991 the Finnish student Linus Torvalds started the operating system kernel **Linux**. The term “open source” became well known in 1998, when the Open Source Initiative was founded. In 2005 Torvalds also developed **Git**, a version control system that a huge number of projects use today.

The browser **Firefox**, the office program LibreOffice and the video player VLC are well-known open-source programs. The mobile phone operating system Android is based on the Linux kernel. Most web servers on the internet also run on Linux. Even the online encyclopedia Wikipedia uses open software and makes its texts freely available.

abschnitte.titel: How it differs from other software
abschnitte.text: With **proprietary software**, the source code stays secret and belongs to a company; examples are many programs from Microsoft or Apple. **Freeware** is free of charge, but its source code is not open. So open source is not the same as free of charge. What matters is the freedom to read, change and pass on the code.

The federal act on the use of electronic means to carry out official tasks, **EMBAG** for short, has been in force since 2024. It requires, in principle, that the federal administration discloses the source code of software it has developed itself. The idea behind it is “public money, public code”. This way cantons, municipalities or companies can also reuse these programs.

begriffe.erklaerung: The commands of a program, written in a way that people can read.
A set of rules that says what you may do with a piece of software.
Software whose source code is secret and belongs to a company.
Free software whose source code, however, is not open.
The group of people who work together on a project.

gewusst: Thousands of people from all over the world have already helped program the Linux kernel.
Linux's mascot is a penguin called Tux.
Many large companies pay employees to work on open-source projects.

teile.einleitung: A category is a group of things that have something in common. When we sort things into categories, we put the world in order and find everything again more quickly. Computers, libraries and shops use categories every day.
wichtigste: A category groups together things with shared features.
The tulip belongs to the category flowers.
The guitar belongs to the category musical instruments.
A jumper belongs in the category clothes, but a banana does not belong to furniture.
In the library you find a book about dinosaurs among the non-fiction books.
Shops have categories such as bread, dairy products or vegetables so that you can find things more quickly.
Computers also sort files, apps and websites into categories.

abschnitte.text: A category is a **group** or class of things that share a common feature. The word vegetables, for example, is the name of a category that includes carrots, leeks and broccoli. The name of the category is a **general term**. The individual things in it are called **specific terms**.

In the shop you find sections such as bread, **dairy products**, vegetables or drinks, where the orange juice is, for example. In the library, **non-fiction books**, novels and comics are kept in different places. At home you sort clothes into the wardrobe and toys into a box. That way you don't have to search for long.

Categories can be nested inside each other like boxes inside boxes. The category animals contains mammals, and this in turn contains cats and dogs. In the 18th century, the Swede **Carl Linnaeus** arranged plants and animals in such a **hierarchy**. His system is the basis for the names experts still use for living things today.

On the computer, you sort files into **folders**, for example pictures, music and documents. App stores divide apps into categories such as games, learning or music. Online shops show menus with categories and subcategories. In many programs you can also mark things with **keywords**, which are also called tags.

Our brain forms categories all the time without us noticing. When you see an animal you don't know, you still recognise that it is a bird. Categories help with **learning**, remembering and explaining. If you are good at categorising, you keep track even when there is lots of information.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of things with shared features.
A word that groups many things together, for example fruit for apple and pear.
A word for a single thing within a category.
A word used to mark files or posts so that you can find them again.

gewusst: Some things fit into several categories: a tomato, for example, is botanically a fruit but is used like a vegetable in the kitchen.
The German-language Wikipedia puts every article into one or more categories.
Even small children spontaneously sort toys by colour or shape.

teile.einleitung: Normalisation is a method for dividing up the tables in a database neatly. The aim is for every piece of information to be stored in only one place. This leads to fewer errors and contradictions.
wichtigste: Normalisation divides large tables into smaller, well-ordered tables.
It prevents unnecessary repetition of data, called redundancy.
The first normal form requires each field to contain only one indivisible value.
The second normal form forbids a non-key attribute from depending on only part of a composite key.
The third normal form removes transitive dependencies between non-key attributes.
The Boyce-Codd normal form makes the third normal form even stricter.
For fast analyses, data is sometimes deliberately denormalised again.

abschnitte.text: In a **relational database**, data is stored in tables with rows and columns. If you write everything into one single huge table, many details are repeated. **Normalisation** breaks this table down step by step into several smaller tables. These are connected to each other by keys so that no information is lost.

Data stored twice leads to so-called **anomalies**. In an **update anomaly**, only one of several copies is changed, and afterwards the data contradicts itself. In a **deletion anomaly**, deleting one record accidentally loses other information. There are also insertion anomalies, where you cannot store something because another detail is still missing.

The **first normal form** (1NF) requires atomic values, so, for example, not several phone numbers in one field. The **second normal form** (2NF) applies to tables with a composite key. Every other attribute must then depend on the whole key and not just on part of it. An example: in a table with pupil number and subject number, the pupil's name does not belong, because it only depends on the pupil number.

The **third normal form** (3NF) forbids a non-key attribute from depending on the key via another non-key attribute. A typical example is the table Customer(CustomerNo, Name, Postcode, Town): the town depends on the postcode and not directly on the customer number. That is why postcode and town are moved into a separate table. The **Boyce-Codd normal form** goes even further and requires every determinant to be a candidate key.

The foundations of normalisation were laid by the British computer scientist **Edgar F. Codd**, who described the relational database model at IBM around 1970. He defined the first three normal forms. Together with Raymond Boyce, he later developed the Boyce-Codd normal form. Today these rules are learned in almost every course on databases.

For a query, normalised databases often have to connect many tables with so-called **joins**. This can become slow with very large amounts of data. For analyses, for example in a **data warehouse**, data is therefore sometimes deliberately stored twice. Redundancy is then accepted in order to speed up queries.

begriffe.erklaerung: The same information is stored more than once.
A column of a table, for example “Name” or “Postcode”.
A column or group of columns that uniquely identifies each row.
An error or contradiction caused by badly organised data.
Connecting two tables through shared values in a query.

gewusst: Experts have a saying to remember: every attribute depends on the key, the whole key and nothing but the key.
There are even a fourth, fifth and sixth normal form, but they are rarely needed in practice.
The Swiss postcode is a classic school example, because a postcode almost always belongs to the same town.

teile.einleitung: Problem decomposition means dividing a big and difficult problem into smaller sub-problems. Each sub-problem is easier to solve than the whole. This way of thinking is one of the most important foundations of computer science, but it also helps in everyday life.
wichtigste: In problem decomposition, you divide a big problem into smaller sub-problems.
In English it is called “decomposition” and is part of “computational thinking”.
With the top-down approach, you start with the whole problem and break it down more and more finely.
You don't need to break down a sub-problem any further if you can solve it directly.
In programming, sub-problems are often written as separate functions or subroutines.
In a team, different people can work on different parts at the same time.
A class party can also be broken down, for example into invitations, food, games and tidying up.

abschnitte.text: Problem decomposition is a method for solving problems. You take a big task and divide it into **sub-problems**. These parts are easier to keep track of and easier to solve. At the end you put the partial solutions back together into an overall solution. In English this is called **decomposition**.

A well-known approach is called **top-down**. You start with the whole problem and think about which big parts it consists of. Then you break each part down again into smaller pieces. This creates a tree of tasks, similar to a family tree. As soon as you can solve a sub-problem directly, you stop breaking it down.

Planning a class party is a big task. You can divide it into invitations, food, games and tidying up. The food can be broken down further into shopping, cooking and laying the tables. Each group in the class takes on one part. That way everything is ready on time, and nobody is overwhelmed.

Anyone who writes a program almost always breaks it down into parts. These parts are written as **functions** or **subroutines**. In a quiz program, the sub-problems would be, for example: showing questions, checking the answer and counting points. Each function can be tested on its own. This makes errors much easier to find.

In 2006 the computer scientist Jeannette Wing made the term **computational thinking** well known. It means thinking like a computer scientist. As well as problem decomposition, it includes recognising patterns, leaving out unimportant details and formulating algorithms. In Switzerland, children learn these ways of thinking in the Lehrplan 21 curriculum in the module media and computer science.

Large programs such as operating systems or games consist of millions of lines of code. Nobody could keep track of something like that all at once. Thanks to problem decomposition, many people work on different parts at the same time. Science, construction and sport also use this method. As early as the 17th century, the philosopher René Descartes recommended breaking difficult questions down into as many small parts as possible.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small part of a big task.
An approach that goes from the whole to the individual parts.
A part of a program that does a particular task and can be used several times.
Thinking through problems in such a way that a computer could solve them.

gewusst: A recipe is also a form of problem decomposition, because it divides a dish into individual steps.
The opposite of top-down is called bottom-up, where you build something big out of small parts.
When building Lego from instructions, a big model is broken down into many small building stages.

teile.einleitung: A process scheduler is a part of the operating system that decides which program may use the processor and when. Because many more programs run on a computer than there are processor cores, it switches between them in a flash. This makes it seem as if they are all running at the same time.
wichtigste: The scheduler decides which process gets the CPU and when.
With first come, first served, processes take their turn in the order they arrive.
With the round-robin method, each process gets a fixed time slice in turn.
Shortest job first minimises the average waiting time if all the running times are known.
With pre-emptive scheduling, the operating system can take the CPU away from a process.
If a process with low priority never gets a turn, this is called starvation.
From 2007 to 2023 the Completely Fair Scheduler was the standard in the Linux kernel.

abschnitte.text: A **process** is a running program, such as the browser or a music player. But a processor core can only work on one process at a time. The **scheduler** shares out the computing time among all the processes. It often switches hundreds of times a second, which is why you don't notice anything.

With **first come, first served** (FCFS), whoever arrived first takes their turn first, like at a checkout. If three processes with running times of 6, 3 and 1 ms arrive in that order, they wait 0, 6 and 9 ms, so 5 ms on average. **Shortest job first** takes the shortest task first and so achieves the lowest average waiting time. But for this, you need to know the running times in advance.

With the **round-robin method**, each process gets a short time slice in turn, often only a few milliseconds. When the time is up, the next one gets its turn, and the interrupted one joins the back of the queue again. This interrupting is called **pre-emptive scheduling**. Modern operating systems such as Windows, macOS and Linux all work pre-emptively.

Important processes, for example for sound or mouse movement, are given a higher **priority**. As a result, it can happen that an unimportant process never gets a turn; this is called **starvation**. The technique of **ageing** prevents this by slowly raising the priority of waiting processes. In the end, every process gets a turn.

From 2007 Linux used the **Completely Fair Scheduler** (CFS) by Ingo Molnár. It tried to give every process as fair a share of computing time as possible. In 2023 it was replaced by a new method called EEVDF. Android mobile phones also use the Linux scheduler and also pay attention to power consumption.

begriffe.erklaerung: A program that is currently running on the computer.
The main processor, the calculating unit of the computer.
The short time a process may calculate before another one gets its turn.
The operating system may interrupt a running process.
A technique in which the priority of waiting processes rises over time.

gewusst: On a normal laptop, several hundred processes are often running at the same time.
Switching between two processes is called a context switch, and it takes a little time itself.

teile.einleitung: In computer science, a process is a program that is currently being run. While a program is just a file lying on the hard drive, the process is the living, running program, so to speak. The operating system manages all the processes and makes sure that they share the processor.
wichtigste: A process is a program being run.
In the simple state model, a process is ready, running or blocked.
The operating system stores the details of each process in a process control block.
In a context switch, the CPU switches from one process to another.
In Unix, a process creates a copy of itself with the system call fork.
Threads of one process share the same address space; separate processes do not.
In Unix and Linux, the init process has the process number 1.
A zombie process has finished, but its return value has not yet been collected.

abschnitte.text: A **program** is a file with commands, like a recipe in a cookbook. A **process** is created when the operating system starts this program, like the actual cooking from the recipe. You can start the same program several times, and then several processes are running. Each process gets its own number, the **process ID** or PID. In the Windows Task Manager or in Activity Monitor on a Mac you can see the running processes.

A process is not always calculating. In the simple model there are three states: **ready**, **running** and **blocked**. Ready means the process is waiting to be given the processor. Running means it is working right now. It is blocked when it is waiting for something, for example a keyboard input or data from the internet.

For each process, the operating system keeps a **process control block**. Among other things, it contains the process number, the state and the contents of the registers. A processor core can really only run one process at a time. That is why the operating system switches back and forth between the processes many times a second. This switch is called a **context switch**, and it happens so fast that everything seems to run at the same time.

In Unix and Linux, a process creates a copy of itself with the system call **fork**. The original process is called the parent process, the copy the child process. This creates a tree of processes. At the very top is the **init process** with the number 1, which is the first to be started when the computer boots. On many of today's Linux systems, this job is done by the program systemd.

A process can have several **threads**, which are strands of execution within the same program. Threads share the same **address space**, that is, the same memory. In this way a web browser can load a page and react to clicks at the same time. Separate processes, on the other hand, each have their own memory. This makes them safer, because an error in one process does not easily disturb the others.

When a child process is finished, it gives a **return value** back to the parent process. As long as the parent process does not collect this value, an entry is left over. This finished but not completely vanished process is called a **zombie process**. If, on the other hand, the parent process dies first, the child becomes an orphan and is taken over by the init process. These funny names are established technical terms among computer scientists.

begriffe.erklaerung: A program that is currently running.
The basic program of the computer, for example Windows, macOS or Linux.
The processor switching from one process to another.
A strand of execution within a process.
The number by which the operating system recognises a process.

gewusst: On an ordinary computer, several hundred processes are often running at the same time, even if you only have a few windows open.
In Linux you can end a process with the command “kill”.
A zombie process needs almost no memory but still takes up a process number.

teile.einleitung: Run-length encoding is a simple method for storing data in a shorter form. Instead of writing down identical characters that come one after another individually, you only note how often the character appears. In this way “AAAABBBCCD” becomes “4A3B2C1D”.
wichtigste: In run-length encoding, identical characters in a row are stored as a count and the character.
In German it is called “Lauflängenkodierung”; in English it is run-length encoding, RLE for short.
Run-length encoding is lossless: no information is lost.
It is especially suitable for pictures with large areas of one colour.
With data that has no repetitions, the result is even longer.
Fax machines used the idea for a long time for black-and-white pages.

abschnitte.text: A sequence of identical characters one after another is called a **run**. **Run-length encoding** writes only the length of the run and the character instead of the whole run. “AAAABBBCCD” becomes “4A3B2C1D”, so ten characters become eight. In English the method is called **run-length encoding**, abbreviated RLE.

A black-and-white picture consists of rows of **pixels**. A row with 10 white, 2 black and 10 white pixels is written as “10W2B10W” instead of writing down 22 letters. The other way round, “3W2B1W” gives the row of pixels WWWBBW. The bigger the areas of one colour, the more the picture is shrunk.

Run-length encoding is **lossless**: from the encoded text you can restore the original exactly. With **lossy** methods such as JPEG, on the other hand, small details that are hardly visible are left out. For texts, programs or numbers, lossless compression is important, because no character may be missing there. Run-length encoding is one of the simplest lossless methods.

If the characters keep alternating, the method brings no benefit. “ABABAB” has 6 characters, but encoded as “1A1B1A1B1A1B” it has 12 characters, twice as many. Photos with many colour transitions hardly have any long runs and so tend to get bigger rather than smaller. That is why RLE is often combined with other **compression methods**.

The **fax machine** used the idea of run lengths for a long time, because a page of text consists mostly of white areas and a few black lines. Older image formats such as BMP or PCX could also store pictures with RLE. In simple computer games and pixel graphics, the method saves storage space. The idea is even found as a step inside modern formats such as JPEG.

begriffe.erklaerung: Rewriting data so that it needs less space.
A sequence of identical characters one after another.
The original can be restored exactly.
A single dot of a digital picture.
Turning the shortened form back into the original data.

gewusst: An empty white picture row with 1,000 pixels can be stored with RLE as “1000W” in only five characters.
When knitting from a pattern such as “5 knit, 2 purl”, you are basically using run-length encoding.
Run-length encoding is so simple that you can easily practise it by hand with paper and pencil.

teile.einleitung: Starting a program is the moment when a program begins to run. However well a program is written, nothing happens without a start. With an educational robot you usually press a start button; on a computer you click on an icon.
wichtigste: Without pressing the start button, a robot does not move off, even if the commands have been entered.
A program always begins with the first command.
The start symbol is often a triangle pointing to the right.
A filled-in square usually means stop, and two vertical lines mean pause.
With an educational robot, the on switch must be switched on first.
Before starting, you put the robot on the starting square.
The direction it faces at the start is important, because all the commands depend on it.

abschnitte.text: A program is a list of **commands**. As long as it has not been started, it just waits. Only when the **program starts** does the computer or robot carry out the first command. Then the other commands follow in order. If you enter commands into a robot and don't press start, it simply stays where it is.

You find the same symbols on many devices. A **triangle** pointing to the right means start or play. A filled-in square means stop. Two vertical lines mean pause. You also know these symbols from music and video apps.

In many Swiss schools, children work with educational robots such as the **Bee-Bot** or the **Thymio**, which was co-developed at EPFL in Lausanne. First the on switch must be switched on. Then you put the robot on the **starting square**. It is important which direction it is facing, because “forward” and “turn left” depend on it. Only when everything is ready do you press start.

On a computer you usually start a program by double-clicking an icon. On a tablet you tap the app once. In programming environments such as Scratch you click on the green flag. The operating system then loads the program into the **memory** and lets the processor carry out the commands. When you switch it on, the computer itself also starts a program first; this is called **booting**.

Before starting, check that all the commands are in the right order. Delete old commands in the robot's memory, otherwise they will be carried out too. Put the robot exactly on the starting square and point it the right way. After starting, watch carefully what happens. If something goes wrong, you can stop it and look for the mistake.

begriffe.erklaerung: The beginning of running a program.
The square on which the robot stands at the beginning.
Starting up a computer after it has been switched on.
Fast storage in which running programs are kept.

gewusst: The word “booting” comes from the English “bootstrap”, a loop on a boot with which you proverbially pull yourself up.
The Bee-Bot looks like a bee and has its buttons on its back.
When a computer starts, dozens of small programs often start up in the background at the same time.

teile.einleitung:
An HTML element is a building block of a website, for example a heading, a paragraph or a picture. Each element is written with what are called tags in angle brackets, such as

for a paragraph. The browser reads these building blocks and uses them to build the page you see on the screen.
wichtigste: HTML elements are the building blocks of every website.

Most elements have an opening tag such as

and a closing tag such as

.

is the biggest heading;

stands for a paragraph of text.
With you include a picture; the attribute alt describes it in words.
<ul> creates a list with bullet points, <ol> a numbered list.
makes a line break and needs no closing tag.
The element <title> sets the text in the browser tab.

abschnitte.text:
**HTML** stands for Hypertext Markup Language, a markup language for websites. An element usually consists of an **opening tag**, the content and a **closing tag** with a slash. So

Hello

becomes a paragraph with the word Hello. Elements can be nested inside each other, so that a kind of tree is formed.

For headings there are six levels, from **

** for the biggest to

for the smallest. Normal text goes into paragraphs with

. A list with bullet points begins with

    , a numbered one with
      , and each item goes in an
    1. . Links to other pages are made with the element and the attribute href.

Many elements have **attributes**, which give extra information. In the picture element , the attribute src says which picture file is to be shown. The attribute **alt** describes the picture in words, so that blind people using a screen reader also find out what can be seen in it. and
are what are called empty elements; they need no closing tag.

Every website begins with the element <html>. Inside it is the **<head>** with invisible information, for example the <title>, which appears in the browser tab. The **<body>** contains everything you see on the page. Newer elements such as <header>, <nav> and <footer> show what job an area of the page has.

HTML was invented around 1990 by **Tim Berners-Lee** at the CERN research centre in Geneva. The world’s first website went online in 1991 and ran on a NeXT computer. Later many new elements were added, such as <video> and <audio> with HTML5. Today a working group of the browser makers looks after the standard as a constantly updated “Living Standard”.

begriffe.erklaerung:
A command in angle brackets, for example

.
Extra information in a tag, for example alt for pictures.
A program such as Firefox or Chrome that shows websites.
Elements sit inside other elements, like boxes inside boxes.
Building websites so that everyone can use them.

gewusst: HTML was invented in Switzerland, at CERN near Geneva.
If you open the page source view in the browser, you can see the HTML elements of any website.
A forgotten closing tag usually does not make the page crash, because browsers quietly repair many mistakes.

teile.einleitung: An artificial neural network is a computer program that is built loosely on the model of the nerve cells in the brain. Many simple calculating units, the artificial neurons, are connected in layers and learn from examples. Today such networks are behind face recognition, translation programs and chatbots.
wichtigste: An artificial neuron forms a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias and applies an activation function.
In 1943 Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts published the first mathematical model of a neuron.
A single perceptron cannot learn the XOR function.
Non-linear activation functions such as ReLU or sigmoid are needed so that several layers can do more than one.
The sigmoid function gives values between 0 and 1.
During training, the weights are adjusted with gradient descent.
If the learning rate is too large, the error jumps back and forth or even grows.

abschnitte.text: In the brain, **nerve cells** pass signals on to other nerve cells. An **artificial neuron** imitates this in a very simplified way: it receives numbers as inputs, multiplies them by **weights**, adds everything up and adds a bias. Then an activation function decides what the neuron outputs. Example: inputs 1 and 2, weights 0.5 and -1, bias 1 gives -0.5, and with ReLU this becomes 0.

A network consists of an **input layer**, one or more hidden layers and an output layer. In a fully connected layer, every neuron is connected to all the inputs. With 100 inputs and 10 neurons, that is 1,000 weights plus 10 biases, so 1,010 trainable parameters. Networks with many layers are called **deep networks**, which is where the term deep learning comes from.

The **activation function** brings a curve, that is non-linearity, into the network. Without it, all the layers together would be just a single linear mapping and could do no more than one layer. The sigmoid function gives values between 0 and 1; the popular **ReLU** outputs negative values as 0 and positive ones unchanged. The universal approximation theorem says that even one hidden layer can approximate any continuous function as closely as you like, if it has enough neurons.

During **training**, the output of the network is compared with the correct answer and the error is calculated. With **gradient descent**, all the weights are moved a small step in the direction in which the error gets smaller, like walking down into a valley. How big these steps are is set by the **learning rate**. If it is much too large, the error jumps back and forth or even grows; if it is too small, learning takes a very long time.

In 1943 Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts described the first mathematical neuron model as a logical switching element. At the end of the 1950s Frank Rosenblatt built the **perceptron**, a neuron that could learn. In 1969 Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert showed that a single perceptron cannot learn the XOR function, which slowed research down for years. With the backpropagation method, fast graphics chips and large amounts of data, the breakthrough came from about 2012, and in 2024 John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton received the Nobel Prize in Physics for their work.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small calculating unit that processes inputs and passes on a result.
A number that decides how important an input is.
A function that turns the sum into the output of the neuron.
A method that changes weights step by step so that the error goes down.
How big the learning steps are during training.

gewusst: Large language models have billions of weights, all of which are adjusted during training.
Graphics cards, originally built for computer games, are today the most important tool for training neural networks.
The LSTM network, co-developed at IDSIA in Ticino, was used for years in speech recognition on millions of mobile phones.

teile.einleitung: An interpreter is a program that reads another program and carries it out directly, step by step. So it does not first translate the code completely, but works through it line by line, so to speak. Well-known languages such as Python are usually run with an interpreter.
wichtigste: An interpreter reads a program and carries it out directly step by step.
Interpreted programs usually run more slowly than compiled ones.
In its standard implementation, Python is usually run by an interpreter.
CPython first translates the source code into bytecode.
REPL stands for Read-Eval-Print Loop.
The Java Virtual Machine runs Java bytecode.
Home computers such as the Commodore 64 had a built-in BASIC interpreter.

abschnitte.text: A computer only directly understands **machine code**, long sequences of zeros and ones. But people write programs in **programming languages** such as Python, which are easy to read. An interpreter is a program that reads this **source code** and carries it out command by command. You can compare it to an interpreter who translates a sentence straight away while the other person is still speaking.

The alternative to the interpreter is the **compiler**. A compiler translates the whole program into machine code beforehand, like a translator who translates a whole book. Compiled programs usually run faster, while interpreted ones are easier to change and test. Many modern languages mix both approaches.

The most widely used implementation of Python is called **CPython**. It first translates the source code into a simple intermediate form, the **bytecode**, and then runs it. Java also works with bytecode, which is run by the **Java Virtual Machine**. JavaScript in web browsers is likewise run by a built-in program that is very cleverly optimised.

Many interpreters have an interactive mode, the **REPL**. The abbreviation stands for Read-Eval-Print Loop: read, evaluate, print and start again. You type in a command like 2 + 3 and immediately see the result 5. This is ideal for quickly trying something out without a separate translation step.

In the 1980s, many **home computers** such as the Commodore 64 had a built-in **BASIC interpreter**. After switching on, you could type in commands straight away and write small programs. The Python language was released by Guido van Rossum at the beginning of the 1990s. Today it is one of the most popular programming languages in the world, including in schools.

begriffe.erklaerung: A program that reads code and carries it out directly step by step.
A program that translates code completely into machine code in advance.
A simple intermediate form of a program that is run by a virtual machine.
The text of a program written by people.

gewusst: The name Python does not come from the snake but from the British comedy group Monty Python.
With an interpreter you can often find a mistake in a program just after the faulty line has been run.
Spreadsheet programs and games also often contain small interpreters for their own commands or formulas.

teile.einleitung: Pseudocode is a way of writing down an algorithm in simple, semi-formal language. It looks similar to a program but does not have to follow strict writing rules. This lets you plan the steps first before translating them into a real programming language.
wichtigste: Pseudocode describes an algorithm in simple, semi-formal language.
A computer cannot run pseudocode directly.
You write pseudocode to plan the steps without worrying about the exact way of writing.
The arrow ← means that a value is assigned to a variable.
After x ← 5 and x ← x + 3, OUTPUT x gives the value 8.
A loop FOR i FROM 1 TO 4 adds 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 and gives 10.
Conditions are often written with IF, THEN and ELSE.

abschnitte.text: Pseudocode is a mixture of everyday language and programming language. “Pseudo” comes from Greek and means roughly “apparent” or “false”. So pseudocode looks like code, but it is not code that a computer can run. It first has to be translated by people into a **programming language** such as Python.

When planning, you want to concentrate on the idea and not on commas or brackets. That is why you first describe an **algorithm** in pseudocode. It is often used in textbooks, exams and scientific articles, because everyone understands it, whatever language they program in. The famous computer scientist Donald Knuth also used such descriptions in his books.

A **variable** is like a labelled box with a value in it. The arrow ← puts a value into it, for example “points ← 0”. With a ← 3, b ← 5, then a ← b and b ← a, both have the value 5 at the end, because the old value of a was overwritten. To swap them, you therefore need a third helper variable.

With **IF ... THEN ... ELSE** the program makes decisions. With number ← 7 and the check whether number MOD 2 equals 0, the output is “odd”, because 7 divided by 2 leaves the remainder 1. A **loop** such as WHILE x < 20: x ← x · 2 doubles x until the condition is no longer true. If x starts at 3, it becomes 6, 12 and finally 24.

Instead of pseudocode, you can also draw the steps. A **flowchart** shows the steps with boxes and arrows. A structogram, also called a Nassi-Shneiderman diagram, shows the steps as rectangles nested inside each other. All these aids help to discover mistakes even before programming.

begriffe.erklaerung: Exact step-by-step instructions for solving a task.
A named storage place for a value.
Storing a value in a variable, often written with ←.
An operation that gives the remainder of a division.

gewusst: There is no single fixed rule for pseudocode; every textbook has its own style.
Many programmers first write their ideas down as pseudocode on paper or on a blackboard.

teile.einleitung: Niklaus Wirth was one of the best-known computer scientists in Switzerland. He invented several programming languages, including Pascal, Modula-2 and Oberon. His idea was simple: programs and computers should be clear, lean and easy to understand.
wichtigste: Niklaus Wirth was born in Winterthur in 1934 and died in 2024.
From 1968 to 1999 he was professor of computer science at ETH Zurich.
He developed the programming languages Pascal, Modula-2 and Oberon.
Around 1980 his team at ETH built the workstation computer Lilith.
In 1984 he received the Turing Award, the most important award in computer science.
His textbook “Algorithms + Data Structures” became a classic.
“Wirth's law” says that software gets slower faster than hardware gets faster.

abschnitte.text: Niklaus Wirth was born on 15 February 1934 in **Winterthur** in the canton of Zurich. Even as a teenager he loved tinkering with model aeroplanes and electronics. He studied electrical engineering at **ETH Zurich** and graduated in 1959. He then went to North America and gained his doctorate at the University of California in Berkeley in 1963.

After a few years at Stanford University in California, Wirth returned to Switzerland. From 1968 to 1999 he was **professor of computer science** at ETH Zurich. He helped to build up computer science there as a subject in its own right. Many of his students later became important experts themselves.

In 1970 Wirth published the language **Pascal**, named after the mathematician Blaise Pascal. Pascal was used in schools and universities all over the world to learn clean programming. **Modula-2** followed in 1978 and **Oberon** in the 1980s, which was also the name of a whole operating system. What all his languages have in common is that they have few, clear rules.

Around 1980 Wirth's team at ETH built the workstation computer **Lilith**. It already had a large screen with graphics and a mouse, which was very modern at the time. Wirth had got the idea during a research stay at Xerox in California. Later his team developed the successor Ceres, on which the Oberon system ran.

In 1984 Niklaus Wirth received the **Turing Award**, which is often called the “Nobel Prize of computer science”. His book “Algorithms + Data Structures” explains how to arrange data cleverly and solve problems step by step. In an essay in 1995 he criticised the fact that programs keep getting bigger and more sluggish. This gave rise to **Wirth's law**: software gets slower faster than hardware gets faster.

Niklaus Wirth died in Zurich on 1 January 2024. His ideas live on in many of today's languages, for example in Delphi, which is based on Pascal. He also strongly shaped the principle of dividing programs clearly into parts, so-called modules. Many experts see him as a role model for simple and well-thought-out technology.

begriffe.erklaerung: An artificial language people use to give commands to a computer.
A very important prize for computer scientists, named after Alan Turing.
The basic program of a computer that controls everything else, for example Windows.
Exact step-by-step instructions for solving a task.

gewusst: The Pascal language came about mainly because Wirth was looking for a clear and simple language for teaching.
The whole Oberon system was so lean that Wirth and his colleague Jürg Gutknecht were able to explain its structure completely in one book.
Niklaus Wirth lived to be almost 90 and remained curious about new technology into old age.

teile.einleitung: A raster graphic is a picture made up of a grid of many tiny coloured dots. These picture dots are called pixels. Photos from digital cameras and mobile phones are raster graphics, as are most pictures on the internet.
wichtigste: A raster graphic stores a picture as a grid of individual coloured dots.
The picture dots are called pixels.
If you enlarge a raster graphic a lot, it looks pixelated and stepped.
Typical file formats are PNG, JPEG and GIF.
The colour depth tells you how many colours a pixel can have.
An uncompressed picture with 100 by 100 pixels and 24-bit colour depth needs 30,000 bytes.
Digital cameras produce raster graphics, which you change with image editing programs.

abschnitte.text: A **raster graphic** is like a mosaic or a fuse bead picture. It consists of many small squares arranged in rows and columns. Each square is a **pixel** and has exactly one colour. From far enough away, the eye does not see a grid but a continuous picture. The counterpart is the **vector graphic**, which describes shapes with lines and curves.

The **resolution** says how many pixels a picture consists of, for example 1,920 by 1,080 pixels. The more pixels, the finer the details. A phone photo today often has ten million pixels or more, which is described in megapixels. If you enlarge a picture a lot, the individual pixels become visible. Edges then look like steps, and the picture looks **pixelated**.

The **colour depth** tells you how many bits are used for the colour of a pixel. With 1 bit only 2 colours are possible, for example black and white. With 4 bits, 16 colours can be shown, because 2 to the power of 4 is 16. Photos mostly use 24 bits, 8 bits each for red, green and blue. This makes over 16 million colours possible.

Raster graphics can need a lot of storage. A picture with 100 by 100 pixels has 10,000 pixels; at 24 bits that is 3 bytes each, so 30,000 bytes. That is why pictures are usually **compressed**. The **JPEG** format is good for photos but loses some quality when saved. **PNG** compresses without loss and is suitable for graphics and screenshots; GIF can also store small animations.

Every **digital camera** and every phone camera produces raster graphics. Screens also show everything as a grid of pixels. Photos are edited with an **image editing program**, such as GIMP or Photoshop. With it you can change the brightness, colours and framing. Pixel art in video games is also deliberately designed as a coarse raster graphic.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single picture dot, from “picture element”.
The number of pixels in the width and height of a picture.
The number of bits per pixel for the colour.
A graphic made of lines and shapes that can be enlarged without loss of quality.
Making a file smaller so that it needs less storage.

gewusst: The word “pixel” is an abbreviation of the English “picture element”.
On a modern phone screen the pixels are so small that you can hardly see them with the naked eye.
Even old mosaics from Roman times work on the same principle as a raster graphic.

teile.einleitung: A photo filter changes how a photo looks, for example its colours, its brightness or its mood. In mobile phone apps, filters can be applied with a single tap, and some even put funny animal ears on faces.
wichtigste: A photo filter changes the colours and mood of a picture.
A black and white filter removes the bright colours.
The sepia filter makes a photo look brownish and old.
The soft focus filter makes a picture soft and blurred.
More contrast strengthens the difference between light and dark.
Bluish colours look cool, reddish and yellowish ones warm.
Beauty filters mean that people on the internet look different from how they look in real life.

abschnitte.text: Originally a **photo filter** was a disc of coloured glass or plastic that you screwed onto the front of a camera lens. Such a filter only let certain light through and so changed the picture. Today most filters are **digital** programs that work out a new version of a photo afterwards. In doing so they change the colour values of every single pixel. Filter apps became well known above all from 2010 onwards with Instagram.

Many filters change the **colour temperature** of a picture. A slightly bluish filter makes a photo look cooler, a yellowish or reddish one warmer, as at sunset. A black and white filter removes all the bright colours and shows only shades of grey. The **sepia** filter colours the picture brownish, so that it looks like an old photo from grandfather’s time. In this way the same moment can have a quite different effect.

If you increase the **contrast**, the difference between light and dark areas becomes stronger. The picture then looks bolder and harsher. With brightness you make a photo lighter or darker overall. The **soft focus** filter makes a picture soft and slightly blurred. The sharpening filter, on the other hand, emphasises edges so that details can be seen more clearly.

Some apps recognise faces in the camera in real time. They then put, for example, **animal ears**, glasses or a crown in the right place. To do this, a program searches the picture for eyes, nose and mouth and follows how they move. Such effects are also called **augmented reality**, that is an enhanced reality. They are fun, but they also show how well computers can analyse pictures today.

There are also filters that make faces smoother, make eyes bigger or change the skin. Photos on the internet therefore often show people differently from how they look in real life. Anyone who constantly sees such pictures easily compares themselves with an ideal that does not even exist. It is therefore worth knowing, when looking at them, that many pictures are **edited**. In some countries, heavily edited advertising photos now have to be labelled.

begriffe.erklaerung: An edit that changes how a photo looks.
A brownish colour tone that makes photos look old.
The difference between light and dark areas in a picture.
A filter that makes a picture soft and blurred.
Enhanced reality, in which digital images are added to the camera picture.

gewusst: The name sepia comes from the ink of the cuttlefish, which used to be used for colouring.
A digital photo consists of millions of pixels, and a filter works out a new colour for each of them.
Photographers still use real glass filters today, for example to reduce reflections on water.

teile.einleitung: Privacy is a person's personal sphere, which concerns only them. It includes your diary, your messages, your photos and also data such as where you live. On the internet in particular, it is important to know how to protect this sphere.
wichtigste: Privacy means deciding for yourself who finds out what about you.
Nobody may read your diary unless you allow it.
You must not secretly look through another child's mobile phone either.
On the internet, “public” means that everyone can see something.
A “private” profile can only be seen by the people you have accepted as friends.
Who may see what you post is set in the app's settings.
Once something has been on the internet, you cannot be sure of deleting it for ever.
In Switzerland, the Federal Constitution and the Data Protection Act protect privacy.

abschnitte.text: Privacy is the part of your life that you do not have to share with everyone. It includes thoughts, feelings, letters, messages and your room. **Personal data** such as your name, address, phone number or date of birth also belong to it. Everyone has a right to have this sphere respected by others. This applies to adults just as much as to children.

On the internet, a distinction is made between **public** and **private**. What is public can be seen by everyone in the world, including strangers. With a private profile, only accepted friends can see your posts. You decide who they are in the app's **settings**. If you send a message to many people, all the recipients can read it and also forward it.

Many apps and games ask for your **location**. This tells them where you are at the moment, and sometimes other users can see it too. In this case children should ask their parents first before agreeing. Often a game does not need the location at all. You can also switch the permission off again later on your phone.

Whatever you put on the internet can quickly be copied, saved or captured with a **screenshot**. That is why a deleted photo has not necessarily disappeared for ever. People talk about the **digital footprint** that everyone leaves online. A good rule is: only post what your teacher or your grandmother could see too. You should also only share photos of other people with their permission.

In Switzerland, Article 13 of the **Federal Constitution** protects everyone's privacy. The **Data Protection Act** regulates how companies and authorities may handle personal data. A revised version of this law has applied since September 2023. Compliance is monitored by the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner, FDPIC for short. The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child also says that children have a right to privacy.

Choose secure passwords and don't tell them to anyone except your parents. Set your profiles on social networks to private. Never give strangers on the internet your address, your school or your phone number. If something seems strange to you, talk to an adult you trust. Respect the privacy of your friends and brothers and sisters too.

begriffe.erklaerung: Rules that protect personal data from misuse.
Details with which a person can be identified, for example name or address.
All the traces you leave on the internet.
Switches in an app with which you decide who may see what.

gewusst: The word “private” comes from the Latin “privatus” and means roughly “for oneself alone”.
Many apps collect more data than they actually need for their task.
Hidden details can also be stored in a photo, for example where it was taken.

teile.einleitung: A context-free grammar is a set of rules that lays down exactly which strings of characters belong to a particular language. Computer scientists use it, for example, to describe what a valid program in a programming language must look like. You can think of it as a building-block system in which placeholders are replaced by characters step by step.
wichtigste: In every rule of a context-free grammar there is exactly one nonterminal on the left.
The grammar with the rules S goes to aSb or ε produces all words of the form a to the power n b to the power n.
Nondeterministic pushdown automata recognise exactly the context-free languages.
In Chomsky normal form only rules of the form A goes to BC or A goes to a are allowed.
The CYK algorithm solves the word problem for such grammars in cubic time.
A grammar is called ambiguous if a word has two different syntax trees.
In 1960 the syntax of ALGOL 60 was described with Backus-Naur form.

abschnitte.text: A context-free grammar consists of four parts: **terminal symbols**, **nonterminals**, rules and a start symbol. Terminal symbols are the real characters that end up in the word, for example a and b. Nonterminals are placeholders, usually written with capital letters such as S or A. The rules say what a placeholder may be replaced by. “Context-free” means that you may always replace a nonterminal, no matter which characters are to its left or right.

The grammar with the rules S goes to aSb or S goes to ε is a classic example. The symbol ε stands for the empty word. S first becomes aSb, then aaSbb, then aaabbb if you put in ε at the end. This produces exactly the words with as many a's as b's, where all the a's are at the front. This language cannot be described with simpler **regular expressions**, but it can with a context-free grammar.

The steps of a **derivation** can be drawn as a tree, the so-called **syntax tree**. At the top is the start symbol, and at the bottom on the leaves are the characters of the finished word. If a word has two different syntax trees, the grammar is **ambiguous**. This is unwanted in programming languages, because otherwise the computer does not know how to understand something like 2 + 3 · 4. That is why grammars are built so that, for example, the rule that multiplication comes before addition is clearly laid down.

In **Chomsky normal form** only two kinds of rules are allowed: A goes to BC or A goes to a single character a. Every context-free grammar can be converted into this form, as long as the empty word is not part of it. For a word of length n you then need exactly 2n minus 1 derivation steps, so 9 for length 5. The **CYK algorithm** uses such grammars to check whether a word belongs to the language. Its running time grows cubically, that is, with n to the power of 3.

For every grammar there is a matching machine that recognises the language. For context-free languages this is the nondeterministic **pushdown automaton**. It has a stack memory on which it can put characters and take them off again, similar to a stack of plates. In this way it can remember, for example, how many a's it has already read and then count the same number of b's. In the Chomsky hierarchy, context-free languages belong to type 2.

The linguist **Noam Chomsky** described such grammars in the 1950s, originally to study human languages.
