In 1960 such a grammar, the **Backus-Naur form**, was used to define the programming language ALGOL 60 precisely. It is named after John Backus and Peter Naur. Today context-free grammars are found in every compiler and parser. They also help when checking data formats such as JSON or when processing arithmetic expressions.

begriffe.erklaerung: A placeholder in a grammar that still has to be replaced.
A real character that appears in the finished word.
The sequence of replacement steps from the start symbol to the finished word.
A model of computation with a stack memory that recognises context-free languages.
A program that breaks a text down according to the rules of a grammar.

gewusst: Correctly nested brackets such as (()()) form a context-free language that cannot be described with simpler regular expressions.
Noam Chomsky is actually a linguist and not a computer scientist.
Whether two context-free grammars produce the same language cannot in general be decided with certainty by any computer.

teile.einleitung: A set diagram is a drawing that uses circles to show which things belong together. Each circle stands for a group, a so-called set, and overlapping circles show what belongs to several groups. It is also known as a Venn diagram.
wichtigste: A set diagram shows which things belong together.
A set is usually drawn as a circle or ring.
Things that belong to two sets go where the circles overlap.
Things that belong to no set go outside all the circles.
With the circles “can fly” and “has feathers”, a duck goes in both circles.
A penguin only goes in the circle “has feathers”, because it cannot fly.
If 5 children have a bike and 2 of them also have a scooter, then 3 children have only a bike.

abschnitte.text: A **set** is a collection of things that share a property, for example “all animals” or “all even numbers”. In a set diagram, each set is drawn as a circle or ring. Everything that belongs to the set goes inside the circle. Whatever does not belong stays outside. So a stone lies outside the circle “animals”.

It gets exciting when two circles overlap. The shared area is called the **intersection**; it contains everything that belongs to both sets. With the circles “red” and “round”, a red ball lies exactly in this overlap. A red cup only belongs in the circle “red”, a green marble only in the circle “round”. Everything in both circles together is called the **union**.

You draw a circle “can fly” and a circle “has feathers”. A duck can fly and has feathers, so it goes in both circles. A penguin has feathers but cannot fly, so it only goes in the circle “has feathers”. A bee can fly but has no feathers, so it only goes in the circle “can fly”. A dog lies outside both circles.

Set diagrams also help with calculating. In the circle “children with a bike” there are 5 children, in the circle “children with a scooter” 4, and 2 children are in both circles. Then 5 minus 2, that is 3 children, have a bike but no scooter. Altogether there are 5 plus 4 minus 2, that is 7 children, because otherwise you would count the 2 twice. The same applies to numbers: if 2, 4 and 6 are in the circle “even numbers”, then 8 belongs in it too.

As early as the 18th century, the Basel mathematician **Leonhard Euler** drew circles to explain logical statements. In 1880 the English mathematician **John Venn** presented the Venn diagrams named after him. In a Venn diagram, all the circles overlap in such a way that every possible combination has its own area. With three circles this gives 8 areas if you count the area outside. Set diagrams in which not all the overlaps are drawn are called Euler diagrams.

In computer science, set diagrams show how **logical operators** work. The intersection corresponds to “and”, the union to “or”. Searches in databases can also be illustrated in this way. At school they are used to sort animals, shapes or numbers. In everyday life they help to show similarities and differences clearly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A collection of things that share a property.
Everything that belongs to two or more sets at the same time.
Everything that belongs to at least one of the sets.
A single thing that belongs to a set.

gewusst: Leonhard Euler from Basel used circles for sets more than a hundred years before John Venn.
A Venn diagram with three circles has exactly 8 areas, including the area outside.
For Venn diagrams with many sets, circles are no longer enough and other shapes are needed.

teile.einleitung: Phishing is a fraud on the internet in which criminals use fake messages to get hold of passwords, bank details or other secret information. The messages often look as if they come from a bank, a parcel service or a well-known online shop. If you know the tricks, you can protect yourself well.
wichtigste: Phishing is fraud using fake emails, messages or websites.
The name comes from the English word fishing.
Reputable banks never ask for passwords by email.
If you move the mouse over a link without clicking, you can see where it really leads.
A targeted attack on a person who has been spied on beforehand is called spear phishing.
In Switzerland you can report phishing to the Federal Office for Cybersecurity.
Time pressure, threats and strange senders are typical warning signs.

abschnitte.text: The term **phishing** comes from the English word fishing. The fraudsters throw out a bait, so to speak, and hope that someone will bite. Instead of fish, they want to catch passwords, credit card numbers or login details. The term appeared in the mid-1990s. The ph instead of f is a nod to the way things are spelled in hacker slang.

The fraudsters send messages that look like real emails from a bank, the post office or an online shop. They say, for example, that the account will be blocked or that a parcel is waiting for a fee to be paid. A **link** leads to a fake website that looks deceptively like the original. Anyone who enters their details there sends them straight to the criminals. Phishing also happens by text message, through chat apps or on the phone.

In **spear phishing**, fraudsters deliberately attack a particular person whom they have spied on beforehand. So they aim precisely at one victim, like with a spear. The message then mentions real names, colleagues or events and therefore seems very believable. Such attacks are often aimed at companies, schools or authorities. Especially with requests for money or data, it is worth checking back through a different channel.

Typical signs are **time pressure** and threats such as “Act within 24 hours”. Often the sender's address is not quite right, or there are strange spelling mistakes. Reputable banks and companies never ask for passwords or codes by email. If you move the mouse over a link without clicking, the browser shows the real destination address. If there is a foreign or odd address there, you should definitely not click.

The best thing is to type the address of the bank or shop into the browser yourself instead of clicking on links in emails. **Two-factor authentication** protects the account even if someone knows the password. Children and young people should show suspicious messages to an adult they trust. In Switzerland you can report phishing and other cyberattacks to the **Federal Office for Cybersecurity** NCSC (as of 2026). If you have already entered your details, you should change your password immediately and, in the case of bank details, phone the bank.

begriffe.erklaerung: A secret word or string of characters with which you log in.
A clickable reference that leads to another website.
A targeted phishing attack on a particular person who has been spied on.
A login in which you need a second proof as well as the password, such as a code on your phone.

gewusst: Phishing by text message is called smishing, and phishing by phone call is called vishing.
Fake websites often have addresses in which only a single letter is different from the original.
The Federal Office for Cybersecurity started its work at the beginning of 2024.

teile.einleitung: Grouping means putting together things that have features in common, for example buttons by colour or animals by their kind. This helps with tidying and finding things again, and it is also an important way of thinking in computer science.
wichtigste: When grouping, you put together things that share a feature.
You can group buttons by colour and building blocks by shape.
Dog, cat and rabbit belong to the group of animals.
In the row apple, pear, banana, hammer, the hammer does not fit.
Bicycle, bus and train form the group of vehicles.
12 children in groups of 3 make 4 groups.
Groups make it easier to find something again.

abschnitte.text: When **grouping**, you put together things that have something in common. This shared thing is called a **feature**. Red, blue and yellow buttons, for example, can be split by colour into three piles. Building blocks can be grouped by shape, size or colour. Depending on which feature you choose, quite different groups are formed.

Anyone who groups also sees what does not belong in a group. In the row apple, pear, banana, hammer, the hammer is not fruit. With eagle, sparrow, blackbird and trout, the **trout** does not fit, because it is a fish and not a bird. Tasks like this train you to look carefully. You have to work out which feature the others have in common.

Grouping also plays an important part in mathematics. If you have 12 children and make groups of 3, you get 4 groups; that is a **division**. When counting large amounts, you often bundle them into groups of ten, which is what our number system is based on. In set theory, a group of things is called a **set**. You can draw such sets clearly with circles.

Computers group things all the time. Files are kept in **folders**, and photos are gathered into albums by date or place. In tables you can group data, for example all pupils by class, to count how many there are in each class. Artificial intelligence programs even find groups in large amounts of data by themselves, which is called **clustering**. In this way music apps, for example, suggest similar songs.

In everyday life, grouping helps you keep things tidy and find them faster. In the supermarket, drinks, vegetables and bread each stand together. At home, cutlery is sorted into drawers with compartments for forks, knives and spoons. In Switzerland, rubbish is separated into groups such as paper, glass, PET and compost. Libraries also arrange books by topic so that you can find them easily.

begriffe.erklaerung: Putting together things that have features in common.
A property such as colour, shape or size by which you recognise something.
In mathematics, a collection of things gathered into one group.
When a computer gathers similar data into groups by itself.

gewusst: Biologists group all living things in one big system, which the Swedish scientist Carl Linnaeus founded as early as the 18th century.
A whale is grouped with the mammals, even though it lives in water and looks like a fish.
The same thing can belong to several groups: a tomato, for example, is red and at the same time a fruit.

teile.einleitung: A password manager is a program that keeps many passwords safely in one place. You only need to remember one single strong password, the master password. This lets you use a different, hard-to-guess password for every account.
wichtigste: A password manager stores many passwords in encrypted form in one place.
You open it with a single password, the master password.
Many password managers create random, strong passwords if you ask them to.
You should not use the same password for all your accounts.
A password manager only fills in passwords on the real web address and so protects against phishing.
The master password must be strong and should also be protected with two-factor authentication.
For important accounts, experts recommend (as of 2026) at least about 12 characters.

abschnitte.text: A **password manager** is like a digital safe for login details. It contains user names, passwords and often notes for each account. Everything is stored **encrypted**, so that strangers can do nothing with the data. Only someone who knows the **master password** can open the safe.

Many people use the same simple password everywhere because they cannot remember so many. But if this password is stolen from one service, criminals immediately try it on other accounts. Then all the accounts are in danger at a stroke. With a password manager you can use a separate, long password for every account.

When you create a new account, the password manager generates a **random** password made of letters, numbers and symbols at the press of a button. When you log in, it fills in the name and password automatically. But it only does this on the real web address for which the password was saved. If you land on a fake **phishing page**, the field stays empty, and that is a warning sign.

There are many different password managers, such as the free software **KeePass**, Bitwarden or 1Password. Password managers are also built into browsers and operating systems today, for example from Apple, Google and Microsoft. The Geneva company Proton also offers one, Proton Pass. Some store the data only on your own device, others sync it over the internet in encrypted form.

The **master password** must be especially strong, for example a long sentence made of several words. For important accounts, experts recommend at least about 12 characters, preferably more (as of 2026). You should also switch on **two-factor authentication**, where you need, for example, a code from your phone. Children should discuss passwords with their parents and otherwise not tell them to anyone.

begriffe.erklaerung: The one main password with which you open the password manager.
Data is converted so that only authorised people can read it.
Fraud using fake websites or messages to steal passwords.
Logging in with two proofs, such as a password and a code from your phone.

gewusst: Guessing a random 16-character password would take an unimaginably long time, even with very fast computers.
Good password managers do not know the master password themselves, which is why the company cannot reset it either.
More and more services offer passkeys, with which you can log in without any password at all.

teile.einleitung: The OSI model is a scheme that explains how computers in a network talk to each other. It divides this communication into seven layers, from the cable to the program. Each layer has its own task and works together with the layer above and the layer below.
wichtigste: The OSI reference model consists of 7 layers.
It was published as a standard by the International Organization for Standardization, ISO.
The lowest layer, the physical layer, describes cables, plugs, radio and individual bits.
A router works mainly on layer 3, the network layer.
The transport layer uses protocols such as TCP to provide the connection between programs.
On the way down, each data packet gets another header at each layer; this is called encapsulation.

abschnitte.text: OSI stands for “Open Systems Interconnection”, the connection of open systems. The model was drawn up by **ISO** and published as a standard in 1984. It is a **reference model**, a kind of map with which you can organise and explain network technology. Thanks to clear layers, devices from different manufacturers can work together.

Layer 1 is the **physical layer**; it describes cables, plugs, radio signals and the transmission of individual bits. Layer 2 is the **data link layer**; here data is packed into frames and sent to devices in the same network, for example by a switch. Layer 3 is the **network layer**, on which routers steer packets across many networks to their destination. This is where the Internet Protocol IP works, for example.

Layer 4 is the **transport layer**, which uses TCP or UDP to set up an end-to-end connection between programs. Layer 5, the session layer, controls the course of a connection. Layer 6, the **presentation layer**, deals with data formats, character encoding and partly with encryption. Layer 7 is the application layer, which programs such as browsers or email work with directly.

When data is sent, it travels down from layer 7 to the cable. Each layer packs the data into its own envelope and writes information on it, the so-called **header**. This packing is called **encapsulation**. At the recipient, the envelopes are unpacked again in reverse order until the message reaches the program.

The internet itself actually uses a simpler model, the **TCP/IP model** with four layers. Even so, in practice people often talk about OSI layers, for example a “layer 3 switch”. So the OSI model is above all a tool for learning and for troubleshooting. When something goes wrong, experts like to ask: is the problem with the cable, with the address or with the program?

To remember the seven layers, many learners use sentences to help them. One English one is “Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away”, from Physical to Application. The first letters stand for the English names of the layers from bottom to top. You can also make up a funny sentence of your own.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fixed rules for how devices exchange data.
A device that forwards data packets between different networks.
A front part with control information placed before the actual data.
A data packet on the data link layer, called “Rahmen” in German.
The International Organization for Standardization, based in Geneva.

gewusst: ISO, which published the OSI model, has its headquarters in Geneva.
Originally, real OSI protocols were meant to replace the internet, but TCP/IP won through.
Wi-Fi and Ethernet cables both work on the bottom two layers of the model.

teile.einleitung: MP3 is a file format with which music and other sounds can be stored in a much smaller form. It deliberately leaves out sounds that our hearing hardly notices. From the late 1990s, MP3 changed the way people collect, swap and listen to music.
wichtigste: MP3 stands for MPEG-1 Audio Layer III.
MP3 was mainly developed at the Fraunhofer Institute in Erlangen.
MP3 uses lossy compression.
When compressing, sounds that the ear hardly notices are left out.
At 128 kbit/s, the amount of data is about 11 times smaller than CD quality.
A 3-minute MP3 file at 128 kbit/s is about 2.9 MB in size.
In an MP3 file, the title and artist are stored in the ID3 tag.

abschnitte.text: MP3 is a method of **audio compression**, that is, of making sound files smaller. The name is an abbreviation of MPEG-1 Audio Layer III. MPEG is a group of experts that sets standards for video and sound. You can recognise MP3 files by the extension .mp3. They can be played on almost every mobile phone, computer and car radio.

MP3 uses knowledge about our hearing, called **psychoacoustics**. For example, when a loud sound is playing, we hardly hear a quieter sound of similar pitch at the same time. MP3 simply leaves out such hidden sounds. That is why it is called **lossy** compression, because the parts that are left out cannot be brought back. Even so, for most people a good MP3 file sounds almost like the original.

How good an MP3 file sounds depends on the **bit rate**, measured in kilobits per second. A music CD contains about 1,411 kbit/s, so an MP3 file at 128 kbit/s is about eleven times smaller. A 3-minute song at 128 kbit/s comes to about 2.9 MB. At 320 kbit/s the music sounds better, but the file is bigger for the same length. Details such as the song title, artist and album are stored in the so-called **ID3 tag**.

MP3 was developed mainly at the **Fraunhofer Institute** for Integrated Circuits in Erlangen. One of the best-known researchers was **Karlheinz Brandenburg**. At the beginning of the 1990s the method was laid down as an international standard. In 1995 the file extension .mp3 was chosen. For testing, the researchers listened countless times to the a cappella song “Tom's Diner” by the singer Suzanne Vega.

Thanks to MP3, lots of songs suddenly fitted onto one hard drive and could be sent over the internet. In 1999 the file-sharing service Napster appeared, through which millions of people swapped music, often without the artists' permission. In 2001 Apple's **iPod** came on the market, and MP3 players became very popular. As a result, the music industry had to reorganise itself completely. Today people mostly listen to music through streaming services, which often use more modern formats such as AAC or Opus.

For a long time MP3 was protected by **patents**, and manufacturers had to pay licence fees. In 2017 the Fraunhofer Institute ended its licensing programme because the most important patents had expired. Since then anyone can use MP3 freely. Although there are now better formats, MP3 is still very widespread. It continues to be popular for audiobooks, podcasts and people's own recordings.

begriffe.erklaerung: Making data smaller so that it needs less storage space.
When making data smaller, parts of it are lost for good.
How much data per second is used for the sound.
The study of how people perceive sounds.
A section in an MP3 file with details such as title and artist.

gewusst: Karlheinz Brandenburg listened to the song “Tom's Diner” so often during testing that Suzanne Vega is sometimes called the “mother of the MP3”.
A CD holds about 80 minutes of music; as MP3 at 128 kbit/s, about 15 hours would fit into the same space.
The file extension .mp3 was decided in 1995 through an internal poll at the Fraunhofer Institute.

teile.einleitung: Logitech is a company that makes accessories for computers, above all mice, keyboards, webcams and headsets. The company was founded in 1981 in the canton of Vaud and is one of the best-known Swiss technology companies. Today Logitech products sit on desks all over the world.
wichtigste: Logitech was founded in 1981 by three people.
It was founded in the canton of Vaud.
Logitech is especially well known for computer mice and keyboards.
The name comes from the French word “logiciel” for software.
The first Logitech mouse was called P4 and came out in 1982.
In 1991 Logitech brought out a wireless radio mouse.
The shares are listed on the SIX Swiss Exchange and on NASDAQ (as of 2025).

abschnitte.text: Logitech is a worldwide company for **computer accessories**. It makes devices with which people operate their computers, games consoles and televisions. The company has its headquarters in the **Lausanne** area and another important site in California. Its products are sold in over a hundred countries. Logitech employs several thousand people on several continents.

Logitech was founded in 1981 by **Daniel Borel**, Pierino Zappacosta and Giacomo Marini. The three had met at Stanford University in California. The company was founded in the small municipality of **Apples** in the canton of Vaud, in a former farmhouse. The name comes from the French word “logiciel”, which means software. The founders had originally wanted to develop mainly software.

In 1982 Logitech brought out its first computer mouse, the **P4**. When Apple and Microsoft spread graphical user interfaces in the 1980s, the mouse became an everyday device. In 1991 Logitech presented a wireless **radio mouse**, an early mouse without a cable. Later came keyboards, webcams, loudspeakers and headsets. By its own account, Logitech had already sold its billionth mouse by 2008.

Under the brand **Logitech G**, the company sells gaming mice, keyboards, steering wheels and headsets for computer games. With Ultimate Ears, portable Bluetooth speakers also belong to the company. For businesses, Logitech makes cameras and devices for **video conferences**. During the coronavirus pandemic from 2020, demand for webcams and headsets rose sharply because many people were working and learning at home. There are also accessories for tablets, such as cases with keyboards.

Logitech's shares are listed on the Swiss stock exchange **SIX Swiss Exchange** and on the American stock exchange **NASDAQ** (as of 2025). Logitech shows that a small Swiss company can become a global corporation. In Lausanne the company works closely with the university EPFL. Most of the devices, however, are made in Asia. Logitech is also trying to use more recycled plastic and to state the CO₂ emissions of its products.

begriffe.erklaerung: Devices you connect to a computer, such as a mouse, keyboard or webcam.
A marketplace where shares in companies are bought and sold.
A part of a company that you can buy.
A computer mouse that is connected to the computer by radio without a cable.

gewusst: Logitech started in a farmhouse in the small village of Apples in Vaud.
The company name actually refers to software, even though Logitech mainly sells devices.
By its own account, Logitech had already sold a billion mice by 2008.

teile.einleitung: The number 147 is a helpline for children and young people all over Switzerland. Anyone who has worries, questions or fears can talk or write to a trained person there at any time, free of charge. Nobody has to be left alone with their problems.
wichtigste: The number 147 helps children and young people in Switzerland with their worries.
A call to 147 costs nothing.
The helpline is run by the Pro Juventute foundation.
You can call 147, but you can also reach it by chat, text message or email.
You may get in touch about any worry, whether it is small or big.
The advice is confidential, and you do not have to give your name.
In an emergency such as a fire, however, you dial 118.

abschnitte.text: **147** is a short telephone number that is easy to remember. Behind it work trained counsellors who listen to children and young people. The service is called “Beratung + Hilfe 147”, which means “Advice + Help 147”, and it can be reached around the clock, including at night and at weekends. The advice is available in German, French and Italian.

147 is offered by the **Pro Juventute** foundation. “Pro Juventute” is Latin and means “for the young”. The foundation was set up in 1912 and has worked ever since for children, young people and families in Switzerland. It also offers, for example, courses on dealing with money and with media.

Not everyone likes to talk about their worries on the telephone. That is why you can also write to 147 in the **chat**, send a text message or send an email. On the website 147.ch you will also find lots of texts and tips on common questions. In this way everyone can choose the way that feels best for them.

You may get in touch about **any worry**; no problem is too small. Common topics are arguments with friends or parents, stress at school, bullying, trouble on the internet or simply sadness and loneliness. The counsellors listen, ask questions and look for a solution together with the child. If necessary, they also say where you can get further help.

Anyone who calls 147 does not have to give their name; this is called being **anonymous**. What you say stays **confidential**, which means it is not simply passed on. This helps many people to talk openly about a difficult subject. You can also call several times if a worry goes on for longer.

147 is there for worries, but not for urgent emergencies. If there is a fire, you dial **118** for the fire brigade. You reach the police on 117, the ambulance service on 144 and the air rescue service Rega on 1414. The European **emergency number** 112 also works in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A conversation in which a trained person listens and helps to find a solution.
Without a name; nobody knows who you are.
What you say is not passed on.
An organisation that uses money and work for a good cause.
A telephone number for urgent danger, for example a fire or an accident.

gewusst: The 147 helpline can be reached day and night on all 365 days of the year.
Adults who are worried about a child can also find help at Pro Juventute; there is a separate advice service for parents.
Many children prefer to contact 147 by chat or text message rather than by telephone.

teile.einleitung: The space bar is the long, wide key at the bottom in the middle of the keyboard. You use it to put a gap between two words, a so-called space. It is the biggest key and is pressed especially often when typing.
wichtigste: The space bar is the longest key on the keyboard.
It is at the bottom in the middle.
You use it to make a gap between words.
Normally you put exactly one space between two words.
In touch typing you press it with your thumb.
In German it is called “Leertaste”; in English space or space bar.
In many games you jump with the space bar, and in video programs it pauses the video or starts it again.

abschnitte.text: The space bar is the longest key on the **keyboard** of computers and typewriters. It is at the bottom in the middle, directly below the rows of letters. When you press it, a **space** appears, which in Switzerland is often called “Leerschlag”. It separates words from each other so that a text stays readable. In English the key is called space or space bar.

The space bar is about six times as wide as a letter key. This means you can easily reach it with either thumb, wherever your hands are. In **touch typing**, your thumbs rest lightly on the space bar and press it at the end of every word. So that the long key goes down evenly even at the edge, there is a small metal bar underneath, the **stabiliser**. Because almost every word ends with a space, it is one of the most frequently pressed keys.

You put exactly one space between two words. Double spaces look untidy and are a common mistake. There is no space before a full stop or comma, but there is one after it. For the computer, a space is a completely normal **character** with its own number; in the ASCII code it is the number 32. There is even a **non-breaking space**, which prevents “5 km”, for example, from being split at the end of a line.

The space bar has other jobs in many programs too. In many **computer games** you use it to make your character jump. In video and music programs it pauses playback or starts it again. In an internet browser it scrolls a web page down a bit. On some mobile phones, tapping the space bar twice automatically gives a full stop followed by a space.

Even the first **typewriters** in the 19th century had a space bar. There it moved the carriage with the paper on by one place without printing a letter. On early models it was often a long wooden or metal bar in front of the keys. Computer keyboards took over this layout. On the on-screen keyboards of smartphones, too, the space bar is the widest key.

begriffe.erklaerung: An invisible character that creates a gap between words, in Switzerland also called “Leerschlag”.
A typing technique in which all ten fingers have fixed keys.
A bar under long keys so that they go down evenly.
A table that gives every character a number.

gewusst: For the computer, a space is not nothing but a character of its own with the number 32.
The space bar is usually the only key you press with your thumb.
There is a programming language called Whitespace whose programs consist only of spaces, tabs and line breaks.

teile.einleitung: The ENIAC was one of the first electronic large computers in the world and was presented in the USA in 1946. It filled a whole room, weighed about 27 tonnes and calculated with thousands of vacuum tubes. It was programmed by a group of women mathematicians who were hardly known for a long time.
wichtigste: ENIAC stands for Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer.
It was developed by John Presper Eckert and John William Mauchly at the University of Pennsylvania in the USA.
The ENIAC was presented to the public in 1946.
It calculated with about 17 500 vacuum tubes and weighed about 27 tonnes.
It was originally meant to calculate trajectory tables for the US Army’s artillery.
It was programmed by replugging cables and setting switches.
Six women mathematicians were the first programmers of the ENIAC.

abschnitte.text: The **ENIAC** (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer) is regarded as one of the first electronic general-purpose computers. It was built from 1943 at the Moore School of the **University of Pennsylvania** in Philadelphia. It was led by the engineers **John Presper Eckert** and **John William Mauchly**. In February 1946 it was presented to the public. Newspapers at the time called it an “electronic brain”.

The ENIAC was a monster: it weighed about 27 tonnes, as much as four elephants, and stood in a room of about 170 square metres. It contained about 17 500 **vacuum tubes**, which looked like small light bulbs and served as switches. There were also thousands of other components and kilometres of cable. It used about 150 kilowatts of electricity and produced a lot of heat. Because tubes often burnt out, technicians constantly had to replace faulty parts.

In the Second World War, the US Army needed precise **trajectory tables** for guns. Calculating such tables by hand took a very long time. The ENIAC could carry out about 5000 additions per second and was therefore much faster than any calculating machine before it. But by the time it was finished, the war was already over. It was then used for many other scientific calculations, for example for weather forecasts.

At that time there were no programs as text on a screen. The ENIAC was programmed by **replugging cables** and setting switches, which could take days. This work was done by six women mathematicians, including **Jean Jennings Bartik**, **Betty Holberton** and Kathleen McNulty. They had to understand the machine themselves from building plans, because there were no instructions. Their achievement was hardly recognised for decades; today they are regarded as pioneers of computer science.

The ENIAC was in use until 1955. It showed that electronic computers are much faster than mechanical ones. The experience gained led to the idea of storing programs in memory like data, which John von Neumann described. Today’s smartphones are millions of times faster and fit into a trouser pocket. Parts of the ENIAC are now on display in museums in the USA.

begriffe.erklaerung: A glass tube that used to serve as an electronic switch.
A very big, powerful computer.
To give a computer exact instructions.
The path that a thrown or fired object takes through the air.

gewusst: One rumour says that when the ENIAC was switched on, the lights in Philadelphia dimmed, but there is no evidence for this.
The achievement of the women programmers only became known decades later, mainly through the research of Kathy Kleiman.
A calculator today is many times more powerful than the whole ENIAC.

teile.einleitung: A grid is an arrangement of squares in horizontal rows and vertical columns, as on a chessboard or in a squared exercise book. Each square has a unique address, for example B2. In computer science, grids are used to steer robots, build games and show pictures made of pixels.
wichtigste: A grid consists of rows and columns.
The horizontal lines are called rows, the vertical ones columns.
You work out the number of squares as rows times columns; with 3 by 3 there are 9.
Each square has an address made of a column letter and a row number, for example B2.
To the right of B2 is C2, and if the rows count from bottom to top, B3 is directly above it.
If a robot may not move diagonally, it needs at least 4 steps from A1 to C3.
Screens consist of a huge grid of pixels.

abschnitte.text: A **grid** is a surface divided into squares of the same size. The squares lie in **rows**, which are the horizontal lines, and in **columns**, which are the vertical lines. A squared maths exercise book, a chessboard or a crossword are examples. You work out how many squares a grid has by multiplying rows by columns. A grid with 3 rows of 3 squares each has 9 squares, and one with 4 by 4 has 16.

So that every square can be found clearly, it is given a **coordinate**. Often the columns are named with the letters A, B, C from left to right and the rows with the numbers 1, 2, 3. The square B2 is therefore in column B and row 2. To its right is C2, to its left A2. If the rows count from bottom to top, B3 is directly above B2, just as on a chessboard, where A1 is at the bottom left.

Many learning robots such as the Bee-Bot move on a grid, going exactly one square per command. From A1 to C1 in the same row, a robot moves 2 squares. If it may not move **diagonally**, it needs at least 2 steps from A1 to B2, one to the right and one up. From A1 to C3 it is at least 4 steps. You simply add up the differences in columns and rows; experts call this the **Manhattan distance**, because the streets in Manhattan are laid out like a grid.

Many games use grids: chess has 8 by 8, that is 64 squares. In Battleships you call out coordinates such as C5 to fire at a square. Sudoku, noughts and crosses and many computer games also build their world out of grid squares. In a program, such a game board is often stored as a **two-dimensional array** with rows and columns.

A screen is a huge grid of tiny points of light, the **pixels**. A Full HD screen has 1920 columns and 1080 rows, which is over two million pixels. Spreadsheets such as Excel also name their cells after the pattern of column and row, such as A1 or D7. Maps such as the Swiss national maps have a coordinate grid with which you can give the exact position of any place.

begriffe.erklaerung: A horizontal line of squares.
A vertical line of squares.
The address of a square, for example B2.
The smallest point of a picture on a screen.

gewusst: On a chessboard, the square at the bottom left from White’s point of view is always called A1.
The Swiss national maps also have a grid with which any point in the country can be given to the nearest metre.
A grid of 10 by 10 squares already has 100 squares, and one of 100 by 100 has 10,000.

teile.einleitung: In programming, a function is a named part of a program that carries out a particular task and can be called again and again. It often receives values as input and returns a result, rather like a function in mathematics.
wichtigste: A function groups commands together under a name.
In Python you define a function with the keyword def.
A Python function without a return statement returns None.
A variable that is only visible in its own function is called a local variable.
A pure function always gives the same result for the same arguments and has no side effects.
A function that receives another function as an argument is called a higher-order function.
With lambda you write short, nameless functions in Python.

abschnitte.text: A **function** is like a small recipe in a program. You write the commands down once, give them a name and can then use them as often as you like. This saves work and makes programs clearer. The values that you pass to a function are called **arguments** or parameters. The result that it gives back is called the return value.

In Python a function begins with the keyword **def**, followed by the name and the parameters, for example def double(x):. With **return**, the function gives back its result. If the return statement is missing, a Python function automatically gives back the value None. Variables that you create inside the function are **local variables**; they are only visible there. Outside the function they do not exist.

Functions in programming are closely related to mathematical functions. If f(x) = 2x + 1, then f(3) gives the value 7. If you put the result in again, you get f(f(3)) = f(7) = 15. A function that always gives the same result for the same arguments and changes nothing else is called a **pure function**. If, on the other hand, a function changes something outside, such as a file, this is called a **side effect**.

Functions can themselves be treated like data. A function that receives another function as an argument is called a **higher-order function**. One example is map in Python, which applies a function to every element of a list. With lambda you write short, nameless functions for this. So list(map(lambda x: x * x, [1, 2, 3])) gives the list [1, 4, 9].

Almost every program consists of many functions that work together. In this way a big problem can be broken down into small parts that are easy to solve. Programming teams share out functions among themselves and test them one at a time. Many ready-made functions are available in **libraries**, for example for calculating or drawing. When a function calls itself, this is called **recursion**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A named part of a program that carries out a task and can be used again.
A placeholder for a value that you pass to a function.
The result that a function gives back.
A variable that is only visible inside its own function.
When a function calls itself.

gewusst: The keyword lambda goes back to the lambda calculus, which the mathematician Alonzo Church developed in the 1930s.
Even the print command in Python is a function that someone else wrote for you.
In Scratch, functions you create yourself are called “My Blocks”.

teile.einleitung: Educational robots are small robots that children and young people use to learn programming in a playful way. You give them a sequence of commands such as “forward” or “turn”, and they carry them out exactly in order. That way you see straight away whether your program works.
wichtigste: An educational robot carries out the commands you give it.
With the command “forward” it moves in the direction it is facing.
Small robots such as the Blue-Bot are given their commands with buttons.
One step of the Blue-Bot is about 15 centimetres long.
Educational robots usually get their energy from a rechargeable battery.
A quarter turn to the right from north makes it face east.
In Switzerland, educational robots are used in the subject media and computer science.

abschnitte.text: **Educational robots** are robots built especially for school and lessons. They are sturdy, easy to use and usually run on a **rechargeable battery**. Well-known examples are the bee-shaped **Bee-Bot** and its brother Blue-Bot, which even nursery children can use. For older pupils there are robots that you program on a computer or tablet.

On the Blue-Bot you press buttons on its back, such as forward, backward, left and right. Every button press is stored, so if the robot is to move forward 4 squares, you press the forward button 4 times. With the go button it starts and carries out the whole **sequence of commands**, about 15 centimetres per step. The Blue-Bot can also be controlled from a tablet via Bluetooth.

An educational robot turns on the spot by a **quarter turn** each time, that is 90 degrees. If it is facing north and turns right once, it faces east. Two quarter turns to the left make a half turn, and it then faces the opposite way. If it moves 3 squares forward and 1 square back, it is 2 squares away from the start.

The educational robot **Thymio** was developed at EPFL in Lausanne together with the art school ECAL. It has lots of sensors and little lights and reacts, for example, to obstacles, clapping or lines on the floor. Thymio can be programmed with blocks on the screen or with text commands. It is used in many Swiss schools.

In the **Lehrplan 21** curriculum, programming is part of the module media and computer science. With educational robots, children practise breaking a task down into small steps and finding mistakes in the program, which is called **debugging**. Older pupils build their own robots with motors and sensors using kits such as LEGO Education. In doing so they learn that a computer does exactly what you tell it, not what you mean.

begriffe.erklaerung: An instruction to the robot, for example “forward”.
A sequence of commands that the robot carries out in order.
A part with which the robot senses something, such as light or obstacles.
An energy store that can be charged again.
Finding and fixing mistakes in a program.

gewusst: The Bee-Bot looks like a bee with yellow and black stripes.
The Swiss educational robot Thymio was created at EPFL in Lausanne.
Educational robots often move on play mats with squares that are exactly as big as one robot step.

teile.einleitung: A flowchart is a drawing that uses boxes and arrows to show the order in which the steps of a process happen. In computer science it is used to plan programs before writing them.
wichtigste: A flowchart shows a process with shapes and arrows.
The arrows show the order of the steps.
Start and end are drawn as a rounded rectangle.
An instruction such as “increase x by 1” goes in a rectangle.
A decision goes in a diamond and has two exits, Yes and No.
Inputs and outputs are drawn as a parallelogram.
In Germany, a flowchart for programs drawn to the standard DIN 66001 is called a program flowchart.

abschnitte.text: A **flowchart** is a kind of building plan for a process. Each step is placed in a shape, and arrows connect the shapes with each other. You read the diagram by following the arrows from the start. In this way you can see at a glance what happens first and what happens next. Flowcharts help you to put your thoughts in order before you program or explain something.

Start and end are drawn as a **rounded rectangle**. An instruction such as “set x to 3” goes in a normal **rectangle**. A question that you answer with Yes or No goes in a **diamond**, from which two arrows lead out. For inputs and outputs, such as “output x”, you use a parallelogram. Thanks to these fixed shapes, everyone understands the diagram in the same way.

If an arrow leads back to an earlier step, a **loop** is formed. An example: set x to 3 and ask whether x is greater than 20. If the answer is No, you double x and go back to the question. So x becomes 6, then 12, then 24, and only then is the answer Yes and 24 is output. Loops save a lot of space, because you do not have to draw steps several times.

So that experts all over the world read flowcharts in the same way, there are **standards**. In Germany, the standard DIN 66001 sets out what a **program flowchart** looks like, and internationally there is the standard ISO 5807. As early as the 1920s, the American engineer Frank Gilbreth drew processes in factories as diagrams. Later, computer pioneers such as John von Neumann used flowcharts to plan programs.

Flowcharts are not only for computers. You can use them to show a recipe, the way to school or brushing your teeth. Companies use them to show who does which task in which order. Instructions for emergencies are also often drawn as a flowchart. At school you learn with them to break a problem down into small **steps**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A drawing with shapes and arrows that shows a process.
A four-sided shape like a square standing on its point, used in a flowchart for decisions.
A part of a process that is repeated several times.
A flowchart for computer programs drawn according to a standard.

gewusst: With flowcharts you can even draw funny decision aids, for example whether you need an umbrella today.
Modern learning languages such as Scratch, with their blocks, look almost like a flowchart put together.
There are plastic stencils for flowcharts, with which you can draw the shapes neatly.

teile.einleitung: A data centre is a building or room full of computers that store and process data. Websites, cloud storage, streaming services and banking systems run here. So that everything works around the clock, a data centre needs a lot of electricity, cooling and security.
wichtigste: In a data centre, many servers stand side by side in cabinets.
The PUE figure is the total energy use divided by the energy use of the IT equipment.
If a centre uses 1.5 MW and the IT uses 1.2 MW of that, the PUE is 1.25.
One rack unit in a 19-inch cabinet measures 1.75 inches, that is 44.45 mm.
Cold and hot aisles prevent cold incoming air and warm outgoing air from mixing.
The term N+1 means there is one component more than needed.
For the highest level, Tier IV, an availability of 99.995 percent is given.

abschnitte.text: A **data centre** contains hundreds to thousands of **servers**, powerful computers without screens. They stand in standardised **19-inch cabinets**, whose height is measured in rack units of 44.45 mm each. Thick fibre-optic lines connect the centre with the internet. When you stream a video or send a message, the data runs through such centres.

Servers get hot when they compute, so cooling is one of the biggest tasks. The cabinets are arranged so that **cold and hot aisles** alternate and the air flows in a targeted way. With **free cooling**, cool outside air or cold water is used instead of refrigeration machines. In Switzerland the cool climate is particularly well suited to this.

Data centres need a great deal of electricity; a large centre uses as much as a small town. How efficient one is shown by the **PUE** figure, the total energy use divided by the use of the IT equipment. A value of 1.0 would be perfect; good modern centres reach about 1.2. The waste heat can be put to good use, for example to heat homes through a **district heating network**.

If a data centre fails, whole companies often come to a standstill. That is why there is **redundancy**: with N+1, there is always one more cooling system or power supply than needed. Batteries and diesel generators take over if there is a power cut. Many companies also run a second centre far away so that operations continue even in a flood or fire.

Switzerland is a popular location because it is politically stable and has a reliable electricity supply. Many data centres are in the Zurich and Geneva areas. Some providers have even converted former **military bunkers** in the Alps into particularly secure data stores. Banks, insurance companies and authorities keep important data there.

begriffe.erklaerung: A powerful computer that provides services for other computers.
A figure that shows how much energy is needed for cooling and technology in addition to the IT.
Extra equipment that takes over immediately if something fails.
Cooling with cool outside air or cold water instead of refrigeration machines.
The standard measure for the height of equipment in a server cabinet.

gewusst: At Tier IV, a data centre may only be down for about 26 minutes a year.
Some data centres use their waste heat to warm indoor swimming pools or greenhouses.

teile.einleitung: In object-oriented programming, a class is a blueprint for objects. It sets out which properties and abilities all objects of this kind have. From a single class you can create as many objects as you like, just as you can build many identical houses from one blueprint.
wichtigste: A class is a blueprint for objects.
A specific object built from this blueprint is called an instance.
When an object is created, the constructor is called automatically.
In Python the initialiser is called __init__ and the first parameter of a method is called self.
A class variable belongs to the class itself and is shared by all instances.
An abstract class cannot be instantiated directly.
In Java, the access modifier private only allows access within the class itself.
The singleton pattern makes sure that there is exactly one instance of a class.

abschnitte.text: A **class** describes how a certain kind of thing is built. A class “Dog” could, for example, set out that every dog has a name and an age and can bark. A particular dog called Bello is then an **object** or an **instance** of this class. You can create as many instances of a class as you like.

The properties of an object are called **attributes**, for example name or colour. The abilities are called **methods**; these are functions such as bark or run. Each instance has its own values for the attributes. A **class variable**, on the other hand, belongs to the class itself and is shared by all instances.

When a new object is created, the program automatically calls a special method, the **constructor**. It gives the object its starting values, for example the dog's name. In Python the initialiser is called __init__. There, the first parameter of every instance method is usually called **self** and stands for the object itself.

With **access modifiers** you decide who may access attributes. In Java, private means that only the class itself can access them. Through **inheritance**, a class can take on the properties of another, for example a class “Dachshund” that inherits from “Dog”. An **abstract class** only serves as a template and cannot be instantiated directly.

Classes first appeared in the programming language **Simula**, which was developed in Norway in the 1960s. Later, languages such as Smalltalk, C++ and Java made object-oriented programming known around the world. Today Python, C# and many other languages use classes too. For common tasks there are proven solutions, the **design patterns**, such as the singleton.

begriffe.erklaerung: A blueprint that describes the properties and abilities of objects.
A specific object created from the blueprint of a class.
A function that belongs to a class and describes what an object can do.
A class takes on the attributes and methods of another class.
A special method that runs automatically when an object is created.

gewusst: In many video games, every game character is an object of a class, for example a class “Enemy”.
In Python, even a simple number like 5 is an object of a class, namely the class int.
The two Norwegians who developed Simula later received the Turing Award, the most important prize in computer science.

teile.einleitung: Peer-to-peer, P2P for short, is a way of connecting computers in a network. All the participants have equal rights; the English word “peer” means an equal. Every computer can offer data and receive data at the same time.
wichtigste: In a peer-to-peer network, every participant is both client and server.
From 1999 the music-sharing service Napster made P2P known worldwide.
With BitTorrent, a tracker brings the participants of a swarm together.
A seeder has the complete file and only uploads.
Many modern P2P networks use a distributed hash table instead of a central server.
Since 2009 the cryptocurrency Bitcoin has been based on a peer-to-peer network.
P2P networks scale well because every new participant also contributes resources.

abschnitte.text: Most networks use the **client-server model**: many clients ask a central server for data, for example a website. With **peer-to-peer** it is different, because every computer is client and server at the same time. The participants, called **peers**, exchange data directly with each other. So there is no need for a big central computer that hands everything out.

In 1999 the American student Shawn Fanning started the music-sharing service **Napster**. Millions of people used it to swap music files directly from computer to computer. Because copyright-protected music was very often copied without permission, the music industry sued. Napster had to shut down in 2001, but it made P2P known all over the world.

**BitTorrent**, developed by Bram Cohen in 2001, splits large files into many small pieces. All the peers downloading the same file form a **swarm** and exchange the pieces with each other. A server called a **tracker** introduces the participants to each other. Someone who has the whole file and only uploads is called a seeder.

Many modern P2P networks even manage without a tracker at all. They use a **distributed hash table**, a kind of address book divided up among all the participants. Each peer knows only a small part but quickly finds the rest through other peers. This means the network keeps working even if individual computers fail.

The internet telephony service **Skype**, launched in 2003, originally used a peer-to-peer architecture. The cryptocurrency **Bitcoin** has been running since 2009 on a P2P network in which thousands of computers together store all payments, without any central bank. Some games also distribute updates via P2P to take the load off their servers. A big advantage is that the network gains more capacity with every new participant.

The technology itself is legal and is used for many useful purposes, such as distributing free software. But anyone who offers protected films, music or games without permission breaks **copyright** law. In Switzerland it is uploading such works in particular that is banned, and BitTorrent automatically uploads while downloading. Malware can also be spread through file-sharing services.

begriffe.erklaerung: A participant with equal rights in a network.
A computer or program that requests data.
A computer that provides data or services for others.
All the peers exchanging the same file at the same time with BitTorrent.
A law that protects the works of artists and creators.

gewusst: With BitTorrent, participants who do not have everything yet and mainly download are called leechers, after the English word for a bloodsucking worm.
Skype was bought by Microsoft in 2011 and shut down in 2025.
The more people share a file via BitTorrent, the faster the download usually becomes.

teile.einleitung: In computer science, an array is a data structure that stores many values of the same type in a fixed row. Each value has a number, the index, through which you can access it at lightning speed. Arrays are among the most important basic building blocks of almost every programming language.
wichtigste: An array stores several elements of the same type under a shared name.
Each element is accessed through its index, which in C, Java or Python begins at 0.
With n elements, the last element has the index n-1.
The elements lie one after another in the working memory without any gaps.
Access through the index always takes the same time, which is written as O(1).
Inserting an element right at the front needs O(n), because all the others have to be moved.
Two-dimensional arrays form tables; an array with 3 rows and 4 columns has 12 elements.

abschnitte.text: Imagine a row of numbered lockers, each with room for exactly one object. An **array** works in exactly the same way: under one name, such as marks, you store many values. The number of a locker is called the **index**. In languages such as C, Java or Python, counting begins at 0, so the first element is marks[0]. If an array has n elements, the last one is marks[n-1].

The elements of a classic array lie one after another in the **working memory** without any gaps. That is why the computer can work out the address of each element directly: start address plus index times the size of one element. If an array begins at address 1000 and each element takes up 4 bytes, the element with index 5 is at 1000 + 5 times 4, which is 1020. This direct access always takes the same time, however big the array is.

Computer scientists describe running time with **big O notation**. Access through the index has the running time O(1), so it is constantly fast. But if you want to insert an element right at the front, all the others have to move one place back, which costs O(n). Searching for a particular value in an unsorted array also needs O(n) in the worst case. If the array is sorted, binary search is much faster.

A classic array has a fixed size. **Dynamic arrays**, such as lists in Python or the ArrayList in Java, can grow. When they are full, they usually reserve twice as much space and copy all the elements across. Because this happens rarely, adding an element at the end still has an **amortised** running time of O(1) on average. In this way dynamic arrays combine fast access with flexibility.

A **two-dimensional array** is like a table with rows and columns. An array with 3 rows and 4 columns contains 3 times 4, which is 12 elements. The programming language C stores such arrays in memory row by row. Two-dimensional arrays are used for game boards such as chess, for tables or for pictures, in which each element is a pixel.

begriffe.erklaerung: A row of values of the same kind; in German called a “Feld”.
A number with which you find an element in the array.
A single value in an array.
How long a program takes in relation to the amount of data.
A way in which data is stored in an organised way in the computer.

gewusst: Arrays start at 0 because of how addresses are calculated: the first element is 0 steps away from the start.
Some older programming languages such as Fortran start counting at 1.
In a computer, a digital photo is often nothing more than a big two-dimensional array of colour values.

teile.einleitung: A half adder is a small electronic circuit that adds together two single bits. It is one of the simplest building blocks from which every computer gets its computing power. If you understand the half adder, you understand how a processor can calculate at all.
wichtigste: A half adder adds two one-digit binary numbers, that is two bits.
It has two inputs and two outputs: the sum and the carry.
The sum bit is produced by an XOR gate.
The carry bit is produced by an AND gate.
If both inputs are 1, it outputs sum 0 and carry 1.
A half adder lacks an input for the carry from the previous digit.
From two half adders and an OR gate you build a full adder.

abschnitte.text: Computers calculate in the **binary system**, that is only with the digits 0 and 1. A half adder adds together exactly two such digits. There are only four possibilities: 0+0, 0+1, 1+0 and 1+1. With 1+1 the binary result is 10, so a 0 in this place and a 1 that is passed on to the next place. This 1 that is passed on is called the **carry**.

A half adder consists of only two **logic gates**. The **XOR gate** gives a 1 when exactly one of the two inputs is 1, and so produces the sum bit. The **AND gate** only gives a 1 when both inputs are 1, and so produces the carry bit. In modern chips, the gates themselves are made of tiny transistors.

A **truth table** shows all the inputs and outputs of a circuit. With 0 and 0, sum and carry are both 0. With 0 and 1, or 1 and 0, the sum is 1 and the carry is 0. With 1 and 1, the sum is 0 and the carry is 1. This small table describes the whole behaviour of the half adder.

abschnitte.titel: From half adder to full adder
abschnitte.text: If you want to add bigger numbers, each digit also has to take the carry from the previous digit into account. That is exactly what the half adder lacks a third input for, which is why it is only called “half”. A **full adder** has three inputs and can be put together from two half adders and an OR gate. In this way it can add three bits at once.

If you connect several full adders one after another, you get an adder for whole numbers with 8, 32 or 64 bits. In the **ripple-carry adder**, the carry is passed on from one full adder to the next, rather like a row of falling dominoes. This is simple, but slow for long numbers. The **carry-lookahead adder** therefore works out the carries in advance and is faster. Adders like these are found in the arithmetic unit of every processor.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest unit of information in a computer; it is either 0 or 1.
A circuit that turns input bits into an output bit according to a fixed rule.
The number that is passed on to the next place when adding.
A table that shows the output of a circuit for every possible input.

gewusst: When you do column addition at school, you do exactly the same as an adder, only with the digits 0 to 9 instead of 0 and 1.
A modern processor can carry out billions of additions per second, and each of them is based on the idea of the half adder.
You can even build a half adder with little lamps, switches or dominoes.

teile.einleitung: An infinite loop is a part of a computer program that repeats itself again and again and never stops. Sometimes this is a mistake, and the program gets stuck. But sometimes it is exactly what is wanted, for instance in traffic light control or a video game.
wichtigste: An infinite loop repeats commands without end.
A common cause of error is that the variable in the condition never changes.
A program in an infinite loop often stops responding and is never finished.
In a console, you usually stop a stuck program with Ctrl + C.
Intended infinite loops exist in traffic lights, games and devices that always have to be ready.
In Scratch, the “forever” block is deliberately an infinite loop.
In 1936 Alan Turing proved that no program can reliably predict for every other program whether it will run for ever.

abschnitte.text: A **loop** repeats commands as long as a condition is met. For example: as long as there are still apples in the basket, take one out. Normally the condition becomes false at some point and the loop ends. In an **infinite loop**, this never happens. The program then goes round in circles, like a hamster in a wheel.

An infinite loop is often caused by a programming mistake, a so-called **bug**. Often the variable in the condition is never changed inside the loop at all. Another example: i starts at 10, and as long as i is not 0, 3 is subtracted. Then i jumps from 1 to -2 and skips the 0, so the loop never ends. “x starts at 1; as long as x is greater than 0, increase x by 1” also runs for ever, because x just keeps getting bigger.

If a program is stuck in an infinite loop, it often stops responding, and the computer sometimes gets slow or warm. In a **console**, such a program is usually stopped with the key combination Ctrl + C. On Windows, stuck programs can be ended in the **Task Manager**. To stop it getting that far, loops are tested carefully to check whether the stopping condition is really reached.

Some programs are not meant to stop at all. A **traffic light control** keeps switching between red, amber and green as long as there is electricity. In Scratch there is the “forever” block for this. Every video game has a **game loop**, a main loop that keeps reading inputs, calculating the game world and drawing the picture again. A microcontroller in a washing machine also runs in an infinite loop and waits for buttons to be pressed.

In 1936 the British mathematician **Alan Turing** asked a famous question: can a program reliably predict for every other program whether it will stop at some point? He proved that this is impossible. This result is called the **halting problem** and is one of the most important theorems of theoretical computer science. It means that there can never be a perfect checking program that finds all infinite loops.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part of a program that repeats commands several times.
A question that is true or false and decides whether the loop goes on.
An error in a computer program.
The main loop of a game, which constantly reads inputs and draws the picture again.
The unsolvable question of whether every program can reliably be predicted to stop.

gewusst: The address of Apple’s former headquarters in California is “1 Infinite Loop”.
A smartphone operating system also basically runs in an infinite loop, constantly waiting for touches and messages.
A simple everyday example of an infinite loop is shampoo instructions such as “lather, rinse, repeat” without saying when to stop.

teile.einleitung: A remote control is a small device with which you control another device from a distance, without getting up. With it you change the channel on the television, open the garage door or steer a toy car.
wichtigste: A remote control controls devices from a distance.
Television remote controls usually send their commands with invisible infrared light.
With a mobile phone camera you can sometimes make this light visible.
The infrared light has to reach the receiver and does not go through walls.
Remote-controlled toy cars and garage doors usually work by radio.
Most remote controls need batteries.
Today many devices can also be controlled remotely with a smartphone.

abschnitte.text: A **remote control** is a transmitter that sends commands to a device. When you press a button, it sends a particular signal, and the device carries out the matching command. With the television, you can change the channel, turn the volume up or down or switch the set off. There are also remote controls for radios, air conditioning, projectors and blinds. To work, most of them need **batteries**.

Most television remote controls send their commands with **infrared light**. Our eyes cannot see this light. At the front of the remote control there is a small light-emitting diode for this, which switches on and off at lightning speed. Each button has its own flashing pattern, rather like Morse code. If you point a mobile phone camera at the remote control and press a button, you can sometimes see a flicker on the screen.

Inside the television there is a **receiver** that catches the infrared light. The light has to reach this receiver, which is why you point the remote control at the device. An infrared remote control does not work through a wall. But because light is reflected by light-coloured walls, it sometimes works by a roundabout route. If an object is in the way, the television does not react.

Remote-controlled toy cars, drones and garage doors are usually controlled by **radio**. Radio waves also go through walls and often reach further than infrared light. In this way a garage door opens with a small remote control even from inside the car. So that not every remote control opens every door, they send a secret **code**. Car keys today also usually open the doors by radio.

The first television remote controls appeared in the USA in the 1950s. One of the earliest was still connected to the television by a cable. Later there were models that worked with beams of light or with **ultrasound**. From about 1980, infrared light won out. Today many devices can also be controlled over wifi with an app on a smartphone.

begriffe.erklaerung: Light that is invisible to our eyes but can carry warmth and signals.
The part of a device that picks up signals.
Sending signals through the air with invisible waves.
A small component that lights up when electricity flows through it, LED for short.

gewusst: A mobile phone camera can often show the invisible infrared light of a remote control as a flicker.
Universal remote controls can imitate the signals of many different devices.
Controlling Mars probes from Earth is also a kind of remote control over millions of kilometres.

teile.einleitung: A MAC address is a hardware address that identifies each network interface of a device, for example the Wi-Fi card of a mobile phone. Devices use it to find each other in a local network. You can think of it a bit like a serial number for the network connection.
wichtigste: MAC stands for Media Access Control.
With Ethernet and Wi-Fi, a MAC address has 48 bits.
The front part, the OUI, reveals the manufacturer of the network interface.
The address FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF means “to all devices in the local network”.
In an IPv4 network, the ARP protocol finds the MAC address that belongs to an IP address.
A switch forwards data to the right port based on the destination MAC address.
Modern smartphones often use random MAC addresses on Wi-Fi so that they cannot be tracked.

abschnitte.text: Every **network interface**, that is, every Wi-Fi chip and every network port, has a MAC address. MAC stands for **Media Access Control**, meaning roughly control of access to the transmission medium. The address is usually set when the device is made. A laptop with Wi-Fi and a network cable port therefore has at least two MAC addresses. Bluetooth devices also have a similar 48-bit address.

With Ethernet and Wi-Fi, a MAC address consists of **48 bits**. It is written as six pairs of hexadecimal digits, for example 3C:22:FB:1A:07:9E. The first three pairs are called the **OUI** and show the manufacturer; these numbers are assigned by the organisation IEEE. The remaining three pairs are set by the manufacturer itself. With 48 bits there are over 281 trillion different addresses.

In a local network, for example at home or at school, data is sent in **frames**. Each frame contains the MAC address of the sender and of the recipient. A **switch** remembers in a table which device is connected to which port and sends the frame there directly. The special address FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF is called broadcast and reaches all devices on the network. If a computer in an IPv4 network wants to reach another device, it uses the **ARP** protocol to ask which MAC address belongs to that device's IP address.

The **IP address** shows where a device is on the internet, similar to a postal address. The MAC address, on the other hand, only applies in the local network, similar to the name on a front door. When a data packet passes a **router**, the IP address stays the same. But the MAC addresses are set again for the next section. In this way a packet travels from network to network until it reaches its destination.

Because the MAC address is fixed, a mobile phone could be recognised anywhere with it, for example in shopping centres with Wi-Fi. That is why modern smartphones often use **random MAC addresses** on Wi-Fi networks. The phone then chooses a different address for each Wi-Fi network. Some routers use MAC filters to only let known devices in. But this is not strong protection, because a MAC address can be faked.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of a device through which it is connected to a network, such as the Wi-Fi chip.
A number system with 16 digits, from 0 to 9 and A to F.
A device that forwards data in a local network directly to the right device.
A device that connects different networks, for example the home network with the internet.
A message to all devices in the local network at the same time.

gewusst: With 48 bits there are over 281 trillion possible MAC addresses.
From the first digits of a MAC address you can often tell which company built the network chip.
The MAC address has nothing to do with Apple's Mac computers.

teile.einleitung: A kilobyte is a unit of measurement for amounts of data, that is, for how much space information needs in a computer. According to the International System of Units, it is exactly 1,000 bytes. All the storage figures on your devices are made up of kilobytes, megabytes and gigabytes.
wichtigste: According to the International System of Units, a kilobyte is 1,000 bytes.
A megabyte is 1,000,000 bytes.
The megabyte lies between the kilobyte and the gigabyte.
A byte consists of 8 bits and is enough for roughly one character.
A text with 2,000 characters needs about 2 kilobytes.
Computers often calculate with 1,024 instead of 1,000, so a 500 GB hard drive appears with only about 465 “GB”.
Internet speeds are usually given in bits per second.

abschnitte.text: The smallest unit of information in a computer is the **bit**, which can only be 0 or 1. Eight bits make a **byte**, and a byte is enough for about one letter. The prefix **kilo** means thousand, as in kilogram or kilometre. So a kilobyte, abbreviated kB, is 1,000 bytes.

After the kilobyte comes the **megabyte** with one million bytes. Then follow the **gigabyte** with one billion and the terabyte with one trillion bytes. So each step is a thousand times as big as the one before. That is why about 500 photos of 2 megabytes each fit onto 1 gigabyte of storage.

Computers calculate in the **binary system**, and there 1,024, that is 2 to the power of 10, is a round number. That is why a kilobyte used to be treated as 1,024 bytes. To avoid confusion, 1,024 bytes are now officially called a **kibibyte**, abbreviated KiB. Because some operating systems calculate with 1,024, they show a 500 GB hard drive with only about 465 “GB”.

A short text message needs only a few bytes, a letter with one page of text about 2 to 3 kilobytes. A phone photo is usually a few megabytes, a song as an MP3 about 3 to 5 megabytes. A feature film in good quality can take up several gigabytes. A short **text file** is therefore normally the smallest file.

How fast data flows through a line is usually given in **bits per second**, not bytes. A connection with 100 megabits per second therefore downloads about 12.5 megabytes per second. That is why a download often takes longer than you might think at first. So watch out for the small b for bit and the capital B for byte.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest unit of information, either 0 or 1.
A group of 8 bits, roughly as much as one character.
Exactly 1,024 bytes, the unit for calculating in powers of two.
One million bytes, that is 1,000 kilobytes.

gewusst: The first home computers often had only a few kilobytes of memory.
A whole book of plain text needs only about as much storage as a single phone photo.
The term kibibyte was introduced in 1998 to end the muddle between 1,000 and 1,024.

teile.einleitung: A punched card is a card made of stiff paper on which information is stored as holes in particular places. For more than a hundred years it was one of the most important ways of storing data and controlled looms, counting machines and early computers. Programmers used to type their programs onto whole stacks of such cards.
wichtigste: On a punched card, information is stored as holes in particular places.
As early as around 1805, punched cards controlled the patterns on Joseph-Marie Jacquard's loom.
In 1890 Herman Hollerith evaluated the census in the USA with punched cards.
Hollerith's company later became the computer company IBM.
The widespread IBM standard punched card had 80 columns.
The holes were punched into the cards with a card punch.
If a stack of cards was dropped, the order of the program lines got mixed up.

abschnitte.text: A punched card is a rectangular piece of **card**. In some places holes are punched, in others not. A hole or no hole stands for a piece of information, similar to 1 and 0 in the binary system. A machine scans the card, in the past with brushes or pins, later with light. The big advantage: **machines** could read, count and sort the cards automatically.

Around 1805 the Frenchman **Joseph-Marie Jacquard** built a loom that was controlled by punched cards. Each card decided which threads were lifted for one row of the fabric. Many cards linked together produced a complicated pattern. This meant that even unskilled workers could weave splendid fabrics. The Jacquard loom is considered an early example of a programmable machine.

In the USA, evaluating the census of 1880 took many years. The engineer **Herman Hollerith** therefore invented machines that could read and count punched cards electrically. In the **census** of 1890, every person got their own card with holes for details such as age or place of residence. This made the evaluation much faster than before. Through mergers, Hollerith's company became the company **IBM** in 1924.

From 1928 the IBM card with rectangular holes became established. It had **80 columns** and 12 rows, and each column could store one character. A card was about 19 centimetres wide and 8 centimetres high. The holes were punched with a **card punch**, which looked like a big typewriter. Each card usually contained exactly one line of a program.

Until the 1970s, many programmers entered their programs into the computer as a **stack of cards**. A larger program consisted of hundreds or thousands of cards. If a stack fell down, the order was jumbled and had to be painstakingly restored. That is why some people drew a diagonal line with a felt-tip pen across the edge of the stack. Later, punched cards were replaced by screens, magnetic tapes and floppy disks.
