Even today, many text windows in programming environments are 80 characters wide, a reminder of the punched card. Some fairground organs also play their tunes from punched cardboard strips. As early as the 19th century, the English mathematician Charles Babbage planned a calculating machine with punched cards. His collaborator **Ada Lovelace** wrote instructions for it that are considered early computer programs. However, this machine was never completed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A piece of card that stores data as punched holes.
A device with a keyboard that punches holes in punched cards.
A survey in which a state counts and questions all its inhabitants.
Something on which information can be kept.

gewusst: The punched card is one reason why many programmers still limit their lines of code to 80 characters today.
The Jacquard loom was more than a hundred years older than the first computer and yet was already controlled by a kind of program.
Some programmers drew a diagonal line across their stack of cards so that they could quickly restore the order after dropping it.

teile.einleitung: “Online” means that a device or a person is connected to the internet; “offline” means the opposite. The words come from English and literally mean “on the line” and “off the line”. Today many devices are online almost all the time, but you can still do a lot offline, and breaks from the screen are important.
wichtigste: Online means: connected to the internet.
Offline means: not connected to the internet.
In flight mode a mobile phone goes offline.
You can look at saved photos offline too.
An online game is played over the internet.
You save offline maps before a journey so that they work without the internet.
A green dot in a chat app often shows that a person is online.
If you have been online for a long time, you should take a break.

abschnitte.text: **Online** comes from English and means “on the line”, that is, connected. **Offline** means “off the line”, that is, without a connection. In the past the words referred to devices that were connected to a line; today they almost always mean the connection to the internet. The words are also used for people: if you can be reached in a chat, you are online.

At home you usually connect to the router via **Wi-Fi**, and when you are out via the **mobile network**. If there is no connection, the screen often shows “No connection” or a crossed-out symbol. If you switch on **flight mode**, the radio connections are turned off and the phone goes offline. On a plane, in tunnels or in remote mountain valleys there is sometimes no signal.

In an **online game** you play over the internet, often with other people in other places. Online shops, online banking and video calls only work with a connection. In chat apps, a green dot next to a name often shows that the person is online right now. In many apps you can switch off this display if you don't want others to see it.

Lots of things work without the internet too: looking at saved photos, listening to downloaded music or writing texts. Before a journey you can save **offline maps** so that navigation works without the internet. Films and audiobooks can also be downloaded beforehand. As soon as the device is online again, new messages and data are brought up to date; this is called **syncing**.

If you are online for a very long time, you often get tired, lose concentration or get dry eyes. That is why it is a good idea to take regular **breaks** and do something offline, for example play outside or meet friends. Many families agree on screen rules, such as no mobile phones during meals or before going to sleep. On many devices you can also see and limit your own **screen time**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Connected to the internet.
Not connected to the internet.
A setting that switches off all the radio connections of a device.
Bringing data on different devices back to the same state.
The time you spend each day on a mobile phone, tablet or computer.

gewusst: The word “online” existed before the internet, for example for devices connected to a telephone line.
Even when you are offline you can write messages; they are sent as soon as there is a connection again.
Some people deliberately do a “digital detox”, a longer break from all online devices.

teile.einleitung: The Pascaline is one of the first mechanical calculating machines in the world. The French mathematician Blaise Pascal began building it in 1642, when he was only 19 years old. With dials and gearwheels it could add numbers, without any electricity at all.
wichtigste: Blaise Pascal began building the Pascaline in 1642.
He originally built it for his father, who had to do a lot of calculating as a tax official.
In 1645 Pascal presented his calculating machine in public for the first time.
The Pascaline was a purely mechanical machine.
Numbers were set with metal dials.
The machine could add directly and passed on the carry to the next column automatically.
Pascal built about 50 trial models before he was satisfied.

abschnitte.text: **Blaise Pascal** was born in 1623 in Clermont in France and was a mathematical talent even as a child. His father Étienne worked in Rouen as a **tax official** and had to add up endless columns of figures by hand. To make his work easier, 19-year-old Blaise began building a calculating machine in 1642. After about 50 trial models, he presented it in public in 1645.

The Pascaline was a brass box about the size of a shoebox. On top it had a row of metal **dials**, one for each place: units, tens, hundreds and so on. Behind them, small windows showed the result. Inside, **gearwheels** turned and passed everything on mechanically.

To enter a number, you turned the dials with a stylus, as on an old telephone dial. If you entered a second number, the machine automatically added it. If a place went above 9, a mechanism passed the **carry** on to the next place. Subtracting was only possible in a roundabout way with so-called complement numbers.

Pascal had about twenty machines built, and in 1649 he received a **privilege** from the French king, a kind of early patent. Even so, the Pascaline was not a business success. The machines were very expensive, difficult to make and often had to be repaired. Some examples have survived to this day, for example in the Musée des Arts et Métiers in Paris.

The Pascaline showed that a machine could take over calculating work that only people had done before. A little earlier, in 1623, the German **Wilhelm Schickard** had already designed a calculating clock, but it was lost. Later Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz built a machine that could also multiply. These inventions are considered early forerunners of pocket calculators and computers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that carries out calculations by itself.
A wheel with teeth that passes turning movements on to other wheels.
If a place becomes greater than 9, one is passed on to the next place.
With moving parts such as levers and wheels, without electricity.

gewusst: Some Pascalines also calculated with old French money, in which one livre had 20 sols and one sol had 12 deniers.
In 1970 a programming language invented by the Swiss Niklaus Wirth was named after Blaise Pascal.
Blaise Pascal was not only an inventor but also a physicist and a philosopher.

teile.einleitung: The e-ID is Switzerland’s electronic identity document, with which you can prove your identity digitally on the internet and in everyday life. It is issued by the state and stored in an app on the smartphone. Voters accepted the e-ID law very narrowly on 28 September 2025.
wichtigste: The e-ID is an official electronic identity document of Switzerland.
On 28 September 2025, about 50.4 percent of voters said yes to the e-ID law.
In 2021 a first e-ID law had been clearly rejected, mainly because private companies were to have issued the e-ID.
The e-ID is stored in the state app swiyu.
The data is kept on the holder’s smartphone.
Getting and using the e-ID is voluntary and free of charge.
You can, for example, prove only that you are of age without revealing any other data.

abschnitte.text: The **e-ID** is an electronic identity, that is a digital version of your identity document. With it you can prove online who you are, for example when dealing with authorities on the internet or opening an account. It is issued by the federal government, and the details come from your passport or identity card. It is stored in a state app, a so-called **wallet** (electronic purse), which is called **swiyu**. Getting and using it is **voluntary** and free of charge, and passports and identity cards will still exist.

On 7 March 2021, voters clearly rejected a first e-ID law. The most important reason was that private companies were to have issued the e-ID. After that, the federal government worked out a new law in which the state itself issues the e-ID. A **referendum** was called against it, and on 28 September 2025 the people accepted the law with about 50.4 percent voting yes. Because it was an optional referendum against a federal law, a **popular majority** was enough, even though the majority of cantons said no.

According to the federal government’s plan, the e-ID data is stored on the holder’s **smartphone** and not in a central database. You decide yourself which details you pass on. When buying alcohol, for example, you only have to prove that you are of age, without showing your name or address. This principle is called **data minimisation**. The state is also not supposed to find out when and where you use the e-ID.

The e-ID is built on a state **trust infrastructure**. This is meant to make other electronic credentials possible too, such as diplomas, driving licences or membership cards. Companies, schools and authorities can issue such credentials, and others can check whether they are genuine. The federal government planned to introduce the e-ID in 2026.

Supporters stressed that the e-ID makes many dealings with authorities simpler and safer. They also said it was better for the state to offer a secure identity document than for big technology companies to take this over. Opponents feared more surveillance and that the e-ID could in practice become compulsory over time. The narrow result shows that the Swiss population was divided on this issue.

begriffe.erklaerung: An electronic identity document with which you can prove who you are digitally.
An app in which you keep electronic identity documents and credentials.
A popular vote on a law passed by parliament.
A majority of all voters in the whole of Switzerland.
Showing only as much data as is really necessary.

gewusst: The e-ID vote of 2025 was one of the narrowest voting results of recent years.
The countries of the EU are also introducing a similar digital wallet for identity documents, the EU Digital Identity Wallet.
The technology of the e-ID is being developed as open source, so that experts can check the code.

teile.einleitung: Secret writing is writing that only people in on the secret can read. For thousands of years people have used it to hide messages from prying eyes, from generals in ancient Rome to children writing invisible messages with lemon juice. Today modern encryption protects every message on your mobile phone.
wichtigste: Secret writing makes sure that only people in on the secret can read a message.
Encrypting means making a message unreadable; decrypting means making it readable again.
To read secret writing, you need the key.
With lemon juice you can write invisibly; careful heating makes the writing visible.
The science of encryption is called cryptography.
Someone who cracks secret writing without the key is a codebreaker.
You must not give the key away to everyone, otherwise everyone can read along.

abschnitte.text: **Secret writing** turns a normal message into a text that outsiders cannot understand. This process is called **encrypting**. Anyone who knows the right **key** can **decrypt** the secret text again and read it. The key is the secret rule, for example “every letter is moved on by three places”. That is why you may only tell it to the people who are meant to read the message.

A special kind of secret writing is **invisible ink**. With lemon juice and a cotton bud you write a message on paper, and once it has dried it is invisible. If you heat the paper carefully, for example with an iron and with the help of an adult, the writing turns brown. The juice changes the paper so that it browns more quickly in those places. Here the message is not encrypted but hidden, which is called **steganography**.

As early as ancient Greece, the Spartans used the **scytale**, a staff around which a strip of leather was wound. The Roman general **Julius Caesar** moved each letter on by three places in the alphabet, so A became D. In the Second World War, the German army encrypted its radio messages with the **Enigma** machine. British codebreakers working with Alan Turing at Bletchley Park were able to decrypt them. This helped the Allies a great deal.

abschnitte.titel: Simple secret writing to try out
abschnitte.text: In the **Caesar cipher** you move all the letters on by a fixed number, so with three places HELLO becomes KHOOR. In a number code you replace each letter by its position in the alphabet: A is 1, B is 2 and so on. Mirror writing is exciting too, as you can only read it properly with a mirror. Codebreakers often count which letter appears most often, because in English, as in German, it is usually E.

The science of encryption is called **cryptography**. Today computers calculate with very long numbers as keys, which nobody can guess. Messenger apps often use **end-to-end encryption**, in which only the sender and the recipient can read the message. Encryption also protects your data in online banking and when shopping on the internet. The small padlock in the address bar of the browser shows that the connection is encrypted.

begriffe.erklaerung: The secret rule or number used to encrypt and decrypt.
The normal, readable message.
The encrypted, unreadable message.
The science of encrypting messages.
Someone who works out secret writing without the key.

gewusst: Leonardo da Vinci wrote many of his notes in mirror writing.
The Enigma had so many possible settings that a person could never have tried them all out.
With the scytale, the Spartans wound a strip around a staff, and only someone with a staff of the same thickness could read the message.

teile.einleitung: Python is a programming language with which you give the computer instructions in an easy-to-read form. It is considered especially beginner-friendly and yet is used by professionals at Google, in science and for artificial intelligence. It does not get its name from the snake but from a British comedy group.
wichtigste: Python was developed by the Dutchman Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991.
The name comes from the British comedy group Monty Python.
In Python, blocks of code that belong together are marked by indentation.
Python is free and runs on Windows, macOS and Linux.
The language is used for websites, data analysis, games and artificial intelligence.
Many schools use Python to learn programming.
Expressions such as 2 ** 10 calculate powers; the result is 1024.

abschnitte.text: Python is a **programming language**, a language in which people write programs. A program called an **interpreter** reads the Python code and carries it out line by line. The language uses many English words such as if, for or print. That is why Python programs can be read almost like a text.

The computer scientist **Guido van Rossum** began working on Python in Amsterdam at the end of the 1980s. The first version appeared in 1991. He chose the name because he was a fan of the television show by **Monty Python**. In 2008 Python 3 came out, a big revised version that is the standard today.

A special feature is **indentation**. Whatever is to be repeated in the body of a loop, for example, is moved a few spaces to the right. Other languages use curly brackets for this. Indentation forces you to write code neatly and clearly.

In Python you calculate much as you do in maths lessons, but with a few symbols of its own. The expression 17 // 5 is an **integer division** and gives 3, because 5 goes into 17 three whole times. With 2 ** 10 you calculate the power 2 to the 10th, that is 1,024. In a **list** such as [10, 20, 30, 40], the index -1 fetches the last element, that is 40. And len("Zürich") counts the letters of the word and gives 6.

Python is now one of the most popular programming languages in the world. Researchers use it to analyse huge amounts of data, for example weather data or measurements at CERN in Geneva. Many applications of **artificial intelligence** are written in Python. Websites, small games and robots can also be programmed with it. With add-on packages, the libraries, Python can be extended almost without limit.

begriffe.erklaerung: An artificial language with which you give a computer commands.
A program that reads code and runs it directly.
Spaces at the beginning of a line that show in Python which lines belong together.
An ordered collection of values, for example numbers or words.
A collection of ready-made code that you can build into your own programs.

gewusst: If you type “import this” in Python, the guiding principles of the language appear, such as “Simple is better than complex”.
Python counts the index from 0, so the first element of a list has the number 0.
For a long time, Guido van Rossum was jokingly called the “benevolent dictator for life” in the Python community.

teile.einleitung: Open data means data that is freely accessible and that everyone may use, process further and pass on. In Switzerland, the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities are publishing more and more such data, for example about weather, traffic or maps.
wichtigste: Open data is data that is freely accessible and may be used and passed on by everyone.
The Swiss portal for open government data is called opendata.swiss.
Since March 2021 the digital geodata of swisstopo have in principle been free of charge.
Since May 2025 MeteoSwiss has made its weather and climate data freely available as open data.
Article 10 of the EMBAG in principle obliges the federal administration to publish its data openly.
Open data should be machine-readable, for example as a CSV file.
Tim Berners-Lee proposed a five-star model for rating open data.

abschnitte.text: **Open data** is data that is freely available to everyone without barriers. You may download it, analyse it, combine it with other data and publish it again. Personal data about individual people is not included; it remains protected. Typical open data includes timetables, measurements, statistics or maps.

On the portal **opendata.swiss**, the Confederation, cantons, municipalities and other bodies collect their open data in one place. Since March 2021 the digital geodata of the Federal Office of Topography **swisstopo** have in principle been free of charge, including national maps and aerial photos. Since May 2025 **MeteoSwiss** has also released its weather and climate data freely. The Federal Statistical Office also publishes many figures openly.

The **EMBAG** is the federal act on the use of electronic means to carry out official tasks. It came into force at the beginning of 2024. Its **Article 10** in principle obliges the federal administration to publish its data as open government data. There are exceptions, for example for data protection or secrets.

For data to be really useful, computers must be able to read it; this is called **machine-readable**. A table as a **CSV file** can be processed directly by a program, whereas a scanned PDF cannot. The inventor of the World Wide Web, **Tim Berners-Lee**, designed a five-star model for this. One star is given for data on the web with an open licence, and linked data reaches the highest level.

Even open data usually has a **licence** that sets out how you may use it. A very common one is **Creative Commons BY**, CC BY for short. It allows almost any use but requires you to name the source. So if you draw a weather map with data from MeteoSwiss, you write next to it where the data comes from.

With open data, companies, researchers, the media and even school classes can carry out their own analyses. This produces, for example, apps for timetables, cycle routes or pollen warnings. Open data makes the work of authorities more open to view; this is called **transparency**. Because the data was collected with taxpayers' money, everyone should be able to benefit from it.

begriffe.erklaerung: A computer program can read and process the data directly.
A simple file format for tables in which the values are separated by commas or semicolons.
A permission with rules about how you may use something.
Data linked to a place on Earth, for example maps or heights.

gewusst: With the free data from swisstopo you can now load whole 3D models of the Swiss Alps onto your own computer.
Many timetable apps use open data from Swiss public transport.
Tim Berners-Lee presented his five-star model in 2010.

teile.einleitung: Computational complexity theory is a branch of computer science that studies how much time and memory a computer needs to solve a problem. So it does not only ask whether a problem can be solved, but how hard it is. One of its big open questions is so important that a million US dollars has been offered for its solution.
wichtigste: Complexity theory studies the effort computers need to solve problems.
The effort is described with big O notation, for example O(n) or O(n²).
Binary search in a sorted list needs only O(log n) steps.
Bubble sort and quicksort need O(n²) in the worst case, merge sort only O(n log n).
Comparison-based sorting cannot be faster than n log n in the worst case.
The question P versus NP is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems of the Clay Institute.
The travelling salesman problem in its optimisation version is NP-hard.

abschnitte.text: For many tasks there are several **algorithms**, that is, ways of solving them. Complexity theory measures how strongly the effort grows when the input gets bigger. It counts the calculation steps, the **running time**, and sometimes also the memory needed. The size of the input is usually called n, for example the number of numbers in a list.

With **big O notation** you describe how fast the effort grows. O(n) means: twice as much data, twice as much work. With **O(n²)** the effort grows with the square, so with ten times more data it takes a hundred times as long. If such an algorithm needs 1 second for 1,000 elements, it needs roughly 100 seconds for 10,000 elements.

**Binary search** halves a sorted list at each step and needs only O(log n) steps. In a million entries it finds any element in this way with about 20 comparisons. Bubble sort and quicksort need O(n²) in the worst case, whereas merge sort needs at most O(n log n). It can even be proved that sorting using only comparisons can never be faster than **n log n**.

The class **P** contains problems that a computer can solve quickly. The class **NP** contains problems for which a proposed solution can be checked quickly, a bit like a sudoku. Nobody knows to this day whether both classes are the same. In 2000 the **Clay Mathematics Institute** included this question in its seven Millennium Prize Problems and offered a prize of one million US dollars.

A famous hard problem is the **travelling salesman problem**. Here you look for the shortest round trip through many towns, for example for a delivery van. The optimisation version is **NP-hard**, which means no fast algorithm for it is known. Interestingly, **encryption** on the internet also relies on certain calculations being very hard.

begriffe.erklaerung: Exact step-by-step instructions for solving a task.
The number of calculation steps an algorithm needs.
A way of writing that shows how fast the effort grows with the amount of data.
At least as difficult as the hardest problems in NP, with no known fast solution.

gewusst: Whoever proves whether or not P equals NP can win a million US dollars.
With binary search you can find a word in a dictionary with a million entries in at most about 20 steps.
Even with 20 towns, there are more possible round trips for the travelling salesman than a person could ever count.

teile.einleitung: A light sensor is an electronic component that measures how bright it is. It turns light into an electrical signal that a device can evaluate. Light sensors are found in mobile phones, street lamps, cars and even educational robots.
wichtigste: A light sensor measures brightness.
Street lamps switch on with a light sensor when it gets dark.
Mobile phones use a light sensor to adjust the brightness of the screen.
Solar lamps in the garden light up at night thanks to a light sensor.
If you cover a light sensor with your finger, it measures darkness.
Cars can use a light sensor to switch on the headlights automatically in a tunnel.
Educational robots recognise a black line because black reflects less light than white.

abschnitte.text: A light sensor is a **sensor**, that is, a measuring device, that reacts to light. When a lot of light falls on it, it gives a different electrical signal than in the dark. A connected microcontroller or a simple circuit evaluates this signal. In this way a device can decide by itself whether to switch something on or off. Brightness is measured in the unit **lux**.

There are different kinds of light sensors. A **photoresistor** lets more current through the brighter it is. A **photodiode** produces a small current when there is light and reacts very quickly. A solar cell can also serve as a simple light sensor, because it gives more voltage in sunshine. A digital camera contains millions of tiny light sensors from which the photo is made.

Many **street lamps** have a twilight switch that turns them on when it gets dark. Solar lamps in the garden charge their battery during the day and light up at night as soon as the sensor reports darkness. In a mobile phone, a light sensor controls the brightness of the screen so that you can see it well in the sun and are not dazzled at night. Many cars automatically switch on their headlights in a tunnel. Automatic blinds come down in strong sunshine and provide shade.

Educational robots often have light sensors on their underside. They shine a small lamp on the floor and measure how much light comes back. White paper reflects a lot of light, a black line only a little. This lets the robot follow a line, which is called a **line follower**. Learning boards such as the Calliope mini or the micro:bit, which are used in Swiss schools, can also measure brightness.

The brightness at a place is called **illuminance** and is measured in lux. In a well-lit classroom it is about 500 lux. Outside in full summer sun it can be over 100,000 lux. Our eyes can adapt to these huge differences, whereas light sensors measure them precisely. That is why photographers and gardeners also use light meters.

begriffe.erklaerung: A component that measures something in the environment, for example light, heat or pressure.
The unit used to measure how brightly a place is lit.
A component that lets more current through when there is more light.
A switch that turns lamps on automatically when it is dark.

gewusst: A phone camera consists of millions of tiny light sensors, one for each pixel.
The micro:bit has no light sensor of its own but measures brightness with its small LEDs.
Full sunlight is about 200 times brighter than a well-lit classroom.

teile.einleitung: An in-app purchase is a purchase you make directly inside an app or a game. This means an app that was downloaded for free can still cost real money. That is why it is important to know how in-app purchases work and how to protect yourself from them.
wichtigste: An in-app purchase is a purchase made inside an app.
Even a free app can cost money through in-app purchases.
Game coins, gems or extras are paid for with real money.
Before you buy something in a game, you ask your parents.
Parents can block in-app purchases with a lock.
Games often put players under pressure with time limits.
A surprise box you can buy in a game is called a loot box.

abschnitte.text: Many apps and games can be downloaded **for free**. The companies then earn money with purchases inside the app, the **in-app purchases**. For example, you buy new characters, clothes for a game character, more lives or a version without adverts. This business model is called **freemium**, from the English words free and premium.

abschnitte.titel: Real money, even if it doesn't look like it
abschnitte.text: Many games use their own **game currencies** such as coins, diamonds or jewels. You buy these with real francs, even if the game only shows colourful stones. This makes it easy to lose track of how much you have already spent. If a pack costs 2 francs and you buy 3 of them, that is already 6 francs.

Some games put you under **pressure** on purpose, for example with messages like “Only 1 minute left! Buy now!”. Others make you wait a long time unless you pay for a shortcut. **Loot boxes** are surprise boxes where you don't know beforehand what is inside, similar to gambling. If you know these tricks, you are less likely to fall for them.

On mobile phones and tablets, parents can set up a **purchase lock**. On Apple devices this works through Screen Time, on Android through the settings in the Play Store or with Family Link. Then every purchase needs a **password** or the parents' approval. In Switzerland, children may in principle only make purchases within the limits of their pocket money without their parents' consent.

Always ask your parents first before you buy something in a game. Read carefully whether a button costs money before you tap it. Set yourself a fixed **budget**, for example part of your pocket money. And remember: many games are fun without buying anything too.

begriffe.erklaerung: A purchase made directly inside an app or a game.
An offer that is free but charges money for extras.
Play money such as coins or gems, which you often buy with real money.
A surprise box in a game that you can buy, with random contents.

gewusst: Today many games companies earn more money from in-app purchases than from selling the games themselves.
Some countries have restricted loot boxes bought with real money because they are similar to gambling.
In the app stores there is usually a note such as “In-app purchases” when an app offers such purchases.

teile.einleitung: The internet protocol suite, often called TCP/IP, is the collection of rules by which devices on the internet talk to each other. It sets out how data is addressed, split into packets, sent and put back together again. Without these shared rules, computers from different manufacturers could not understand each other at all.
wichtigste: The internet protocol suite is also called TCP/IP after its most important protocols.
Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn are considered its fathers.
From 1 January 1983 the ARPANET had to use TCP/IP.
An IPv4 address has 32 bits.
TCP sets up connections with the three-way handshake SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.
UDP works without a connection and without a delivery guarantee.
DNS translates names such as admin.ch into IP addresses.
HTTPS uses port 443 by default.

abschnitte.text: The protocol suite is built in **layers**, each of which takes on one task. At the bottom is the network access layer, such as Ethernet or Wi-Fi. Above that comes the **internet layer** with the IP protocol, then the transport layer with TCP and UDP. At the very top is the application layer with protocols such as HTTP, DNS or email.

The **Internet Protocol** gives every device an address and sends data packets from router to router. An IPv4 address has 32 bits and is written as four numbers, for example 192.168.1.10. In a network with the mask /24, 8 bits are left for devices, which gives 254 usable addresses. The **Time to Live** field is reduced by one at each router so that packets do not circle the network endlessly.

**TCP** makes sure that all data arrives completely and in the right order. To do this, it first sets up a connection with the **three-way handshake**: SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK. **UDP** does without this; it is connectionless and faster, but has no delivery guarantee. UDP is therefore suitable for video calls or online games, where a lost packet is less bad than a delay.

People find names easier to remember than numbers, which is why there is the **Domain Name System**. DNS translates a name such as admin.ch into the matching IP address. Many services run on a computer at the same time; they are told apart by **ports**. HTTP normally uses port 80, the encrypted HTTPS port 443.

In 1974 Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn presented their ideas for a protocol that could connect different networks. Later it was split into the two parts TCP and IP. On 1 January 1983 the ARPANET switched to TCP/IP for good, and many people see this day as the birthday of the internet. Because IPv4 addresses were running out, its successor IPv6 was created.

begriffe.erklaerung: An agreed rule for exchanging data.
A small piece of data with a sender and destination address.
The number by which a device can be reached on the network.
A number that identifies a particular service on a computer.
A device that forwards packets between networks.

gewusst: With IPv4 there are only about 4.3 billion addresses, fewer than there are people on Earth.
On its way through the internet, a data packet can travel through more than a dozen routers, often in fractions of a second.
In 2004 Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn received the Turing Award for TCP/IP, a kind of Nobel Prize for computer science.

teile.einleitung: An application programming interface, API for short, is a kind of agreement through which different programs can talk to each other. You can think of it like a restaurant menu: it shows what you can order without you having to know the kitchen. Almost every app today uses APIs, for example for weather data, maps or payments.
wichtigste: API stands for “Application Programming Interface”.
An API sets out how one program can use the functions of another program.
Web APIs today mostly exchange their data in the JSON format.
Roy Fielding described the REST architectural style in his doctoral thesis in 2000.
To read a resource, a REST API usually uses the HTTP method GET.
The older protocol SOAP wraps messages in XML envelopes.
With rate limiting, you limit how many requests a client may make.
In 2021 the US Supreme Court decided in the case Google v. Oracle that Google was allowed to use the Java API as fair use.

abschnitte.text: An **application programming interface** connects two programs. It describes exactly which questions you may ask and which answers come back. The program that asks is called the **client**. The client does not need to know how the other program works inside. It is like a plug socket: you plug the cable in and get electricity without knowing the power station.

A weather app gets its forecasts from a weather service through an API. A timetable app asks for train connections through an API. Online shops use APIs to process payments by card or TWINT. The operating system of your mobile phone also offers APIs so that apps can use the camera or GPS. This means developers don't have to program everything themselves.

Many APIs work over the internet and are therefore called **web APIs**. A very common style is **REST**, which the computer scientist Roy Fielding described in 2000. In it, data is addressed like addresses on the web. With the HTTP method GET you read data, with POST you send new data. The answers usually come in the text format **JSON**, which people and computers can read easily.

Before REST, the protocol **SOAP** was widespread. It wraps every message in an XML envelope. SOAP is regulated very precisely, but it is also more cumbersome. Today there are other techniques, for example GraphQL, in which the client says exactly which data it wants. Which technique fits depends on the task.

Many APIs require an **API key** so that the provider knows who is asking. With **rate limiting**, the number of requests a client may make per minute or hour is limited. This prevents a server from being overloaded. Functions that are due to be removed soon are marked as **deprecated**, that is, out of date. Developers then have time to adapt their programs.

The company Oracle sued Google because Google had rebuilt parts of the Java API for Android. The dispute lasted about ten years and went all the way to the **Supreme Court** of the USA. In April 2021 the court decided that this use was allowed as **fair use**. Many programmers were relieved, because rebuilding interfaces is common in computer science. The judgment is considered important for the whole software industry.

begriffe.erklaerung: Abbreviation for application programming interface, through which programs exchange data.
The program that makes a request.
A simple text format for data, for example {"name": "Lumi"}.
A widely used blueprint for web APIs.
Out of date: a function that will soon be removed.

gewusst: SBB and many Swiss authorities also offer open data through APIs.
The name REST stands for “Representational State Transfer”.
When you log in to another app with an existing account, an API is working in the background.

teile.einleitung: A hyperlink, link for short, is a clickable reference that leads to another web page, file or place. Links connect billions of pages on the internet into one big network. The World Wide Web with its links was invented in 1989 at CERN in Geneva.
wichtigste: A hyperlink is usually just called a link.
When you click on a link, another page or file opens.
Text links are often blue and underlined, and over a link the mouse pointer often turns into a hand.
Pictures and buttons can also be links.
In HTML you make a link with the element <a> and the attribute href.
A link whose target no longer exists is called a dead link.
You should not click on links in messages from strangers.

abschnitte.text: A **hyperlink** is a connection in a digital document. If you click on it, you jump to another page, to a picture, a video or another place on the same page. On a computer you click with the mouse; on a tablet or mobile phone you tap on it with your finger. Text links can often be recognised by their blue colour and underlining. Links you have visited are sometimes shown in purple.

Because links connect pages with each other, the internet is also called the **World Wide Web**. The British researcher **Tim Berners-Lee** developed the idea in 1989 at the CERN research centre in Geneva. He wanted researchers to be able to link their documents with each other easily. In 1991 the first website went online. The term **hypertext** for linked texts had already been coined in the 1960s by the American Ted Nelson.

Websites are written in the language **HTML**. A link there looks something like this: Next. The attribute href contains the target of the link, and between the tags is the visible text. With target="_blank" the page opens in a new tab. If the target begins with mailto:, a click opens the email program.

An **absolute link** contains the whole address with https:// at the start. A **relative link** points from the location of the current page, for example to a file in the same folder. Anchor links lead to a particular place on the same page, for example to a chapter. If a linked page is deleted or moved, a dead link is created, which shows an error message such as “404 Not Found”. Search engines use links to find new pages and to judge how important they are.

Not every link is harmless. Fraudsters send messages with links that lead to fake pages in order to steal passwords. This is called **phishing**. That is why it is best not to click on links from strangers. If you move the mouse over a link on a computer without clicking, you can usually see at the bottom of the window where it really leads. If in doubt, ask an adult.

begriffe.erklaerung: Short for hyperlink, a clickable reference.
The address of a web page, for example with https:// at the start.
The language in which websites are written.
A link whose target no longer exists.
Fraud with fake messages and pages in order to steal data.

gewusst: You can still visit the very first website in the world, from CERN, today.
Wikipedia articles often contain dozens of links, with which you can jump from topic to topic for hours.
The “a” in the HTML element <a> stands for “anchor”.

teile.einleitung: Konrad Zuse was a German engineer and inventor who is considered one of the fathers of the computer. In 1941 in Berlin he completed the Z3, the world's first working, freely programmable and fully automatic digital computer. One of his computers even worked for several years at ETH Zurich.
wichtigste: Konrad Zuse was born in Berlin in 1910 and died in 1995.
His first computer, the Z1 of 1938, was purely mechanical.
The Z3 of 1941 was made mainly of relays and is considered the first working programmable computer.
Zuse's computers worked with the binary system, that is, only with 0 and 1.
The Z3 was destroyed in a bombing raid in 1943.
With the Plankalkül, Zuse designed one of the first high-level programming languages.
From 1950 ETH Zurich rented his Z4 computer.

abschnitte.text: Konrad Zuse was born on 22 June 1910 in **Berlin**. He studied civil engineering and then worked as a structural engineer in the aircraft industry. There he had to do a great many long and boring calculations by hand. So he had the idea of building a machine that would do the calculating automatically. Zuse was also a talented **painter** and died in 1995 in Hünfeld in the German state of Hesse.

abschnitte.titel: The Z1 in the living room
abschnitte.text: Zuse built his first computer from 1936 in his parents' flat in Berlin. The **Z1** was finished in 1938 and worked purely mechanically with many thin metal sheets and pins. It already calculated with the **binary system**, that is, only with the digits 0 and 1. Unfortunately the mechanics often worked unreliably. A replica of the Z1 is now in the German Museum of Technology in Berlin.

In May 1941 Zuse completed the **Z3** in Berlin. Instead of metal sheets, he used about 2,000 **relays**, electrical switches that click when they switch over. The machine read the program from a punched strip of cinema film. The Z3 could, for example, add, multiply and work out square roots. In 1943 it was destroyed in a bombing raid during the Second World War; a replica is now in the Deutsches Museum in Munich.

In the 1940s Zuse designed his own programming language, the **Plankalkül**. With it he wanted to write down calculation rules not only for numbers but also for tasks such as chess moves. The Plankalkül is considered one of the world's first high-level **programming languages**. Because the war and the post-war period hindered his work, it was only fully published in 1972. It was only put into practice on a computer many years after Zuse's death.

Towards the end of the war, Zuse was able to rescue the **Z4** from Berlin and bring it to southern Germany. In 1950 **ETH Zurich** rented the machine and used it for scientific calculations until 1955. At that time the Z4 was one of very few working computers in Europe. The experience gained helped ETH later build its own computer called ERMETH. The original Z4 is now in the Deutsches Museum in Munich.

In 1949 Zuse founded the company Zuse KG, which built several hundred computers. It was later taken over by Siemens. Today Zuse is considered, together with researchers from the USA and Great Britain, one of the most important **computer pioneers**. Many schools, prizes and institutes bear his name.

begriffe.erklaerung: An electrical switch that is turned on and off by electric current and clicks audibly as it does so.
A number system that only has the digits 0 and 1.
An artificial language used to give commands to a computer.
A computer that works with digits rather than continuous quantities.

gewusst: Konrad Zuse built his first computer in his parents' living room.
In 1950 ETH Zurich was one of the first universities in Europe with its own working computer, although it was only rented.
Zuse painted many pictures and sold some of them under an artist's name.

teile.einleitung: Pattern recognition means discovering regularities, similarities and repetitions. People do this all the time, for example when recognising faces or continuing a sequence of numbers. In computational thinking, pattern recognition is an important step for solving problems cleverly, and computers use it for things like face recognition or spam filters.
wichtigste: Pattern recognition means finding similarities and repetitions.
It is one of the basic building blocks of computational thinking.
With number sequences you look for the rule, for example “times 3”: 2, 6, 18, 54, 162.
If commands repeat in a program, you can use a loop.
Spam filters recognise unwanted emails by typical patterns.
Many smartphones unlock the screen using face recognition.
Square numbers such as 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 continue with 36.

abschnitte.text: A **pattern** is something that repeats in a regular way. Pattern recognition means noticing such regularities and finding a **rule** for them. In **computational thinking** it is one of several basic building blocks, alongside breaking problems down, abstraction and designing algorithms. If you recognise a pattern, you can often transfer a solution to many similar tasks.

In the sequence 2, 6, 18, 54, each number is multiplied by 3, so the next one is 162. In 3, 5, 9, 17, 33 the gaps double, so 65 comes next. The sequence 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 consists of **square numbers**, and 36 comes next. In A, C, E, G one letter is always skipped, so I follows.

For 1 square made of matchsticks you need 4 matches, for 2 squares in a row 7 and for 3 squares 10. With each new square exactly 3 matches are added, because one side is shared. So the rule is: 3 times the number of squares plus 1. That is why you need 31 matches for 10 squares, without having to lay them all out.

If the same two commands appear eight times in a row in a program, that is a pattern. You can simplify it with a **loop** that repeats the commands eight times. This makes the program shorter, clearer and less prone to errors. Recurring tasks are also often put into a **function** that can be called several times.

In computer science, pattern recognition is also a field of research, closely linked to **artificial intelligence**. A spam filter recognises unwanted emails by typical patterns that it has learned from many example emails. Many smartphones unlock using **face recognition**, others with a fingerprint. Speech recognition, reading postcodes on letters and recognising road signs in cars are also based on pattern recognition.

begriffe.erklaerung: A regularity that repeats.
A series of numbers or characters following a particular rule.
A part of a program that repeats commands several times.
Thinking through problems in such a way that a computer can help to solve them.
A method that recognises people by their face.

gewusst: People are so good at recognising patterns that they even see faces in clouds, plug sockets or the fronts of houses.
The number of spirals in a sunflower often follows the Fibonacci sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 and so on.
Swiss Post has the addresses on letters read by machines that recognise handwriting patterns.

teile.einleitung: The ERMETH was the first computer built in Switzerland. Its name stands for “Elektronische Rechenmaschine der ETH” (electronic calculating machine of ETH), and it was created in the 1950s at ETH Zurich.
wichtigste: ERMETH means Elektronische Rechenmaschine der ETH, the electronic calculating machine of ETH.
It was the first computer built in Switzerland.
The project was led by the mathematician Eduard Stiefel at ETH Zurich.
The calculating unit contained about 1500 vacuum tubes.
A heavy magnetic drum served as working memory.
The ERMETH calculated with the decimal system and was in use until 1963.
Today you can see it at the Museum of Communication in Bern.

abschnitte.text: The **ERMETH** was built in the 1950s at the Institute for Applied Mathematics at ETH Zurich. At that time there were only a few computers in the world, and you could not simply buy one in a shop. Switzerland therefore wanted to develop its own computer. From 1956 the machine did calculations for research and industry. It was in use until 1963.

The project was led by the mathematics professor **Eduard Stiefel**. His team included the researchers Heinz Rutishauser and Ambros Speiser. Rutishauser later became famous for his work on the programming language Algol. Before the ERMETH was finished, ETH rented the German computer Zuse Z4 from 1950. This allowed the researchers to gain experience with computers early on.

The calculating unit consisted of about 1500 **vacuum tubes**, which look like small light bulbs and served as switches. A heavy, rotating **magnetic drum**, on which numbers were stored magnetically, served as working memory. Unlike today’s computers, the ERMETH did not calculate with zeros and ones but in the **decimal system**, with the digits 0 to 9. The machine was so big that it filled a whole room. It used a lot of electricity and got warm while doing so.

With the ERMETH, experts solved difficult calculations that would have taken weeks by hand. These included calculations for engineers, for instance for building **dams**. Researchers in physics and mathematics also used it. For its time the machine was fast; today every mobile phone is millions of times faster.

After it was taken out of service, the ERMETH was preserved. Parts of it are now in the **Museum of Communication** in Bern. There it shows visitors how the history of computers in Switzerland began. It is regarded as an important monument of Swiss technological history.

begriffe.erklaerung: A glass component that used to serve as an electrical switch in computers.
A rotating cylinder on which data is stored magnetically.
The number system with the ten digits 0 to 9 that we use in everyday life.
The Swiss Federal Institute of Technology, a well-known university in Zurich.

gewusst: The ERMETH was so big that it filled a whole room, even though it could calculate much less than a calculator today.
Before the ERMETH was finished, ETH calculated with a rented computer from Germany, the Zuse Z4.
Vacuum tubes often broke and had to be replaced regularly.

teile.einleitung: Post-quantum cryptography is encryption that is meant to remain secure even once there are large quantum computers. Such computers could crack many of today's methods, such as RSA. That is why experts around the world are developing new mathematical methods of protection.
wichtigste: Quantum computers could break today's public-key methods such as RSA.
In 2024 the US agency NIST published the standard ML-KEM as FIPS 203.
ML-KEM and ML-DSA are based on mathematical lattices.
The signature method SLH-DSA is based on hash functions.
To counter Grover's algorithm, the key length of AES is doubled.
In March 2025 NIST also selected the code-based method HQC.
The hybrid approach combines classical and post-quantum methods.

abschnitte.text: Quantum computers calculate with **qubits** and can solve certain tasks much faster than normal computers. In 1994 the mathematician Peter Shor showed with **Shor's algorithm** that a large quantum computer could split numbers into factors quickly. This would make RSA and methods using elliptic curves insecure. There is not yet a quantum computer big enough to do this.

Attackers could already be collecting and keeping encrypted data today. As soon as a powerful quantum computer exists, they could then decrypt the data. This danger is called **“harvest now, decrypt later”**. That is why secret data that has to stay protected for a long time is already being switched to new methods now.

Post-quantum methods are based on problems that, as far as we know today, even quantum computers cannot solve quickly. The most important are **lattices**, regular patterns of points in a great many dimensions. Other methods use hash functions or error-correcting codes, such as the **McEliece method** from 1978. Symmetric methods such as AES remain secure if their key length is doubled, because Grover's algorithm only gives part of the advantage.

The US standards institute **NIST** started a worldwide competition for new methods in 2016. In August 2024 the first standards appeared: ML-KEM (FIPS 203, from Kyber), ML-DSA (FIPS 204) and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205, formerly SPHINCS+). In March 2025 HQC was added as an extra key exchange method. A candidate called **SIKE**, on the other hand, was broken in 2022 with an ordinary computer in about an hour.

Many companies rely on a **hybrid approach**, in which a classical and a post-quantum method are used at the same time. If one of them is broken, the other still protects. Messengers such as Signal and iMessage, as well as modern browsers, already use such methods. But switching over all systems will take many more years.

begriffe.erklaerung: A computer that calculates with qubits according to the rules of quantum physics.
The science of encrypting messages.
A regular pattern of points on which many new methods are based.
Using an old and a new method at the same time.
The National Institute of Standards and Technology of the USA.

gewusst: For years the SIKE method was considered promising, but in 2022 it was cracked with just a single processor core.
The idea of the McEliece method is almost 50 years old and is still considered secure.

teile.einleitung: Landau symbols are mathematical signs such as O, Ω and Θ that describe how fast a function grows. In computer science they show how strongly the effort of an algorithm increases when the input gets bigger. This lets you compare programs without having to measure exact seconds.
wichtigste: The Landau symbols are named after the mathematician Edmund Landau.
The O symbol gives an upper bound for growth.
The symbol Ω (omega) describes a lower bound.
f ∈ Θ(g) means that f grows exactly as fast as g.
The function 3n² + 5n + 7 belongs to the class O(n²), because only the largest term counts.
With an O(n²) algorithm, the running time roughly quadruples when n doubles.
Trying out all the orders of n towns takes O(n!) steps.

abschnitte.text: Landau symbols describe the **growth** of functions for very large values. You are not interested in exact numbers, only in how fast something increases. The best known is the big **O**, pronounced “big O”. If you write f ∈ O(g), it means: f grows at most as fast as g, apart from a fixed factor. There are also Ω for lower bounds and Θ for exactly the same growth.

abschnitte.titel: Only the most important part counts
abschnitte.text: With Landau symbols you leave out **constant factors** and smaller terms. The function 3n² + 5n + 7 therefore belongs to O(n²). For n equal to 1,000, 3n² is three million, whereas 5n is only 5,000. So the term with the greatest growth decides almost everything. This produces simple classes that are easy to compare with each other.

The most common **complexity classes** are, from slowest to fastest growth: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(2ⁿ) and O(n!). O(1) means constant effort, no matter how big the input is. Two nested loops over n elements give O(n²). With **exponential** growth such as 2ⁿ, the effort doubles as soon as n gets just one bigger. For large n, 2ⁿ grows much faster than any power such as n² or n³.

A traveller wants to visit n towns and find the shortest route for this. If you simply try out all the orders, there are n! possibilities, that is n **factorial**. With 5 towns that is 120 orders, with 10 towns already over 3.6 million. With 20 towns it would be more than 2 quintillion, which even fast computers can no longer manage. This problem is called the **travelling salesman problem**.

The big O was introduced in 1894 by the German mathematician Paul Bachmann. **Edmund Landau** (1877 to 1938) used and spread the notation in his books on number theory, which is why the symbols bear his name. Landau also added the little o. In the 1970s the American computer scientist **Donald Knuth** made the symbols Ω and Θ known in computer science. Today they are part of the basic knowledge of every computer science degree.

begriffe.erklaerung: A limit that a function does not exceed for large values.
A limit below which a function does not fall for large values.
The product of all numbers from 1 to n, written n!.
Growth in which the value multiplies at every step.

gewusst: The number 20! has 19 digits and is greater than 2 quintillion.
With a million numbers, an O(n log n) sorting method is about 50,000 times faster than an O(n²) method.
The big O originally stood for the German word “Ordnung”, meaning order.

teile.einleitung: A check digit is an extra digit at the end of or within a number that lets you detect typing and reading mistakes. It is calculated from the other digits according to a fixed rule. You can find check digits on barcodes, books, bank accounts and even on the AHV number.
wichtigste: A check digit is used to detect typing mistakes.
It is calculated from the other digits according to a fixed rule.
In the barcode on a product, the check digit is right at the end.
If the check digit does not fit, the scanner at the checkout usually does not accept the code.
A good check digit often also detects two swapped digits.
In the Swiss IBAN there are two check digits straight after “CH”.
The ISBN on a book also contains a check digit.

abschnitte.text: A **check digit** is a digit that carries no new information but is only used for checking. It is calculated from all the other digits of a number. Whoever reads or types in the number later does the calculation again. If the result does not match the check digit, you know: a mistake has happened here. However, the check digit usually does not reveal which digit is wrong.

Imagine a code in which the last digit is the **sum** of the others. Then 2 3 4 has the check digit 9, because 2 plus 3 plus 4 equals 9. The code 1 2 4, on the other hand, is wrong, because 1 plus 2 makes 3 and not 4. But this simple rule has a weakness. If you swap two digits, the sum stays the same and the mistake is not noticed.

Almost every product in the shop has a barcode with a 13-digit **EAN number**. The last digit is the check digit. The digits are multiplied alternately by 1 and by 3 before being added up. This **weighting** means that many swaps are detected. If the scanner misreads a line, the check digit does not fit and the till does not beep.

Every book has an **ISBN**, which since 2007 has usually had 13 digits and also contains a check digit. With the older 10-digit ISBN, the check digit could also be an X, which stands for the number 10. The Swiss **IBAN** for bank accounts begins with CH and two check digits, which are worked out with a calculation using the number 97. The 13-digit AHV number, which begins with 756, also ends with a check digit. Credit card numbers are checked with the so-called Luhn method.

People easily make typing mistakes, especially with long numbers. Without a check digit, money could be transferred to the wrong account or the wrong product could be charged. With a check digit, the system notices the mistake immediately and asks for a new entry. This saves time, money and trouble. Check digits are a simple example of **error detection**, an important topic in computer science.

begriffe.erklaerung: A control digit with which mistakes in a number are detected.
The number under the barcode on products.
International number for books.
International account number for bank accounts.

gewusst: The check digits of the IBAN detect almost all simple typing mistakes.
Check digits are also hidden in train ticket codes and on many ID documents.
The 756 at the beginning of the AHV number is Switzerland's international country code.

teile.einleitung: JPEG is a very widespread format for storing pictures, and above all photos, in a space-saving way. Almost every digital camera and every mobile phone saves photos as JPEG. The trick is this: the picture is made much smaller by leaving out details that the eye hardly notices.
wichtigste: JPEG is especially suitable for photos.
JPEG stands for Joint Photographic Experts Group.
The JPEG standard was adopted in 1992.
For compression, JPEG splits a picture into blocks of 8 × 8 pixels.
JPEG pictures often have the extension .jpg.
A low quality level gives a smaller file with more picture errors.
If a JPEG is saved again and again, the quality gets a little worse each time.

abschnitte.text: JPEG is a **file format** for pictures, which you can recognise by extensions such as .jpg or .jpeg. The name comes from the **Joint Photographic Experts Group**, an international group of experts that developed the method. The standard was adopted in 1992. Since then, JPEG has been the most important format for photos on the internet, on cameras and on mobile phones.

An uncompressed photo would be huge, because the colour has to be stored for every single pixel. JPEG therefore splits the picture into small **blocks** of 8 × 8 pixels. In each block, fine details that the human eye hardly sees are simplified or left out. Because information is lost in the process, this is called **lossy compression**.

When saving, you can usually choose a **quality level**. A high quality gives a nice picture but a larger file. A low quality saves a lot of space, but you can see **artefacts**, small blocks and blurred edges. If a JPEG is edited and saved again often, these errors build up.

JPEG is ideal for **photos** with soft colour transitions, such as landscapes, people or animals. It is rather unsuitable for screenshots with text, logos or drawings with sharp edges. There, visible smudges appear around the letters. For such pictures it is better to use the **PNG** format, which saves without loss.

Almost all photos you take with a mobile phone or look at on the internet are JPEG pictures or similar formats. A phone photo as a JPEG is often only a few megabytes in size. Without this compression, the files would be many times larger. Newer formats such as **HEIC** or WebP can store pictures in an even more space-saving way.

begriffe.erklaerung: The way data is stored in a file, recognisable by the extension.
Making a file smaller so that it needs less storage space.
A single dot of a digital picture.
A visible picture error caused by strong compression.

gewusst: The extension .jpg has only three letters because older operating systems did not allow longer file extensions.
A JPEG can often shrink a picture to a tenth of its original size without you noticing much.
Photos are mostly saved as JPEG because the files are small and still look good.

teile.einleitung: In a database table, a primary key is the column or group of columns that uniquely identifies each row. It works like an ID number for every record. Without a primary key, the database would not know for sure which entry is meant.
wichtigste: A primary key must be unique and must not be empty (NULL).
A table has exactly one primary key, but it can consist of several columns.
A primary key made of several columns is called a composite key.
A surrogate key is an artificial key, such as a running number.
All the minimal combinations of columns that could serve as the primary key are called candidate keys.
A person's name is usually not a good primary key, because several people can have the same name.
The database system usually creates an index for the primary key automatically, often as a B-tree.

abschnitte.text: In a **relational database**, data is stored in tables, and each row is a **record**. The **primary key** is the value by which every record is uniquely recognised. It has to meet two conditions: it is **unique**, so it appears only once, and it must never be empty. In databases, empty values are called NULL.

A person's name is not a good primary key, because there are, for example, many people called Anna Müller. Numbers assigned specially for this purpose are better, such as a pupil number or an item number. In Switzerland the 13-digit **AHV number** serves as a unique personal number; it always begins with 756. Because of data protection, however, it may not simply be used everywhere.

All the minimal combinations of columns that could serve as the primary key are called **candidate keys**. One of them is chosen as the primary key. If it consists of several columns, for example class and seat number, it is called a **composite key**. A **surrogate key**, on the other hand, is an artificial number with no meaning of its own, which is often counted up automatically.

Primary keys are needed to link tables to each other. In a table of loans, for example, you can store the number of a book and the number of a child. Such a column, which points to the primary key of another table, is called a **foreign key**. That way you do not have to write out the details of the book again each time.

So that the database can find a record quickly, it usually creates an **index** for the primary key automatically. This is like the index in a thick book. This index is often built as a **B-tree**, a structure that allows very fast searching. In this way the database finds a row in a fraction of a second, even among millions of entries.

The relational database model was described by the British computer scientist **Edgar F. Codd** around 1970 at the company IBM. Unique keys play a central role in it. In the database language **SQL** you define a primary key with the words PRIMARY KEY. Today almost all websites, apps and companies use such databases.

begriffe.erklaerung: A row in a table, for example all the details about one child.
An empty value in a database; a detail is missing.
A column that refers to the primary key of another table.
A directory with which the database finds entries quickly.
A language for querying and changing databases.

gewusst: The number 756 at the beginning of the AHV number is Switzerland's international country code.
The ISBN on the back of a book is also a kind of key that uniquely identifies every book.
In many databases, every new entry automatically gets the next free number as its key.

teile.einleitung: On the internet you can write and play with lots of people, including ones you do not know. But behind a profile there may be someone quite different from what the picture and the name suggest. If you know a few simple rules, you stay safe online and know what to do when something feels odd.
wichtigste: You can never know for sure who is behind a profile on the internet.
Children should only chat with people they also know in real life.
If a stranger wants to meet up, tell your parents straight away.
You always tell an adult you trust about secrets with strangers from the internet.
You turn down presents from strangers in games.
You do not give out personal details, for example whether you are home alone.
With the Block and Report functions you can protect yourself.

abschnitte.text: On the internet anyone can make a **profile** with any name and picture they like. A profile that looks like a ten-year-old child may in reality belong to an adult. That is why you never know for sure who is writing to you. Most people online are friendly, but some want to trick or take advantage of others. So the rule is: strangers on the internet remain strangers, even if they write nicely.

Some messages are **warning signs**. These include someone saying “This is our secret” or wanting your parents not to find out. Questions such as “Are you home alone?” or “Where do you live?” are also suspicious. You should also be careful if someone offers you **presents** such as game currency or wants to lure you into another app to chat privately. And if someone suggests meeting up, that is a clear sign to tell adults straight away.

Only chat with people you also know in real life. Do not give away **personal details** such as your address, school, phone number or passwords. Do not send photos to strangers. In games and apps, set things up so that only friends can write to you. It is best not to answer suspicious questions at all.

Almost all apps and games have a **Block** function. With it, a person can no longer send you messages or find you. With **Report** you inform the people who run the app, who can check the profile and shut it down. Take a screenshot of the messages first, so that you can show them to adults. Blocking is not rude; it is clever.

If something seems odd to you or frightens you, tell your **parents**, a teacher or another adult you trust. You will not get into trouble, even if you did something wrong before. In Switzerland you can call or chat with the Pro Juventute helpline on **147** around the clock, free and anonymously. The police also help if someone is being threatened. Getting help is always right.

begriffe.erklaerung: The page with a name and picture that someone shows of themselves in an app.
A function with which a person can no longer contact you.
A function with which you point out a problem to the people who run an app.
A photo of what can be seen on the screen at that moment.
Information such as your name, address, school or phone number.

gewusst: The Pro Juventute number 147 does not appear on a phone bill, so you can call it in complete confidence.
In many games and apps, parents can set things up so that children only get messages from confirmed friends.
Adults are also taken in by fake profiles on the internet, so being careful matters for everyone.

teile.einleitung: A finite automaton is a simple mathematical model of a machine that is in one of a few states. It reads symbol by symbol and switches from state to state according to fixed rules. Finite automata are used to describe drinks machines, traffic lights, lifts and also the search for words in texts.
wichtigste: A finite automaton has a finite number of states and changes them when it reads input symbols.
A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) consists of states, an alphabet, a transition function, a start state and final states.
A non-deterministic automaton (NFA) may have several next states for the same symbol.
Every NFA can be turned into a DFA with the powerset construction; 4 states become at most 16.
Finite automata recognise exactly the regular languages.
No finite automaton can recognise the language of all words of the form a to the n, b to the n.
In a Mealy machine, the output depends on the state and on the symbol read.

abschnitte.text: Imagine a **drinks machine** that charges 2 francs per can. It is in a state such as “0 francs paid”, “1 franc paid” or “2 francs paid”. Each coin put in makes it switch to a new state, and when the amount is right it gives out the can. A **finite automaton** works in exactly this way: it has only a finite number of states and knows fixed rules for each change. But it has no other memory, so it only knows which state it is in at the moment.

A **deterministic finite automaton**, DFA for short, is described by five parts. These include the set of states, the **alphabet** of allowed symbols and the **transition function**, which says where to go for which symbol. Then there is a start state and a set of final states. If reading a word ends in a final state, the word is accepted. Automata are usually drawn as circles for states and arrows for transitions.

In a DFA, there is exactly one next state for every state and every symbol. A **non-deterministic automaton** (NFA), on the other hand, may have several possibilities. Surprisingly, both kinds can recognise exactly the same languages. With the **powerset construction**, an NFA is turned into a DFA, and n states become at most 2 to the power of n, so with 4 states, 16. Michael Rabin and Dana Scott described these ideas in 1959.

The sets of words that a finite automaton recognises are called **regular languages**. One example is the set of all binary numbers whose value is divisible by 3; for this a minimal DFA with 3 states is enough. Regular languages are closed under union and intersection, among other things, which is shown with a product automaton. The **Myhill-Nerode theorem** describes when a language is regular and gives the smallest possible automaton. The language of all words a to the n, b to the n, on the other hand, cannot be recognised by any finite automaton, because for this it would have to count arbitrarily far.

Finite automata are found in many devices, such as traffic lights, lift controls, washing machines and ticket machines. Programs use them to search for patterns in texts, for example with regular expressions. Compilers also use automata to split program code into individual words. If the automaton also produces output, it is called a **Mealy machine** when the output depends on the state and the symbol. In a Moore machine, by contrast, the output depends only on the state.

begriffe.erklaerung: The situation an automaton is in at the moment.
The set of all symbols the automaton can read.
A change from one state to another when a symbol is read.
A state in which a word is accepted as correct.
A set of words that a finite automaton can recognise.

gewusst: Michael Rabin and Dana Scott received the Turing Award in 1976 for their work on non-deterministic automata.
Many characters in video games are controlled by state machines, for instance with states such as “patrol”, “chase” and “flee”.
An automaton that checks binary numbers for divisibility by 3 needs only three states, however long the number is.

teile.einleitung: A filter bubble forms when websites and apps mainly show you content that fits your previous clicks and opinions. You then see more and more of the same and hardly notice other points of view. The term was coined by the American internet activist Eli Pariser.
wichtigste: The term filter bubble was coined by Eli Pariser in his book of 2011.
Filter bubbles form mainly because algorithms choose content according to previous clicks.
In an echo chamber, like-minded people confirm each other’s views.
Confirmation bias is the tendency to believe mainly information that supports your own opinion.
A danger for democracy is that other opinions are hardly noticed any more.
How strongly filter bubbles work is disputed in research.
The best help is to read different sources and opinions on purpose.

abschnitte.text: A **filter bubble** is like an invisible shell around each person on the internet. Search engines, social networks and video platforms remember what you click on, like and share and how long you look at something. From this they work out what you might like and show you more of it; this is called **personalisation**. So each person sees a slightly different internet.

The American **Eli Pariser** described the phenomenon in 2011 in his book “The Filter Bubble”. He noticed, for example, that different people got quite different results from the same Google search. His worry was that the programs decide, without us noticing, what we get to see. Since then the term has been used around the world.

The choice is made by **algorithms**, that is computer programs with fixed rules. Their aim is usually for you to stay on the platform as long as possible, because that is how it earns money from advertising. Anyone who watches a lot of football videos soon gets almost nothing but football suggested, and it works in the same way with opinions. On top of that comes **confirmation bias**: people prefer to click on things that support their own opinion.

Closely related is the **echo chamber**, a group in which like-minded people confirm each other’s views, like an echo that throws your own voice back at you. For **democracy** this can be a problem, because other opinions are hardly noticed any more and arguments become sharper. In Switzerland, where voters vote on issues several times a year, it is particularly important to know different arguments. However, researchers disagree about how strongly filter bubbles really work; some studies show that many people still use different sources.

Deliberately read different **sources**, for example several newspapers, radio and television, not only posts in one app. Also follow people or channels that have a different view, and listen to their arguments. In many apps you can reset recommendations or switch to a feed in time order. And ask yourself with every piece of news: who wrote this, and why am I seeing it right now?

begriffe.erklaerung: A situation in which you see almost only content online that fits your own preferences.
A program with fixed rules that, here, chooses which content you see.
A group in which like-minded people confirm each other’s views again and again.
The tendency to believe mainly what supports your own opinion.
Adapting content to the interests of an individual person.

gewusst: Two friends searching for the same word can see quite different results on their phones.
There are filter bubbles in real life too, for instance when you only talk to people who think the same way.
Some platforms do not show on their start page what is new, but what they think you will find particularly exciting.

teile.einleitung: Ransomware is a malicious program that encrypts data on a computer and then demands a ransom. The word is made up of the English “ransom” and “software”. Such extortion hits private individuals, companies, hospitals and municipalities.
wichtigste: Ransomware encrypts data and demands a ransom for decrypting it.
The ransom usually has to be paid in a cryptocurrency such as Bitcoin.
Ransomware often gets onto the computer through an infected email attachment.
If you notice an attack, you should disconnect the device from the network immediately.
Experts and authorities advise not to pay any ransom and to report the incident.
In double extortion, the criminals also threaten to publish stolen data.
In May 2017 the ransomware WannaCry paralysed hundreds of thousands of computers worldwide.
Regular backups are the best protection.

abschnitte.text: **Ransomware** is a particularly dangerous kind of malicious program. It **encrypts** photos, documents and other files so that you can no longer open them. Then a message appears demanding a ransom. The criminals promise to send the key if you pay. The money is usually demanded in a **cryptocurrency** such as Bitcoin, because it is harder to trace.

abschnitte.titel: How it gets onto the computer
abschnitte.text: Very often, ransomware comes through an infected **email attachment** that looks like an invoice or a parcel slip. Fake links, unsafe downloads and outdated software with security holes are also ways in. With companies, attackers sometimes use stolen passwords for remote access. The criminals are often part of well-organised gangs. Some even rent out their malicious software to other criminals.

Frequent victims are **hospitals** and **municipal administrations**, because they urgently depend on their data. The criminals hope that such victims will pay quickly. Schools, companies and private individuals are also attacked. In **double extortion**, the attackers also steal the data and threaten to publish it on the internet.
