In Switzerland, for example, the Bern software company Xplain was attacked in 2023, which also affected data of the federal administration.

The first known ransomware is considered to be a program from 1989 that was sent out on floppy disks. **WannaCry** became famous worldwide in May 2017. It spread by itself through a security hole in older versions of Windows. Within a few days, hundreds of thousands of computers in over 100 countries were affected. In Great Britain, hospitals had to postpone operations because their computers no longer worked.

abschnitte.titel: What to do in an attack?
abschnitte.text: If you notice that files are being encrypted, you should **disconnect** the device **from the network** immediately. This stops the malicious software spreading to other devices. Experts and authorities advise paying **no ransom**, because there is no guarantee that you will get the data back. You would also be financing further attacks. In Switzerland you can report incidents to the Federal Office for Cybersecurity NCSC and file a complaint with the police.

The most important protection is a regular **backup copy**. It should be kept separately from the computer, for example on an external hard drive that is not permanently connected. The operating system and programs should always be up to date. It is better not to open unknown attachments and links. An antivirus program also helps to recognise known malicious software.

begriffe.erklaerung: Money that extortionists demand in order to give something back.
Converting data so that it can only be read with a key.
A safety copy of data.
Digital money such as Bitcoin that works without a bank.

gewusst: WannaCry was slowed down because a young security researcher happened to find a built-in kill switch in the program.
For some ransomware there are free decryption programs, for example on the website “No More Ransom”.
Some ransomware gangs run their own help chats for their victims, like a customer service.

teile.einleitung: The lambda calculus is a mathematical model that describes what calculating with functions actually means. It was developed in the 1930s by Alonzo Church, even before there were real computers. Although it consists of only a few simple rules, you can use it to calculate everything a computer can calculate.
wichtigste: Alonzo Church developed the lambda calculus in the 1930s.
In the lambda calculus everything consists of variables, functions and applying functions.
Beta reduction puts an argument into a function, so (λx.x) y becomes y.
Alpha conversion is the renaming of bound variables.
Natural numbers are usually represented as Church numerals.
The Y combinator makes recursion possible even though functions have no names.
The programming language Lisp of 1958 was directly influenced by the lambda calculus.

abschnitte.text: The lambda calculus is a very small formal language. There are only three kinds of expressions: **variables** such as x, **abstractions** such as λx.x and **applications**, in which you apply a function to something. An abstraction is a function without a name. λx.x, for example, means “take x and give back x”, which is the identity function. The Greek letter lambda λ gave the calculus its name.

In the lambda calculus, calculating is done only by replacing. In **beta reduction**, you put the argument in everywhere the variable appears in the function. So (λx.x) y simply becomes y. **Alpha conversion** allows bound variables to be renamed, because λx.x and λz.z mean the same thing. If an expression cannot be simplified any further, it is in its **normal form**.

In the pure lambda calculus there are no built-in numbers. Even so, you can rebuild them with functions, the so-called **Church numerals**. The number 2 is a function that applies another function twice, and the number 3 applies it three times. In the same way you can represent truth values, pairs and operations such as addition. The **Y combinator** even allows functions that call themselves.

Not every calculation in the lambda calculus comes to an end. The famous expression (λx.x x)(λx.x x), usually called **Ω**, turns back into itself at every reduction. So it runs forever, much like a program in an endless loop. However, the **Church-Rosser theorem** says: if an expression has a normal form, it is unique. Whatever order you calculate in, you then get the same result.

The American mathematician **Alonzo Church** presented the lambda calculus in the 1930s at Princeton University. At about the same time, Alan Turing described his Turing machine. Later it turned out that both models can calculate exactly the same things. This led to the **Church-Turing thesis**: everything that can be calculated at all can be calculated with these models. Church, by the way, was Alan Turing's doctoral supervisor.

The lambda calculus is the basis of **functional programming**. In 1958 John McCarthy developed the programming language **Lisp**, which was directly influenced by it. Languages such as Haskell or OCaml are also built on it. Python, JavaScript and Java today have so-called lambda expressions for small functions without names. In Python, for example, you write lambda x: x * 2 for a function that doubles a number.

begriffe.erklaerung: A function without a name, written with λ, for example λx.x.
The calculation step in which an argument is put into a function.
An expression that cannot be simplified any further.
A way of representing a number as a function that applies another function as many times as the number says.
A lambda expression without free variables.

gewusst: In the lambda calculus there are really only functions, and yet you can solve any computable task with it.
The logo of the programming language Haskell contains a lambda symbol.
Alonzo Church was the doctoral supervisor of Alan Turing, one of the most famous computer scientists.

teile.einleitung: Git is a version control program with which you save all the changes to files step by step. In this way you can go back to an earlier version at any time and work on the same project with many people at once. Linus Torvalds developed Git in 2005, and today millions of programmers around the world use it.
wichtigste: Git is a distributed version control system.
Linus Torvalds, the creator of Linux, developed Git in 2005.
Before that, the Linux developers used the program BitKeeper.
With git add, changes go into the staging area; with git commit they are saved.
Branches make it possible to work on new ideas without disturbing the main version.
By default, Git identifies its objects with the hash function SHA-1.
The platform GitHub, where many Git projects are kept, was bought by Microsoft in 2018.

abschnitte.text: Git is a tool for **version control**. At every save point it remembers exactly what all the files of a project looked like. So later you can see who changed what and when, and you can undo mistakes. Git is **distributed**, which means that each person has a complete copy of the project with its whole history on their computer. That is why you can also work without an internet connection.

The developers of the Linux operating system first used the program **BitKeeper**. When its free use ended in 2005, **Linus Torvalds** wrote a program of his own within a few weeks: Git. It was meant to be fast, reliable and suitable for very large projects. Soon afterwards he handed over the lead to Junio Hamano, who has looked after Git ever since. Git is free software and may be used by everyone at no cost.

A project folder under Git control is called a **repository**. With git add you place changes in the **staging area**, a kind of preparation area. With git commit you save them as a new save point with a short description. The command git pull fetches changes from others, combining the steps fetch and merge; git push sends your own changes up. With git stash you put changes aside for a while without committing them.

A **branch** is a separate line of development. In it you can try out a new feature without putting the main version at risk. When the work is finished, the branch is brought back with a merge. **HEAD** is the pointer to the commit or branch that is currently checked out. In the file **.gitignore** you set which files Git should not track, for example temporary files.

Every commit receives a unique identifier, which Git calculates with the hash function **SHA-1**; newer versions also support SHA-256. Many projects are kept on platforms such as **GitHub** or GitLab, where people can manage and discuss code together. GitHub was founded in 2008 and bought by Microsoft in 2018. Today Git is by far the most widely used version control system. Texts, websites and scientific work are also managed with it.

begriffe.erklaerung: A project folder with all the files and their whole history.
A saved state of the project with a description.
A separate line of development, a branch in the project.
Bringing two lines of development together.
A calculation that turns data into a short, unique identifier.

gewusst: In Britain, “git” is a joking insult, and Torvalds said in fun that he names projects after himself.
The first version of Git was written in only about ten days.
Today Git manages huge projects such as the Linux kernel, with many thousands of contributors.

teile.einleitung: A robotic lawn mower is a small self-driving lawn mower that cuts the grass all by itself. It drives over the lawn, goes back to its charging station when its battery is low and then carries on mowing. It is practical, but it can be dangerous for animals such as the hedgehog.
wichtigste: A robotic lawn mower mows the lawn by itself.
Many robotic mowers recognise the edge of the lawn by a wire in the ground.
The sharp blades are on the underside.
The small cuttings stay on the lawn as fertiliser.
Robotic mowers usually go over the lawn a little almost every day.
In heavy rain, many go back to their charging station.
Hedgehogs in particular are at risk from robotic mowers at night.

abschnitte.titel: What is a robotic lawn mower?
abschnitte.text: A robotic lawn mower is a **robot** that mows the lawn without help from people. It runs on a **rechargeable battery** and drives to its charging station by itself to recharge. The blades are well protected on the underside. Usually they are small blades like razor blades on a rotating disc. One of the first robotic mowers for gardens came on the market in the 1990s.

abschnitte.titel: How does it find its way?
abschnitte.text: With many models, a **boundary wire** lies in the ground at the edge of the lawn. A weak signal flows through the wire, which the robot senses, so that it turns round. Newer devices find their way with precise **satellite navigation** or with cameras and no longer need a wire. Many drive criss-cross at random, others mow in neat strips. Sensors notice when the robot bumps into an obstacle.

A robotic mower usually goes over the lawn a little almost every day. Each time it only cuts off a few millimetres. The fine cuttings stay on the ground and serve as natural **fertiliser**; this is called **mulching**. That is why there is no grass to collect. In heavy rain, many robotic mowers go back to their charging station, because wet grass does not cut well.

The blades are very sharp, so small children must not play on or next to a robotic mower while it is running. If you lift the robot, the blades stop immediately thanks to a **lift sensor**. Even so, it should only be allowed to run under supervision when children or pets are in the garden. Many devices have a PIN lock against theft. They can often be controlled with an app on a mobile phone.

The **hedgehog** is out and about at dusk and at night, looking for beetles and worms in the grass. When in danger it does not run away but rolls up into a ball. As a result it is easily badly injured by robotic mowers that run at night. Nature conservation organisations in Switzerland therefore recommend only letting robotic mowers run during the day. A wild corner with long grass also helps hedgehogs, insects and other animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wire in the ground that shows the robotic mower where the lawn ends.
Leaving finely cut grass on the ground as a natural fertiliser.
The place where the robot charges its battery.
A component that measures something, for example whether the robot is being lifted.

gewusst: When in danger, a hedgehog rolls up instead of running away and so cannot get out of the way of a robotic mower.
Because a robotic mower only cuts a little each day, the lawn often becomes thicker than with occasional mowing.
Robotic mowers are much quieter than petrol lawn mowers because they run on electricity from the battery.

teile.einleitung: A decision tree is a model that breaks a decision down into a series of simple yes-or-no questions. You start at the top at the root and, depending on the answer, follow a branch until you reach a leaf with the result. In machine learning, a computer learns such trees by itself from example data.
wichtigste: A decision tree consists of a root, branches and leaves.
In classification, the leaves contain the predicted class.
The ID3 algorithm chooses the feature with the greatest information gain.
A node with equal numbers of examples of two classes has an entropy of 1 bit.
With 3 examples of class A and 1 of class B, the Gini impurity is 0.375.
In pruning, branches that are not very useful are removed.
Random forest and gradient boosting combine many trees.

abschnitte.text: A decision tree is usually drawn upside down, with the **root** at the top. At each inner **node** there is a question about a feature, for example “Is it raining?”. Depending on the answer, you follow a different branch downwards. At the end you land in a **leaf**, which in classification contains the predicted class, such as “take the bike” or “take the bus”. In this way every decision can be followed as a path from the root to a leaf.

In **machine learning**, an algorithm builds the tree from example data. For each node, it looks for the question that best splits the examples into groups that are as pure as possible. The classic **ID3 algorithm** by Ross Quinlan from the 1980s chooses the feature with the greatest **information gain**. Other well-known methods are C4.5 and CART. The splitting is repeated until the groups are pure enough.

How mixed a group is can be measured, for example, with **entropy**. If a node contains equal numbers of examples of two classes, the entropy is 1 bit, which is the greatest possible disorder with two classes. Another measure is the **Gini impurity**: you subtract the squares of the class shares from 1. With 3 examples of class A and 1 of class B, this gives 1 minus 0.5625 minus 0.0625, which is 0.375. A node with only one class has an impurity of 0.

A very deep tree can learn the training data by heart, including random exceptions. Then it makes more mistakes with new data; this is called **overfitting**. What helps against it is **pruning**, in which branches that are not very useful are removed afterwards. You can also limit the depth of the tree from the start.

A **random forest** combines many decision trees that are trained on random subsets of the data and features. At the end the trees vote, and the majority decides. In **gradient boosting**, trees are built one after another, with each new tree correcting the mistakes of the ones before. Such methods are among the most accurate methods for table data.

A big advantage of decision trees is that their decisions are easy for people to **follow**. With deep neural networks this is much harder. That is why decision trees are used, for instance, in medicine, in banks or in quality control. They also help without a computer, for example as identification keys for plants or as a flow chart in an emergency.

begriffe.erklaerung: A place in the tree where a question is asked.
An end point of a decision tree with the result.
A measure of how mixed a group of examples is.
A model learns training data by heart and fails with new data.
Sorting things into fixed groups, called classes.

gewusst: Identification keys for plants and animals are really decision trees on paper.
In German, a random forest is called a “Zufallswald”, a forest of chance.
A decision tree with only one single question is called a decision stump in English, like the stump of a tree.

teile.einleitung: In theoretical computer science, a formal language is a set of words formed from the characters of a fixed alphabet. Formal languages are used to describe exactly how programming languages are built and what computers can recognise at all.
wichtigste: An alphabet is a finite, non-empty set of characters, such as {a, b}.
A word is a finite sequence of characters from the alphabet.
Σ* denotes the set of all words over the alphabet Σ.
A formal language over Σ is a subset of Σ*.
The empty word ε has length 0.
Concatenation joins words together: “ab” and “ba” become “abba”.
There are languages that no Turing machine can recognise.

abschnitte.text: In the theory of formal languages, an **alphabet** is a finite, non-empty set of characters. It is often written with the Greek letter Σ, for example Σ = {a, b}. A **word** is a finite sequence of characters from this alphabet, such as “abba” or “b”. The length of a word is the number of its characters. The **empty word** ε consists of no characters at all and therefore has length 0.

The set of all words over Σ is written as Σ*, and it is infinitely large. A **formal language** is simply a subset of Σ*, that is a selection of words. One example is the language of all **palindromes** over {a, b}, all words that read the same forwards and backwards, such as “aba” or “abba”. Another example is the language of all words of even length. All valid Python programs together also form a formal language.

You can calculate with words. **Concatenation** joins two words together, so “ab” with “ba” gives the word “abba”. For a language L, L* denotes all words that can be formed by joining together any number of words from L, including zero words. This is called the Kleene star, after the mathematician Stephen Kleene. You can also count: over {a, b} there are 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 words with at most 3 characters, counting the empty word.

To describe a language, you often use a **grammar**, that is rules for how words are formed. In the 1950s the American linguist Noam Chomsky arranged grammars according to their power. This arrangement is now called the **Chomsky hierarchy**. Among the simplest languages are the regular languages, which can be recognised by finite automata. Programming languages are usually described with context-free grammars.

A **Turing machine** is an imagined model of a computer that Alan Turing described in 1936. Every Turing machine can be described by a finite text, so there are only countably many of them. Formal languages, on the other hand, are uncountably many, that is “more” than can be numbered one by one. That is why there must be languages that no Turing machine recognises. This insight shows that computers too have fundamental limits.

begriffe.erklaerung: A finite, non-empty set of characters from which words are formed.
The word with no characters, written ε, with length 0.
Joining two words together.
Rules that set out which words belong to a language.
An imagined, very simple model of a computer.

gewusst: If a program has a typing mistake, the computer notices because the text does not belong to the formal language of the programming language.
Formal languages are also used to describe genetic sequences made of the four letters A, C, G and T.
The search function of many programs uses regular expressions, which come directly from the theory of formal languages.

teile.einleitung: In a relational database, a foreign key is a column that refers to a record in another table. In this way tables can be linked with each other, for example pupils with their courses.
wichtigste: A foreign key refers to the primary key or a unique column of a table.
Referential integrity means that every foreign key value refers to an existing record.
If the relationship is optional, a foreign key column may contain NULL.
With ON DELETE CASCADE, dependent records are deleted as well when a record is deleted.
Without a deletion rule, the database system refuses to delete a record that is still referred to.
A foreign key can also refer to the same table.
With JOIN you link tables through foreign and primary keys.

abschnitte.text: A **relational database** stores data in tables with rows and columns. Each row is a record, for example a pupil. So that every record can be identified clearly, the table has a **primary key**, such as a number like pupil_id. A **foreign key** is a column in another table that contains exactly such numbers. In this way the database knows which record belongs to which.

A table “Class” contains the classes with the number class_id. In the table “Pupil”, the class_id of each child’s class is stored as a foreign key. For a **many-to-many relationship**, in which many pupils attend many courses, you need a linking table, such as “Enrolment”. It contains the foreign keys pupil_id and course_id, which together form its primary key. In the database language SQL, such tables are linked with the command **JOIN**.

The database makes sure that a foreign key does not point to nothing. This rule is called **referential integrity**: every foreign key value must refer to an existing record. In SQL a foreign key may only refer to a primary key or a unique column. If a relationship is optional, the column may also contain NULL, which means “no value”. A pupil without a fixed course would then, for example, have NULL entered.

If you want to delete a record that foreign keys still refer to, the database system refuses by default. In this way no links are broken by accident. With the option **ON DELETE CASCADE** you can specify that dependent records are automatically deleted as well. With ON DELETE SET NULL, the foreign key is set to NULL instead. Which rule fits depends on the task.

A foreign key can also point to the same table. In a table “Employee”, each person has a column manager_id, which again refers to an employee. In this way a whole **organisation chart** can be stored in a single table. The relational model on which all this is based was presented by the computer scientist **Edgar F. Codd** in 1970. Today almost all banks, online shops and school administrations use such databases.

begriffe.erklaerung: A column that clearly identifies each record in a table.
A column that refers to the key of a record in a table.
The rule that every reference points to an existing record.
A language used to query and change databases.
A special value in databases that means “no value present”.

gewusst: Without foreign keys, you would have to store the same details, such as the name of a class, again for every single pupil.
Orders in an online shop are linked to customers and items through foreign keys.
The word relational comes from relation, which in mathematics means a table of relationships.

teile.einleitung: NP-complete problems are among the most difficult tasks known to computers. A finished solution can be checked quickly, but nobody knows a fast method for finding one. Anyone who could solve a single one of these problems quickly would have solved all of them at a stroke.
wichtigste: An NP-complete problem lies in the class NP, and every NP problem can be reduced to it in polynomial time.
In 1971 the Boolean satisfiability problem (SAT) was shown to be the first NP-complete problem.
In 1972 Richard Karp published a famous list of 21 NP-complete problems.
If a polynomial-time algorithm were found for a single NP-complete problem, P would equal NP.
The halting problem is NP-hard but not NP-complete.
The question of whether there is a cycle that visits every node of a graph exactly once is NP-complete.

abschnitte.text: In computer science, problems are sorted into **complexity classes** according to how much computing time they need. The class **NP** contains problems whose solutions can be checked quickly. A problem is **NP-complete** if it lies in NP itself and every other NP problem can be reduced to it. So it is at least as hard as any other problem in NP.

The most important tool is called **reduction**. You translate a problem A into a problem B, and so quickly that the translation only needs polynomial time. If you can then solve B, you have automatically solved A as well. To show that a new problem is NP-complete, you usually reduce an already known NP-complete problem to it.

In 1971 the computer scientist **Stephen Cook** proved that the satisfiability problem **SAT** is NP-complete. Independently, Leonid Levin in the Soviet Union reached the same result, which is why it is called the Cook-Levin theorem. In 1972 **Richard Karp** showed that 21 other well-known problems are NP-complete as well. Since then, thousands of such problems have been found.

One example is the question of whether a graph has a cycle that visits every node exactly once, the so-called **Hamiltonian cycle**. Colouring a map with only three colours and the **knapsack problem** also belong to this group. 3-SAT is interesting, in which each clause has three literals: it is NP-complete, whereas 2-SAT can be solved in P. The knapsack problem is considered “weakly” NP-complete, because it can be solved in pseudo-polynomial time with dynamic programming.

abschnitte.titel: NP-hard is not the same thing
abschnitte.text: A problem is called **NP-hard** if it is at least as hard as all NP problems but does not itself have to lie in NP. The famous **halting problem** is such a case. It asks whether a program will ever stop, and it cannot be solved at all. That is why it is NP-hard but not NP-complete.

Many practical tasks such as timetables, route planning for delivery vans or packing containers are NP-complete. For large cases you therefore usually cannot calculate a perfect solution in a reasonable time. Instead, people use **approximation methods** or rules of thumb that quickly give a good but not necessarily the best solution. Even so, modern SAT solvers often manage surprisingly large tasks.

begriffe.erklaerung: The computing time only grows moderately when the task gets bigger.
A problem is translated into another one so that it can be solved with it.
The question of whether variables can be set to true and false in such a way that a logical formula is true.
A network of points (nodes) connected by lines (edges).

gewusst: Even popular puzzles such as generalised sudokus on grids of any size are NP-complete.
The standard book on the subject by Michael Garey and David Johnson from 1979 already lists about 300 NP-complete problems.
Nobody knows for certain to this day whether NP-complete problems really can never be solved quickly.

teile.einleitung: HTML is the language in which websites are built. It tells the browser what is a heading, a paragraph, a picture or a link. Almost every page on the internet that you look at consists at its core of HTML.
wichtigste: HTML stands for Hypertext Markup Language.
HTML is a markup language and not a programming language.
HTML was invented by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in Geneva.
A typical HTML file has the extension .html.
A modern HTML5 document usually begins with <!DOCTYPE html>.
Between <body> and </body> is the visible content of the page.
A simple text editor is enough to write HTML.

abschnitte.text: HTML is a **markup language**. This means that texts are given markings that set out their meaning. The **browser** reads these markings and uses them to build the page on the screen. The word “hypertext” means texts that are connected with each other by **links**.

The markings are called **tags** and are written in angle brackets. Usually there is a start tag and an end tag, for example

and

for a paragraph.

stands for a big heading, for a link and for a picture. Together with the content between them they form an **element**.

A modern document begins with the line <!DOCTYPE html>. After that comes the element <html>, which encloses everything. In the **head** between <head> and </head> there is information such as the title of the page. In the **body** between <body> and </body> is everything that you see on the page.

The British physicist **Tim Berners-Lee** developed HTML from 1989 onwards at the research centre **CERN** near Geneva. He wanted researchers to be able to exchange and link their documents easily. Together with HTTP and the first web browser, this is how the **World Wide Web** came about. Today HTML keeps being developed further; the current form is called HTML5.

HTML only sets out what is on a page and how it is structured. **CSS** takes care of colours, fonts and layout. For a page to move or react to clicks, **JavaScript** is needed. These three languages work together on almost every modern website.

begriffe.erklaerung: A language that gives texts markings to set out their meaning.

A marking in angle brackets, for example

for a paragraph.
A program for looking at websites, for example Firefox, Chrome or Safari.
A clickable reference that leads to another page or place.

gewusst: The very first website in the world went online at CERN in 1991 and can still be visited today.
In almost every browser you can right-click and choose “View page source” to see the HTML of a page.
The page you are reading right now is also built with HTML.

teile.einleitung: Quicksort is one of the best-known and fastest methods for sorting a list. It chooses one element as the “pivot” and divides the other elements into smaller and larger ones. These parts are then sorted further in the same way until everything is in order.
wichtigste: Quicksort was invented by the British computer scientist Tony Hoare around 1960.
The method divides the list into smaller and larger values using a pivot element.
On average, quicksort has the running time O(n log n).
If you always take the first element as the pivot, the worst case occurs with data that is already sorted.
The usual version of quicksort is not stable.
For the recursion stack, quicksort needs O(log n) extra memory on average.
A random pivot or the median of three elements makes the worst case unlikely.
Introsort starts with quicksort and switches to heapsort if the recursion gets too deep.

abschnitte.text: Quicksort was developed by **Tony Hoare**, a British computer scientist. He had the idea around 1959, when he was working on machine translation in Moscow and had to sort words. The method was published in 1961. Hoare later received the Turing Award, the highest honour in computer science. Quicksort is still used in many programming languages today.

First you choose an element of the list, the **pivot element**. All smaller elements go to the left, all larger ones to the right. This step is called **partitioning**. Then you sort the left and the right half in exactly the same way. Because the method calls itself, it is an example of **recursion** and of the principle of “divide and conquer”.

Take the list 7, 3, 9, 1, 5, 2 and choose 3 as the pivot. Only 1 and 2 are smaller than 3, so 2 elements end up on the left. On the right are 7, 9 and 5. Now the left group and the right group are each sorted on their own. At the end you get 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 9.

On average, quicksort needs about n times log n steps, written **O(n log n)**. That is much faster than simple methods such as bubble sort. In the worst case, however, it needs about n times n steps. This happens, for example, if you always take the first element as the pivot and the list is already sorted. Then the pivot is the smallest element every time, and the list is divided very unevenly.

To avoid the worst case, the pivot is chosen cleverly. One possibility is the **median of three**, that is, the middle value of the first, middle and last element. Another is a randomly chosen pivot, so that no particular input is always unfavourable. The **introsort** method even switches to heapsort if the recursion gets too deep. Introsort is often used in the C++ standard library, among others.

Quicksort sorts directly in the list and needs only a little extra memory, on average O(log n) for the recursion stack. In practice it is often faster than other methods with the same running time. But the usual version is not **stable**. This means that elements of equal size can lose their original order. If stability is important, you use merge sort, for example.

begriffe.erklaerung: The comparison element at which the list is divided.
Dividing the list into smaller and larger elements.
A way of writing that shows how strongly the computing time grows with the amount of data.
A sorting method is stable if equal elements keep their order.

gewusst: Tony Hoare was born in 1934 in Colombo in Sri Lanka.
Hoare chose the name “quicksort” himself, and it simply means “quick sorting”.
There are videos in which folk dancers dance out quicksort and other sorting methods.

teile.einleitung: A search engine for children is a search engine made especially for children. It only shows websites that have been checked by experts beforehand. This way children can search the internet and hardly ever come across content that is not suitable for them.
wichtigste: A search engine for children only shows checked pages.
Experts on children and media check the pages.
Well-known search engines for children are fragFINN, Blinde Kuh and Helles Köpfchen.
You type a search word into the search engine.
The results appear in the list of results.
Search engines for children usually show fewer results than normal search engines.
If you find something strange, you show it to an adult.

abschnitte.titel: What is a search engine for children?
abschnitte.text: Normal **search engines** search billions of websites, including many that are not suitable for children. A search engine for children only searches a selected list of pages, a so-called **allow list** or whitelist. These pages have been checked beforehand. This makes searching much safer for children.

The pages are looked at by **experts** on children and media, for example media educators. They make sure that the content is understandable, suitable for the age group and free of dangerous material. Too much advertising can also be a reason not to include a page. That is why there are fewer results, but the results are more suitable.

In German-speaking countries, **fragFINN**, **Blinde Kuh** and Helles Köpfchen are well known. Blinde Kuh is one of the oldest search engines for children and started back in the 1990s. These services come from Germany but can also be used well by children in Switzerland. Some search engines for children also offer knowledge articles, games or news for children.

Type a suitable **search word** into the search box, for example “hedgehog” or “volcano”. After searching, the **list of results** appears with titles and short descriptions. Read through them quickly and click on the result that fits best. If you find nothing, try a different or more precise word.

Even a search engine for children is not perfect, because websites can change. If you find something strange or unpleasant, show it to an **adult**. Never give away your name, your address or photos of yourself on the internet. As you get older, you gradually learn to use normal search engines critically and safely too.

begriffe.erklaerung: A program on the internet that finds websites for a search word.
The list of results that appears after a search.
A list of checked, permitted websites, also called a whitelist.
The word you type into a search engine.

gewusst: The name Blinde Kuh comes from the German name of the well-known children's game blind man's buff, where you search with your eyes covered.
A search engine for children only searches a tiny fraction of the whole internet.
Many schools set a search engine for children as the home page on school computers.

teile.einleitung: In the shortest path problem, you look in a network of points and connections for the shortest or cheapest route from one place to another. Navigation apps solve exactly this task when they show you the fastest route. The best-known method of solving it is the algorithm of the Dutch computer scientist Edsger W. Dijkstra.
wichtigste: In computer science, a network of points and connections is called a graph.
The weight of an edge tells you how long or expensive a connection is.
The shortest path is the one with the smallest sum of weights, not the one with the fewest edges.
Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest paths from a starting point.
Edsger W. Dijkstra came from the Netherlands.
Dijkstra does not work reliably with negative edge weights.
The A* algorithm also uses an estimate of the remaining distance.
In a network without weights, breadth-first search finds the path with the fewest edges.

abschnitte.text: A road network, a railway network or a computer network can be shown as a **graph**. The places are called **nodes**, the connections between them **edges**. Each edge has a weight, for example the length in kilometres or the travel time in minutes. What you are looking for is the route with the smallest sum of these weights.

From A to B it is 4 km, from B to C 3 km, from A to C 9 km, from C to D 2 km and from B to D 8 km. The direct route A, C, D is 11 km long, and the route A, B, D is even 12 km. The route A, B, C, D has more edges, but at 9 km it is the shortest. This shows: it is not the number of edges that counts but the **sum of the weights**.

The Dutchman **Edsger W. Dijkstra** published his method in 1959. The algorithm starts at the starting point and always takes the unfinished node with the smallest known distance. From there it checks whether other places can be reached more quickly via this node. It only works reliably if there are no **negative weights**; for that case there is the Bellman-Ford algorithm.

If all the edges have the same weight, **breadth-first search** is enough: it first examines all the neighbours, then their neighbours and so on. The **A* algorithm** of 1968 also uses an estimate of the remaining distance, for example the straight-line distance to the destination. This lets it search specifically in the direction of the destination, and it is often much faster than Dijkstra. A* is often used in computer games so that game characters can find their way.

Navigation apps and route planners such as the SBB online timetable are constantly calculating shortest or fastest routes. On the internet, **routers** look for the best route for data packets. Parcel services also plan their delivery rounds with such methods. With very large networks such as the European road network, clever precalculations are used as well so that the answer is there in a fraction of a second.

begriffe.erklaerung: A network of nodes and edges.
A point in the graph, for example a place.
A connection between two nodes.
A number on an edge, such as length or travel time.
Exact step-by-step instructions for solving a problem.

gewusst: Dijkstra is said to have thought up his famous algorithm in about twenty minutes on a café terrace in Amsterdam, without pen and paper.
The shortest route does not have to be the fastest, because a longer motorway is often quicker than a short mountain road.
Computer game characters also use shortest-path algorithms to walk round obstacles.

teile.einleitung: An IP address is a number that makes every device in a network such as the internet uniquely identifiable. It works much like a postal address: only if you know it does data arrive at the right place. There are two kinds, the older IPv4 and the newer IPv6.
wichtigste: Every device on the internet needs an IP address.
An IPv4 address consists of 4 numbers separated by dots.
Each of these numbers is between 0 and 255.
Addresses such as 192.168.1.5 are private addresses for home networks.
IPv6 was introduced because IPv4 addresses were running out.
The blocks of an IPv6 address are separated by colons.
In a home network, the DHCP service hands out IP addresses automatically.
The address 127.0.0.1 always stands for your own computer.

abschnitte.text: IP stands for **Internet Protocol**, the basic rule for how data is sent on the internet. Data travels in small packets, and each packet carries the address of the sender and of the recipient. These addresses are the **IP addresses**. Without them, the routers on the internet would not know where to send a packet next.

An **IPv4 address** consists of four numbers separated by dots, for example 192.168.0.15. Each number is between 0 and 255, because it is stored in exactly 8 bits. So an IPv4 address has 32 bits in total. This means there are only about 4.3 billion different addresses, and that is too few for the whole world.

Because IPv4 addresses were running out, **IPv6** was developed. An IPv6 address is 128 bits long and is written in blocks separated by **colons**. It also contains letters from a to f, because it is written in the base-16 system. With IPv6 there are so unimaginably many addresses that every grain of sand on Earth could get several.

At home, usually only the **router** gets a public address on the internet. The devices behind it, such as a mobile phone, laptop or games console, get **private addresses**, often beginning with 192.168. The router hands these out automatically with the **DHCP** service. The special address 127.0.0.1 is called localhost and always means your own computer.

Nobody wants to remember long strings of numbers. That is why there is the **Domain Name System**, DNS for short, which works like a telephone directory. When you type in a name such as a web address, DNS looks up the matching IP address. Only then can your browser load the website.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number by which a device in a network is uniquely identified.
A device that forwards data packets between networks, for example between a home network and the internet.
A service that automatically assigns an IP address to devices on the network.
A system that translates website names into IP addresses.

gewusst: IPv6 offers about 340 undecillion addresses, a number with 39 digits.
The address 127.0.0.1 exists on every computer, and it always leads back to that computer itself.
Many devices in your household share the same public IP address of the router on the internet.

teile.einleitung: Packet switching is the way data is sent on the internet. A message is split into many small packets, which travel through the network individually. At the destination the packets are put back together again.
wichtigste: With packet switching, data is split into small packets and sent individually.
The counterpart is circuit switching, with a fixed, reserved channel.
In the 1960s the Briton Donald Davies coined the term “packet”.
The ARPANET of 1969 used packet switching and is considered the forerunner of the internet.
Packets can take different routes and arrive in a different order.
With store-and-forward, a node receives a packet completely and then passes it on.
The usual maximum payload (MTU) with Ethernet is 1,500 bytes.

abschnitte.text: With **packet switching**, a large message, such as a photo, is divided into many small **data packets**. Each packet gets a kind of address label with the sender, the recipient and a number. The packets then travel through the network individually, via many intermediate stations. At the destination, the computer puts them back together in the right order.

In the past, the telephone network worked with **circuit switching**. A fixed channel between two telephones was reserved for the whole call, even when nobody was speaking. With packet switching, on the other hand, many users share the same lines. This makes much better use of the network and makes it more robust if a line fails.

Special devices, the **routers**, look at the address of each packet and send it on. They often work on the **store-and-forward** principle: first the packet is received completely, then passed on. Because packets can take different routes, they sometimes arrive in a different order. Protocols such as TCP then sort them again and request lost packets once more.

An Ethernet frame normally carries at most 1,500 bytes of payload; this is called the **MTU**. Sending such a packet over a line with 12 Mbit/s takes 1 millisecond, because 1,500 bytes are 12,000 bits. If an IPv4 packet is larger than the MTU of the next line and splitting is not forbidden, it is divided into **fragments**. The recipient then puts these parts back together.

In the 1960s two researchers thought about this idea independently of each other: **Paul Baran** in the USA and **Donald Davies** in Great Britain. Davies coined the English term “packet”. In 1969 the **ARPANET** went into operation in the USA, the first larger network with packet switching. Today's internet later developed from it.

Today almost all data transmission uses packet switching, from emails and videos to online games. Phone calls are now also mostly transmitted as data packets. In Switzerland, Swisscom switched the old analogue landline network to internet telephony by around 2018. The idea from the 1960s is therefore the basis of modern communication.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small piece of a message with address details.
A device that forwards packets between networks.
The largest packet size that fits over a line in one go.
A unit of data; one byte consists of 8 bits.

gewusst: Paul Baran wanted to design a network that would still work even if many nodes failed.
The first message on the ARPANET was supposed to be “LOGIN”, but after the letters “LO” the system crashed.
A single photo from a mobile phone is often split into thousands of packets before it is sent.

teile.einleitung: The pigpen cipher, also called the Freemasons’ cipher, is a simple secret script in which each letter is replaced by a sign made of lines and dots. The signs come from a noughts and crosses grid and an X, and today you often come across the code in puzzles.
wichtigste: The signs are made of the lines and dots of grids.
The basic shapes are a grid like the one for noughts and crosses and an X.
A noughts and crosses grid has 9 squares.
Dots tell apart letters with the same grid shape.
In English the code is called pigpen, because the signs look like little pens for pigs.
In the 18th century the Freemasons often used it.
The code is not secure encryption and is easy to crack.

abschnitte.titel: What the secret script looks like
abschnitte.text: In the **pigpen cipher**, each letter is replaced by a small geometric sign. First you draw the basic shapes: a grid like the one for **noughts and crosses** with 9 squares and a big X with 4 spaces. You write the letters into the spaces in order. The sign for a letter is then exactly the shape of the lines around its space. In the end, a word looks like a row of corners, boxes and angles.

Because the alphabet has 26 letters, one grid and one X are not enough. That is why you draw each basic shape twice, once without and once with **dots** in the spaces. The dots therefore tell apart letters that would otherwise have the same grid shape. This gives 9 + 9 + 4 + 4 = 26 signs. There are, however, different versions of how the letters are shared out among the spaces.

The Freemasons are an association whose members meet in what are called **lodges**. In the 18th century they often used this grid code, for instance for notes. That is how it got its German name, which means Freemasons’ alphabet. In English it is called **pigpen**, because the signs look like little enclosures for pigs. Similar grid scripts are probably even older, though.

The pigpen cipher is a **substitution**, which means that each letter is always replaced by the same sign. Codes like this are easy to crack. You simply count which sign appears most often, because in English, as in German, that is usually the letter E. This method is called **frequency analysis**. For real secrets the code is therefore not safe; today mathematical methods on the computer are used for that.

Today you often come across the pigpen cipher in **escape rooms**, treasure hunts and puzzle books. Children like to use it to write secret messages to friends. The code also sometimes turns up as a puzzle in computer games and films. It is a nice way into **cryptography**, the science of encryption. Once you know it, you can draw it from memory without any help.

begriffe.erklaerung: A script that only people who know the key can read.
An encryption in which each letter is replaced by another sign.
A method of cracking codes by counting which signs appear most often.
The science of encrypting messages.

gewusst: The English name pigpen refers to a pen for pigs, because the signs look like small enclosures.
You do not need a table to decode it if you remember the grids.
On some old gravestones in the USA there are inscriptions in this grid code.

teile.einleitung: Merge sort is a sorting method that keeps halving a list, sorts the small parts and then cleverly merges them together. The name comes from the English word “merge”, meaning to combine. Merge sort is fast and reliable even with very large amounts of data.
wichtigste: John von Neumann presented merge sort in 1945.
Merge sort splits a list until only single elements are left.
A list with 1,024 elements has to be halved 10 times for this.
Two sorted lists of 4 elements each are merged with at most 7 comparisons.
Merge sort is stable, so equal keys keep their order.
When sorting an array, merge sort usually needs O(n) extra memory.
With Timsort, Python uses a method that combines merge sort with insertion sort.

abschnitte.text: Merge sort is a **sorting algorithm**, that is, a set of instructions for putting data in order. It works on the principle of **divide and conquer**. A big, difficult task is broken down into smaller, simple tasks. At the end the partial solutions are put back together. The Hungarian-American mathematician **John von Neumann** presented the method in 1945.

First merge sort halves the list, then halves each half again, and so on. In the end only single elements are left, and a list with one element is automatically sorted. With 1,024 elements you have to halve 10 times, because 2 to the power of 10 is 1,024. With a million elements it is only about 20 halvings. This number of levels grows with the **logarithm** of the length of the list.

Then the parts are merged step by step. Each time you compare the front elements of the two sorted lists and take the smaller one first. In this way 1, 4, 7 and 2, 3, 9 become the list 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 9. For two lists of 4 elements each you need at most 7 comparisons, because after each comparison one element is fixed and the last one falls into place by itself. This combining is called **merge** in English.

Merge sort always needs about n times log n steps, written **O(n log n)**. This applies in the best as well as the worst case. Simple methods such as bubble sort, on the other hand, need O(n²) steps for large lists and are then much slower. One disadvantage of merge sort is the extra memory. When sorting an array, it usually needs as much space again as the data itself, that is O(n).

Merge sort is a **stable** sorting method. If two entries have the same sorting key, their original order is kept. If you sort a class list first by name and then stably by mark, children with the same mark are still in alphabetical order. Because merge sort reads the data in sequence, it is particularly well suited to very large files on **storage media**. Such files often do not fit completely into the main memory.

The programming language Python uses **Timsort**, which Tim Peters developed in 2002. Timsort combines merge sort with insertion sort and takes advantage of the fact that real data is often already partly sorted. Java also sorts lists of objects with Timsort. Quicksort is another well-known fast method that manages without much extra memory. Merge sort is one of the standard examples in computer science lessons.

begriffe.erklaerung: Step-by-step instructions for putting data in order.
A strategy in which you break a problem down into smaller parts and solve them.
Equal entries keep their original order when sorted.
The number that tells you how often you have to halve a number until 1 is left.

gewusst: Merge sort is older than almost all programming languages, because John von Neumann described it as early as 1945.
With a million numbers, merge sort needs only about 20 million comparisons, but a simple O(n²) method needs up to a trillion.
You can easily try out merge sort yourself with playing cards by putting small sorted piles together.

teile.einleitung: Influencers are people who have lots of fans on social networks such as Instagram, TikTok or YouTube. With their photos and videos they influence what others think, buy or find beautiful. For many of them it is a job that earns them money.
wichtigste: The English word “influence” means “Einfluss” in German.
A follower is someone who follows an account on a social network.
Many influencers earn money by advertising for companies.
Paid posts must be labelled as advertising.
With product placement, a product is shown clearly in return for payment.
Micro-influencers have a smaller but loyal fan base.
Fake followers are bought or automated accounts that pretend someone is popular.

abschnitte.text: An **influencer** is a person who regularly publishes content on the internet and reaches lots of people with it. Typical topics are fashion, make-up, sport, travel, food, video games or animals. The fans are called **followers**, because they follow the account and see new posts. Some influencers have a few thousand followers, others several million.

Many influencers work together with companies, which is called a **collaboration**. The company pays money or gives products, and the influencer shows them in videos or photos. With **product placement**, a product is built into a post where it is easy to see. On YouTube, well-known channels also get part of the income from the adverts shown before the videos.

If a post is paid for, this must be clearly visible, for example with “Advert” or “Ad”. This way you can tell **advertising** apart from an honest opinion. In Switzerland, the Swiss Commission for Fairness in Advertising, among others, makes sure that advertising does not deceive people. Hidden advertising is considered unfair to viewers.

Influencers are divided into different groups according to the number of followers. **Micro-influencers** have a few thousand followers, who are often especially loyal to them. Big stars with millions of fans reach a huge number of people at once. Small influencers are interesting for companies because their fans often trust them a lot.

Not everything influencers show is real. Many photos are edited or improved with filters, and the perfect life is often staged. Some even buy **fake followers** to seem more popular than they are. So it is worth asking: who is earning money here, and is it really true?

begriffe.erklaerung: Someone who follows an account and sees its posts.
Cooperation between an influencer and a company in return for money or products.
A product is built clearly into a post in return for payment.
Internet platforms such as Instagram or TikTok where people share content.
An effect that changes photos or videos and often makes them look nicer.

gewusst: For many young people, “influencer” is a dream job today, but only a few can really make a living from it.
Animals such as dogs or cats also have their own accounts with millions of followers.
Some influencers work with a whole team of camera operators, video editors and managers.

teile.einleitung: The internet is a worldwide network of billions of computers, mobile phones and other devices that exchange data with each other. Through the internet we write messages, watch videos, look for information and learn. It began in 1969 as a small research network in the USA and today it is hard to imagine everyday life without it.
wichtigste: The internet connects computers all over the world.
Its forerunner is the ARPANET, which started in the USA in 1969.
The World Wide Web is a service that uses the internet.
Every website has an address, the URL, for example https://www.admin.ch.
Swiss internet addresses often end in .ch.
With a search engine you can find content on the internet.
You do not give strangers on the internet personal details such as your address.
If something on the internet frightens you, you tell an adult.

abschnitte.text: The **internet** is a network of many smaller networks that all use the same rules, the **protocols**. Data is split into small packets and sent to its destination along different routes. The connections run over copper cables, fibre-optic cables, radio and even cables on the seabed. At the end of 2024, about 5.5 billion people worldwide were using the internet.

In 1969 the **ARPANET** in the USA connected a few university computers for the first time. In the 1970s, Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn developed the TCP/IP rules that still hold the internet together today. In 1989 Tim Berners-Lee invented the **World Wide Web** at CERN in Geneva, and in 1991 the first website went online. From the mid-1990s the internet came into many homes.

The internet and the web are not the same thing. The internet is the network; the **World Wide Web** is a service on it that connects web pages with links. Email, video calls and online games also use the internet but are not the web. Every website has a **URL**, a complete address such as https://www.admin.ch.

abschnitte.titel: How you get onto the internet
abschnitte.text: At home, a **router** connects the devices to the internet, often wirelessly via **Wi-Fi**. When you are out and about, your mobile phone uses the mobile network. With the browser you open websites, and with a **search engine** you find content on a keyword. Addresses from Switzerland often end in .ch; this ending is managed by the SWITCH foundation on behalf of the Confederation.

On the internet the rule is: you do not give strangers personal details such as your **address**, phone number and passwords. Not everything on the internet is true, so it is worth checking information. If something frightens you or seems strange, you talk to an adult you trust. In Switzerland, the number 147 from Pro Juventute also helps, free of charge and around the clock.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fixed rule for how computers exchange data.
A device that connects your home network to the internet.
A wireless network without cables that lets devices get onto the internet.
The complete address of a website.
A service that finds websites for a search term.

gewusst: The first message on the ARPANET was supposed to be “LOGIN”, but after the letters “LO” the system crashed.
A large part of the world's data traffic runs through fibre-optic cables on the seabed.
The World Wide Web was invented near Geneva.

teile.einleitung: A false report is a piece of news that is not true but looks as if it were. In English such reports are often called fake news, and on the internet in particular they often spread very quickly.
wichtigste: A false report is a piece of news that is not true.
In English, false reports are also called fake news.
False reports often want to frighten or outrage people.
The source of a piece of news shows where it comes from.
Before passing on an astonishing piece of news, you should check whether it is true.
When many people share a false report, many people also believe it.
If you are unsure, it is best to ask an adult.

abschnitte.text: A **false report** is a piece of news with false content. Some come about by mistake, because someone did not check carefully. Others are deliberately made up to deceive people or to make money. In German, a false report in a newspaper used to be called a **Zeitungsente**, a “newspaper duck”; in English it is called a canard. Today people often speak of fake news.

On the internet, anyone can send a message to many people with a few clicks. False reports are often exciting, funny or frightening, which is why they are shared particularly often. When many people share a report, it seems more believable, even though it is false. In chats such as class groups, such reports sometimes go round within minutes. **Chain letters** with threats also belong here.

Many false reports want to **frighten** you or make you angry. Often there is no clear source, or it just says “A friend heard that...”. Capital letters, lots of exclamation marks and the demand “Forward to everyone now!” are warning signs. Pictures can also deceive, because they are easy to edit or take out of a different context. Today computer programs can even create pictures and voices artificially.

First ask yourself what the **source** is, that is where the news comes from. Check whether well-known newspapers, the radio or television are reporting the same thing. Children’s news, for example from SRF Kids, explains news in an understandable way and checks it beforehand. If you are unsure, ask an adult such as your parents or your teacher. And only pass on a piece of news once you are sure that it is true.

False reports can frighten people or make people look bad unfairly. They can also lead people to make wrong decisions, for instance about their health. In a democracy such as Switzerland, people need correct information in order to be able to vote. That is why it is important for everyone to learn to check news critically. This ability is called **media literacy**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A piece of news that is not true; in English also called fake news.
The place or person that a piece of news comes from.
A message that demands that you send it on to many people.
The ability to use media wisely and to check news.

gewusst: In German, a false report in a newspaper has long been called a “Zeitungsente”, a newspaper duck.
Experts who check reports to see whether they are true are called fact-checkers.
On 1 April, some newspapers deliberately publish funny false reports as April Fools’ jokes.

teile.einleitung: Pixel art is an art form in which pictures are put together from small, clearly visible squares. Each square is a pixel and has exactly one colour. This style is best known from old video games, but it is still very popular today.
wichtigste: Pictures in pixel art consist of small squares.
The word pixel means picture dot.
A single pixel has exactly one colour.
A picture with 8 by 8 pixels has 64 pixels altogether.
Pixel art is especially often seen in old video games.
The more pixels a picture has, the finer and more detailed it becomes.
Without a computer you can create pixel art on squared paper or with fuse beads.

abschnitte.text: Every picture on a screen consists of tiny dots, the **pixels**. The word is formed from the English “picture element” and means **picture dot**. Each pixel shines in exactly one colour. Normally they are so small that you can hardly see them with the naked eye.

In **pixel art**, the pixels are deliberately made big and visible. Artists place every single dot carefully by hand. They often use only a few colours, which are called a **palette**. A small picture of 8 by 8 pixels has 64 squares, and even with that you can draw a heart, a mushroom or a face.

Pixel art came about out of necessity: early games consoles and computers had very few pixels and colours. Games such as **Space Invaders** from 1978, Pac-Man or Super Mario Bros. from 1985 had to show their characters with just a few dots. The screen of the Game Boy from 1989 had only 160 by 144 pixels and four shades of grey. The characters in such games are called **sprites**.

You can also create pixel art without any computer at all. On **squared paper**, you simply colour in individual boxes. With **fuse beads**, you put patterns onto a pegboard and then iron them together. Mosaics made of little stones, cross-stitch embroidery or Lego pictures work on the same principle.

The number of pixels in a picture is called its **resolution**. The more pixels a picture has, the finer and more detailed it looks. A phone photo today often consists of many millions of pixels. In pixel art, on the other hand, the low resolution is intended and is part of the style.

Even today, many new games deliberately come out in pixel style, such as Stardew Valley or Terraria. The game **Minecraft** uses small pixel textures of 16 by 16 dots for its blocks. With free programs and apps, anyone can create pixel pictures and small animations themselves. Pixel art is now considered an art form in its own right with many fans.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single coloured dot on a screen.
The number of pixels a picture is made of.
The selection of colours used for a picture.
A small character or object in a video game.

gewusst: A Full HD screen has 1,920 by 1,080 pixels, that is, over two million.
Mario was given a cap and a moustache partly because hair and a mouth were almost impossible to draw with just a few pixels.
In some cities, artists stick small pixel figures made of tiles onto the walls of buildings.

teile.einleitung: A regular expression is a short string of characters that describes a pattern for texts. With it, a computer can check in a flash whether a text matches this pattern or find all the matching places. It is often abbreviated to “regex”, from the English “regular expression”.
wichtigste: A regular expression describes a pattern used to search or check texts.
Regular expressions were introduced by the mathematician Stephen Kleene in the 1950s.
Kleene's theorem says that regular expressions and finite automata describe the same languages.
The star means any number of times, the plus at least once.
The expression (ab)*, for example, describes the word ababab.
^[0-9]{4}$ describes exactly four digits, such as a Swiss postcode.
With Thompson's construction, you build an automaton from a regular expression.
Backreferences such as \1 go beyond the power of regular languages.

abschnitte.text: A **regular expression** is like a wanted poster for texts. Instead of searching for a particular word, you describe a **pattern**. For example: “four digits in a row” or “a word that begins with a and ends with d”. Programs can use it to search, check and replace texts. Almost all programming languages and many text editors support regular expressions.

Some characters have a special meaning. The **star** * means “any number of times, including none”, the **plus** + means “at least once”. The vertical bar | means “or”, and brackets group parts together. Square brackets contain allowed characters, so [0-9] means “one digit”. The character ^ stands for the beginning and $ for the end of the text.

The expression (ab)* matches the empty word, ab, abab and ababab. The expression a(b|c)*d matches every word that begins with a, ends with d and has only b and c in between, for example abccbd. With ^[0-9]{4}$ you check whether someone has entered exactly four digits, as with a **Swiss postcode**. Similar patterns check whether an email address looks roughly right. Regular expressions also save a lot of time when searching and replacing in long documents.

The American mathematician **Stephen Kleene** described regular expressions in the 1950s. He wanted to use them to study what simple calculating machines can recognise. In his honour the star operator is also called the **Kleene star**. In the late 1960s, Ken Thompson built regular expressions into text editors. Later this led to the well-known Unix tool grep.

In theoretical computer science, regular expressions belong to the **formal languages**. **Kleene's theorem** states that regular expressions and finite automata describe exactly the same languages. A finite automaton is a simple machine with a few states that reads character by character. With **Thompson's construction**, you build a nondeterministic automaton with epsilon transitions from a regular expression. However, some practical extensions such as backreferences go beyond regular languages.

begriffe.erklaerung: Short form of regular expression.
A description of which texts match and which do not.
A simple imaginary machine that reads characters and changes its state as it does so.
The character *, which means “any number of times”.

gewusst: The name of the grep tool comes from an editor command meaning “globally search for a regular expression and print”.
A badly built regular expression can keep a computer busy for so long that whole websites go down.
There are puzzle games, so-called regex crosswords, in which every row has to match a pattern.

teile.einleitung: A photo album is a collection of photos that you keep in order and like to look at again. In the past, pictures were stuck into a book; today most photo albums are digital, on the mobile phone or the computer.
wichtigste: A photo album is for collecting and looking at photos.
Digital photo albums are found on the mobile phone or computer.
It makes sense to sort photos by date.
People often write next to a photo where and when it was taken.
A printed book of your own photos is called a photo book.
In a slideshow, photos are shown one after another.
You make a backup copy of important photos so that they do not get lost.

abschnitte.text: A paper **photo album** is a book with thick pages into which you stick or slot photos. Often thin tissue paper separates the pages so that the pictures do not stick to each other. Next to the photos you write where and when they were taken. Such albums have existed since the 19th century, shortly after photography was invented. In many families, old albums tell the story of grandparents and great-grandparents.

Today most people take photos with a **smartphone**. The pictures end up automatically in a gallery or photo app on the mobile phone or computer. There you can sort them into **digital albums**, for example “Holidays in Ticino” or “Birthday”. Many apps sort photos by themselves according to date, place or even recognised faces. A digital album needs no room on the shelf, but it does need storage space on the device.

So that you can find a photo again, **order** is important. The easiest way is to sort by date, because cameras store the date a picture was taken automatically. You can also create albums for topics, people or places. It is best to delete blurred or duplicate photos, otherwise the collection becomes confusing. Good file names and descriptions also help when you search.

Digital photos can be lost if a mobile phone breaks or is stolen. That is why you make a **backup copy** of important pictures. You can copy them to an external hard drive, a USB stick or a **cloud** on the internet. The safest way is to keep the photos in two different places. In this way memories are kept even after many years.

From digital photos you can have a printed **photo book** made, which looks like a real book. This is a popular present, for example for grandparents. In a **slideshow**, photos are shown one after another on a screen, often with music. In the past, slides were shown on the wall with a projector for this. Today it also works on the television or a tablet.

begriffe.erklaerung: An ordered collection of photos, on paper or digital.
A printed book with your own photos.
A presentation in which photos are shown one after another.
An extra copy of data in case the original is lost.
Storage space on the internet, on computers run by providers.

gewusst: A single smartphone today can store tens of thousands of photos, more than would fit into hundreds of paper albums.
The word album comes from Latin and originally meant white tablet.
Photos often store invisible extra information such as the date, the time and sometimes the place where they were taken.

teile.einleitung: A recommender system is a computer program that suggests content or products you might like. Such programs are found in video platforms, music apps, online shops and social networks. They learn from what you watch, click on or buy.
wichtigste: A recommender system suggests content that you might like.
It typically uses data about what you have watched or clicked on so far.
In collaborative filtering, recommendations are based on the behaviour of similar users.
Content-based recommendations are based on features of the content you like.
Platforms want good recommendations so that users stay longer.
In 2006 Netflix offered a prize of 1 million US dollars for a better recommendation algorithm.
In the cold start problem, there is hardly any data yet about new users.

abschnitte.text: A **recommender system** picks out, from huge amounts of content, the items that could suit a particular person. A video platform has millions of videos, and nobody could look through them all. The recommender system sorts them and shows a small selection, for example under “For you” or “You might also like”. For this it uses data about what you have watched, clicked on, liked or bought so far. How long you watch a video can also play a part.

In **collaborative filtering**, the program looks for people with similar taste. If many people who, like you, enjoy football videos have also watched a particular skiing video, it will be suggested to you too. For this the program does not even need to know what the video is about. Online shops use this, for example, under “Customers who bought this item also bought”.

In **content-based recommendations**, the program looks at features of the content itself. If you have already read several crime novels, an app recommends more crime novels. Features can be genre, author, topic, length or style of music. Many services combine both approaches and today use **machine learning**.

In 2006 the streaming service **Netflix** offered a prize of 1 million US dollars for a better recommendation algorithm. Researchers from all over the world took part, and in 2009 a team won that had improved the predictions by ten percent. A well-known difficulty is the **cold start problem**: there is hardly any data yet about new users or new content. That is why some apps ask at the start which topics you like.

Recommendations help you to discover new things and save time. But platforms mainly want users to **stay as long as possible**, because then they can show more advertising. Anyone who is only ever shown similar things can end up in a **filter bubble** and hardly see other opinions any more. You can influence the suggestions yourself by deleting your history or choosing “Not interested”. It also helps to search for other topics yourself on purpose now and then.

begriffe.erklaerung: An exact set of calculating instructions that a computer follows.
Recommending what people with similar taste liked.
There is not yet any data about new users or content.
You see almost only content that fits your own opinion.
A list of the content you have already watched or searched for.

gewusst: The winning algorithm of the Netflix Prize was never fully used in everyday operation because it was so complex.
A large part of what people watch on streaming platforms was suggested to them by the recommender system.
In the EU, very large platforms must also offer a feed that is not based on personal data.

teile.einleitung: Input and output describe how information gets into a computer and comes out again. When you type on the keyboard, that is input; when the screen shows something, that is output. Every computer program also reads input, processes it and outputs a result.
wichtigste: Input means data gets into the computer; output means results come out.
The IPO principle stands for input, processing, output.
In Python, you read input from the keyboard with input().
input() always returns a string (str).
With int(), you turn text that has been typed in into a whole number.
With print(), you output something on the screen in Python.
Keyboard and mouse are input devices; screen and printer are output devices.

abschnitte.text: Almost every job a computer does follows the **IPO principle**: input, processing, output (in German called EVA). On a calculator, for example, you type in 3 + 4; that is the input. The processor calculates; that is the processing. The display shows 7; that is the output. Input and output are often abbreviated as I/O.

**Input devices** bring data into the computer, for example the keyboard, mouse, microphone, camera or scanner. **Output devices** pass results on to us, such as the screen, loudspeakers, headphones or printer. Some devices can do both. A **touchscreen** shows pictures and at the same time recognises where it is touched. A hard drive also takes in data and gives it out again.

In the programming language Python, the function **input()** reads input from the keyboard. It always returns a **string**, that is text, even if you type in a number. That is why, if someone types in the number 5 at a = input(), print(a + a) outputs 55, because two texts are joined together. If you want to calculate, you turn the text into a whole number with int(), for example in age = int(input("Age? ")).

With the function **print()**, Python outputs something on the screen. Several values are separated by a space, so print("A", "B") outputs A B. Whatever is in quotation marks is output exactly as it is, which is why print("3 + 4") shows 3 + 4 and not 7. Normally a line break follows every output. With end="" in print("Hello", end="") you prevent it, and the next output appears on the same line.

A program without input always does exactly the same thing, and a program without output shows no result. Only input and output make programs **interactive**, so that you can play or work with them. Good programs also check input so that a wrong input, such as a letter instead of a number, does not cause a crash. Sensors in robots, cars or weather stations are also inputs, while motors and lamps are outputs.

begriffe.erklaerung: Data that comes into the computer or a program.
Results that the computer displays, prints or plays.
A text, that is a sequence of characters; in Python the type str.
Input, processing, output as the basic sequence of every computer.
A device that is connected to the computer, such as a mouse or printer.

gewusst: Early computers received their input through punched cards with holes punched into them.
The first program that many people write just outputs “Hello World”.
A games console with vibration in the controller also uses the sense of touch as output.

teile.einleitung: Shutting down means switching a computer off properly. The computer first closes all programs calmly and saves important data before the power is switched off. This is much safer than simply pulling out the plug.
wichtigste: You switch a computer off properly by shutting it down.
If you simply pull out the plug, data can be lost.
Before shutting down, you should save your work.
In Windows you find the command for shutting down in the Start menu.
The power symbol is usually a circle with a line at the top.
When restarting, the computer goes off and straight back on again.
In sleep mode the computer is asleep but quickly ready again.

abschnitte.text: A computer is constantly working with many programs and files at the same time. When shutting down, the **operating system** asks all the programs to close. After that it writes any data still open to the **storage** and closes all the files properly. Only right at the end does the device switch itself off.
