abschnitte.titel: Why not just pull out the plug?
abschnitte.text: If the power suddenly goes, the computer can no longer finish saving open files. Then texts, pictures or saved games can be lost. In the worst case the **operating system** itself is damaged and no longer starts properly. So the rule is: only hold the power button down for a long time if the computer has completely **frozen**.

abschnitte.titel: How to do it step by step
abschnitte.text: First save your work and close the programs. In Windows you click on the **Start menu** at the bottom left and then on the **power symbol**. There you choose “Shut down”. On a Mac you find the command in the Apple menu at the top left, and on a mobile phone you usually hold down the side button.

When **restarting**, the computer shuts down and starts again straight away. This often helps when something no longer works properly, or after an update. In **sleep mode**, everything that is open stays in the working memory, and the computer uses only very little electricity. With one key press it is then ready again in a few seconds.

A computer that runs all night uses **electricity** unnecessarily. That is why you shut it down in the evening when you no longer need it. You save even more with a **power strip with a switch**, because some devices still draw a little electricity even when switched off. This is good for your wallet and for the environment.

begriffe.erklaerung: Ending the computer’s work in an orderly way and switching it off.
The main program that controls the computer, for example Windows, macOS or Android.
Switching the computer off and straight back on again.
A sleeping state in which the computer uses little electricity and wakes up quickly.

gewusst: The power symbol combines a 1 for “on” and a 0 for “off”.
Many computer problems can be solved with a simple restart.
Even a computer that is switched off can still use a tiny bit of electricity on standby.

teile.einleitung: A chain letter is a message that asks you to send it on to as many other people as possible. In the past chain letters came by post; today they usually come through chat apps or social networks. They often promise good luck or threaten bad luck, but none of it is true.
wichtigste: A chain letter is a message meant to be sent on.
Threats in chain letters are not true: nothing will happen to you.
Good luck promised for sending it on doesn't exist either.
Chain letters spread quickly because everyone sends them on to many people.
It was usually written by someone unknown.
Threatening or pushing is a typical warning sign.
The best thing is to delete a chain letter.
If a chain letter frightens you, you talk to your parents.

abschnitte.text: A chain letter is a message with a request to **send it on** to others. In this way it forms a long chain of recipients. In the past, such letters came on paper by post. Today they spread mainly through **chat apps**, emails and social networks.

If every person sends the message on to 5 others, after one round it is 5 people, after two rounds 25 and after three rounds 125. After only 10 rounds it would be almost 10 million. This rapid growth is called **exponential growth** or the **snowball principle**. That is why chain letters reach a huge number of people in a short time.

Many chain letters work with **fear**, for example: “Send this on, or something will happen to you!”. Others promise luck, money or love if you forward them. Some claim that a well-known app will soon cost money, or contain **false reports**. Almost always the text comes from someone **unknown**, and nobody can check the claims.

The most important thing: a chain letter cannot do anything to you, whatever it says. The best thing is simply to **delete** it and not send it on. If a message frightens you, talk to your parents or a teacher. In Switzerland, for example, the Pro Juventute advice service on the number **147** offers help for children and young people around the clock.

Some chain letters ask you to send money to the person at the top of a list. Such **pyramid schemes** only work as long as new people keep joining, and most people lose their money in the end. In Switzerland such schemes are banned. Chain letters that ask for passwords or personal details are also dangerous.

begriffe.erklaerung: A message that demands to be sent on to many others.
A message that is not true but looks like a real one.
Growth in which a number multiplies again and again and very quickly becomes huge.
A fraud in which only the first people win and those who join later lose their money.

gewusst: Chain letters existed long before the internet; they used to be sent by post.
Many chain letters turn up again almost unchanged every few years.
In Switzerland, 147 is the telephone number on which children and young people can get advice free of charge.

teile.einleitung: In mathematics and computer science, a graph is a network of points connected by lines. The points are called vertices or nodes, the lines edges, and graphs can be used to describe railway networks, friendships or the internet.
wichtigste: A graph consists of vertices and edges.
In a railway network, the stations are the vertices and the lines between them the edges.
The degree of a vertex is the number of its edges.
For one-way streets you need a directed graph.
If each edge carries a number such as a distance, the graph is called weighted.
A connected graph without cycles is called a tree.
If 5 people all shake hands with each other, the graph has 10 edges.

abschnitte.text: A **graph** consists of **vertices**, which are drawn as points, and **edges**, which connect two vertices. What the vertices and edges mean depends on the example. In a graph of a school class, the people can be the vertices and friendships the edges. A graph of this kind is not the same as the graph of a function from maths lessons. All that matters is what is connected to what, not exactly how you draw it.

A railway network such as that of the SBB can be shown as a graph: the **stations** are the vertices and the lines between them the edges. Road maps, electricity networks and the internet are also huge graphs. Social networks store who is friends with whom as a graph too. Navigation apps use graphs to find the shortest route. There are well-known methods for this, such as the algorithm by Edsger Dijkstra from 1959.

If a connection may only be used in one direction, the edge is drawn as an arrow. Such a graph is called **directed**, and it fits, for example, a road network with one-way streets. If each edge carries a number, for example a distance in kilometres or a travel time, the graph is **weighted**. In this way a computer can work out which route is fastest. Both properties can also be combined.

The **degree** of a vertex tells you how many edges it is connected to. If a vertex is connected to 4 others, it has degree 4. A graph is connected if you can get from every vertex to every other one along edges. A connected graph without cycles is called a **tree**; one example is a family tree. If 5 people all shake hands with each other, this gives 5 times 4 divided by 2, that is 10 edges.

The Basel mathematician **Leonhard Euler** is regarded as the founder of graph theory. In 1736 he looked into whether it was possible to take a walk in the city of Königsberg that crossed each of its seven bridges exactly once. Using a kind of graph, Euler showed that this is impossible. This puzzle is now called the **Seven Bridges of Königsberg** problem. So graph theory has its roots with a Swiss researcher.

begriffe.erklaerung: A point in a graph, for example a station.
A connection between two vertices.
The number of edges attached to a vertex.
A graph whose edges are arrows and only go in one direction.
A connected graph without cycles.

gewusst: Leonhard Euler, the founder of graph theory, came from Basel and used to be shown on the Swiss ten franc note.
Search engines treat the whole internet as a huge graph of web pages and links.
In every graph, the sum of all the degrees of the vertices is twice the number of edges.

teile.einleitung: In computer networks, a port is a number that shows which program on a computer a message is meant for. The IP address is like the address of a house, and the port is like the number of the flat in the house. This lets a computer handle websites, emails and games over the network at the same time.
wichtigste: Ports are numbers from 0 to 65535.
The ports from 0 to 1023 are called “well-known ports”.
Unencrypted HTTP uses port 80 by default.
SSH for secure remote access uses port 22.
SMTP transfers emails between mail servers via port 25.
An IP address and a port number together form a socket.
As its source port, a browser usually uses a random, high port.

abschnitte.text: A **port** is part of the addressing in the network protocols TCP and UDP. The port number is 16 bits long, so it ranges from 0 to **65535**. When a data packet arrives, the operating system looks at the destination port number. That way it knows whether the packet belongs to the web server, the email program or a game.

Ports 0 to 1023 are the **well-known ports** for important services. Unencrypted HTTP uses port 80, encrypted HTTPS port 443. SSH uses port 22, SMTP for emails port 25 and the name system DNS port 53. The organisation IANA manages the list of which service gets which number.

When you open a website, your browser sends a request to port 443 or 80 of the web server. As its own sender port, it chooses a random, high **dynamic port**, usually above 49152. The combination of IP address and port is called a **socket**. A connection is therefore uniquely described by two sockets, one at the browser and one at the server.

A router at home normally does not let any requests from outside into the home network. With **port forwarding** you can set it so that requests to a particular port go to a device in the home network. Some game servers or cameras need this. Because open ports can also give attackers a way in, you should only set up the forwarding you need.

With the open-source tool **Nmap** you can search computers for open ports. Experts use it to check their own networks for weak points. A firewall blocks ports that are not needed. Scanning other people's computers without permission is not allowed and can have legal consequences.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that determines which program on a computer receives data.
The combination of IP address and port number as the end point of a connection.
A network protocol that transfers data reliably and in the right order.
A protective program that blocks unwanted connections.
A router setting that passes requests to a port on to a particular device.

gewusst: Thousands of connections can run over different ports on a single computer at the same time.
The name “port” comes from the English word for a harbour, through which data comes in and goes out.

teile.einleitung: Grace Hopper was an American mathematician and computer pioneer who lived in the 20th century. She developed one of the first compilers, helped to shape the programming language COBOL and rose to the rank of admiral in the US Navy.
wichtigste: Grace Hopper was born in New York in 1906 and died in 1992.
From 1944 she worked on the early mainframe Harvard Mark I.
In 1947 her team found a moth causing a fault in a computer.
In 1952 she developed one of the first compilers.
She played a major part in the programming language COBOL for business applications.
She served in the US Navy for a long time and finally became an admiral.
Her nickname was “Amazing Grace”.

abschnitte.text: **Grace Hopper** was born in New York on 9 December 1906. Even as a child she took alarm clocks apart to understand how they worked. She studied mathematics and physics and in 1934 gained a doctorate in mathematics at Yale University. After that she taught as a professor of mathematics. She died on 1 January 1992.

During the Second World War, Grace Hopper joined the **US Navy** in 1943. From 1944 she worked at Harvard University on the **Harvard Mark I**, one of the first large computers in the USA. The machine was about 15 metres long and calculated with electromechanical parts. Hopper wrote programs for it and produced a detailed manual. She stayed in the Navy, with breaks, until 1986 and finally became an admiral.

In 1947 Grace Hopper’s team was looking for a fault in the Harvard Mark II computer. They found a **moth** that had got caught in a relay. The moth was stuck into the logbook with a note saying that a real “bug” had been found. The English word bug for a fault in technology already existed before. But through this story it became the famous term for **program errors**.

At that time, programs had to be written laboriously in number codes. Grace Hopper had the idea that computers could translate programs themselves. In 1952, with the A-0 system, she developed one of the first **compilers**, that is a translation program. Later she created the language FLOW-MATIC, which worked with English words. From 1959 the programming language **COBOL** was built on it; she played a major part in it, and it is still used in banks today.

Grace Hopper gave many talks and was known for her vivid explanations. With a **piece of wire** about 30 centimetres long she showed how far light travels in a nanosecond. Because of her achievements people called her “Amazing Grace”. A warship of the US Navy, the USS Hopper, bears her name. In her honour, the Grace Hopper Celebration takes place every year, a big conference for women in **computer science**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A program that translates program text into commands that the computer understands.
A programming language for business applications that uses many English words.
The English word for a fault in a program or device.
A billionth of a second.

gewusst: The moth from 1947 is still stuck in the original logbook, which is kept in a museum in the USA.
When she retired from the Navy at the age of 79, Grace Hopper was one of the oldest serving officers in the USA.
She is said to have had a clock in her office that ran backwards, to show that things can be done differently.

teile.einleitung: The entity-relationship model, ER model for short, is a method for planning the data for a database clearly. In it you draw which things there are, what properties they have and how they are connected. The model was presented by Peter Chen in 1976 and is still learnt in computer science lessons today.
wichtigste: Peter Chen presented the ER model in 1976 in a well-known specialist article.
Entities are things or people about which data is stored.
Properties such as name or date of birth are called attributes.
In Chen notation, a relationship is shown with a diamond.
Relationships have cardinalities such as 1:1, 1:n or n:m.
In the relational model, an n:m relationship is implemented with its own table with two foreign keys.
Crow’s foot notation is named after the branching end of the line.

abschnitte.text: Before you build a **database**, you have to think about what data you want to store. The ER model helps with this through a simple drawing, the **ER diagram**. The computer scientist **Peter Chen** presented it in 1976 in a well-known specialist article. The model does not depend on any particular software and is therefore understood by experts and non-experts alike.

An **entity** is a thing or a person about which data is stored, such as a particular pupil or a course. Entities of the same kind are grouped into an entity type, for example “Pupil”. The properties of an entity type, such as name or date of birth, are called **attributes**. A **relationship** connects entities, for example “pupil attends course”. In Chen notation, entity types are drawn as rectangles, relationships as diamonds and attributes as ellipses.

The **cardinality** tells you how many entities can take part in a relationship. With 1:1, each element belongs to exactly one other, for example a country and its capital. With 1:n, a class has many pupils, but each pupil belongs to exactly one class. With n:m, each pupil attends several courses, and each course has several pupils. In **crow’s foot notation**, a branching line end that looks like a bird’s foot marks the “many” side.

For a relational database, the ER model is translated into **tables**. Each entity type becomes a table, and each attribute a column. In a 1:n relationship between class and pupil, the **foreign key** goes in the pupils’ table, that is on the n side. An n:m relationship needs its own relationship table with two foreign keys, for instance a table “Enrolment” with pupil and course.

A **weak entity** can only be clearly identified together with another entity. An example is a room in a building: there is a room 12 in many buildings, and it only becomes unique when the building is given as well. In Chen notation, weak entities are drawn with a double frame. Such details help to avoid errors in the database later on.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thing or a person about which data is stored.
A property of an entity, such as name or age.
How many entities can take part in a relationship.
A column that refers to a row in another table.
An attribute that clearly identifies each entity, such as a number.

gewusst: Peter Chen was born in Taiwan and did his research in the USA.
In an ER diagram, the primary key is often shown underlined.
Crow’s foot notation is now more widespread in many database programs than the original Chen notation.

teile.einleitung: A logic gate is a small electronic circuit that calculates an output from one or more inputs with the values 0 and 1. Logic gates are the basic building blocks of every computer and every mobile phone. In a modern processor, billions of them work together.
wichtigste: An AND gate only gives a 1 if all inputs are 1.
An XOR gate outputs a 1 if the inputs are different.
A NOR gate gives a 1 if both inputs are 0.
An XNOR gate gives a 1 if both inputs are the same.
Every Boolean function can be built using only NAND gates or only NOR gates.
A truth table for three inputs has 8 rows.
A classic CMOS NAND gate with two inputs consists of 4 transistors.

abschnitte.text: A logic gate processes **signals** that have only two states: 0 and 1. Electrically, this usually means “no voltage” and “voltage”. The gate has one or more inputs and one output. Which value comes out at the output depends on the inputs according to fixed rules. These rules come from **Boolean algebra**, a kind of arithmetic for true and false.

The **AND gate** only outputs 1 if all inputs are 1. The OR gate gives 1 as soon as at least one input is 1. The NOT gate simply turns the value round. NAND and NOR are an AND or OR followed by a NOT, so a NOR outputs a 1 with two zeros. The **XOR gate** gives 1 if the inputs are different, the XNOR if they are the same.

What a gate does is shown in a **truth table**. It contains all possible combinations of inputs with the output for each. With two inputs there are 4 rows, with three inputs 8 and with n inputs 2 to the power of n rows. With **De Morgan's laws** you can rearrange expressions. For example, NOT(A AND B) is the same as (NOT A) OR (NOT B).

NAND and NOR are special gates; they are called **universal**. Using only NAND gates you can build any other logic circuit, and the same is true for NOR. This makes the manufacture of chips much simpler. If you combine an XOR gate and an AND gate, you get a **half adder**, which can add two bits. Many such adders make up the arithmetic unit of a processor.

Today logic gates are made of tiny **transistors**, which work like switches. In the widespread CMOS technology, a NAND gate with two inputs needs exactly 4 transistors. A modern mobile phone processor contains many billions of transistors on a few square centimetres. Earlier computers used relays or vacuum tubes for this. In 1937 the American **Claude Shannon** showed that Boolean algebra can be calculated with electrical circuits.

begriffe.erklaerung: A kind of arithmetic with only two values, true and false or 1 and 0.
A table that shows what comes out for every combination of inputs.
A tiny electronic component that works as a switch or amplifier.
A circuit of gates that adds two single bits.

gewusst: The on-board computer of the Apollo moon missions was built almost entirely from NOR gates.
Boolean algebra is named after the English mathematician George Boole, who invented it in the 19th century, long before computers.
You can even build logic gates in the computer game Minecraft with redstone.

teile.einleitung: A list is an ordered series of things, usually written one below the other. Shopping lists, class lists and to-do lists help us not to forget anything and to keep track. Computers also work with lists all the time, for example the playlist or the contacts list on your phone.
wichtigste: A list is a series of entries, usually one below the other.
A single thing on a list is called an entry.
Before going shopping you write a shopping list.
You tick off finished tasks on a to-do list.
The class list shows which children are in the class.
Numbered entries are easier to count.
In computer science, a list is an important way of storing data.

abschnitte.text: A **list** is a collection of things in a particular order. Each thing on the list is called an **entry**. Usually the entries are written one below the other so that you can read them quickly. If your shopping list has bread, milk, cheese and apples on it, it has 4 entries.

Before going shopping you write a **shopping list** so that you don't forget anything. The **class list** shows which children are in a class. A guest list for a party has the names of the guests on it. A timetable, a results list on sports day or a table of contents are also lists.

A **to-do list** contains tasks you still want to do. When a task is done, it is ticked off or crossed out. If you have a list of 6 names and cross out 2, 4 are left. Many people find it motivating to see their list getting shorter.

Lists can be ordered in different ways, for example alphabetically, by date or by importance. If you number the entries 1, 2, 3, it is easier to **count** them and to refer to a particular entry. A list with bullet points instead of numbers is called a bulleted list. On websites there are separate HTML elements for both kinds: <ol> for numbered lists and <ul> for unordered lists.

Computers also store a lot of data as a **list**, such as the songs in a playlist or the contacts on a mobile phone. In programming languages such as Python, you write a list in square brackets, for example ["bread", "milk", "cheese"]. The computer can add new entries, delete entries or **sort** the list. It is important to know that in many programming languages the first entry has the number 0 and not 1.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single thing on a list.
Which entry comes first and which comes after it.
Marking a finished entry with a tick.
Arranging entries according to a rule, for example alphabetically.
The number under which an entry appears in a list.

gewusst: Many programming languages start counting list entries at 0 instead of 1.
More than 4,000 years ago, people in Mesopotamia were already writing lists on clay tablets, for example about supplies.
People who write a shopping list often buy fewer things they don't actually need.

teile.einleitung: The computer mouse is a small input device that you use to move the pointer on the screen and click on things. It got its name because the cable looks like a mouse's tail. It was invented in the 1960s, and one of the best-known mouse companies in the world comes from Switzerland.
wichtigste: The computer mouse is called that because its cable looks like a tail.
If you push the mouse to the right, the pointer moves to the right.
You usually click with the left mouse button.
The right mouse button usually opens a small menu.
With the scroll wheel you scroll up and down.
Laptops often have a touchpad instead of a mouse.
A wireless radio mouse needs batteries or a rechargeable battery.

abschnitte.text: The **computer mouse** is an **input device** that you push across the desk with your hand. Every movement of the mouse is passed on to the **mouse pointer** on the screen: pushing it to the right moves the pointer to the right, pushing it forward moves it up. So that it glides well, people often put it on a mouse mat. The name comes from the cable, which sticks out of the device like a mouse's tail.

With the **left mouse button** you select or open something, and a quick double-click often starts a program. The right button usually opens a small menu with more options, the context menu. The **scroll wheel** between the buttons is used to scroll up and down. If you hold the button down and pull a picture to another place, this is called **drag and drop**.

In the past, the mouse had a **ball** underneath that rolled when you pushed it and so reported the movement. Today most mice have an optical sensor with an LED or a laser. A tiny camera chip takes thousands of pictures of the surface every second and so detects every movement. A wireless mouse without a cable sends the data by radio or Bluetooth and needs batteries or a rechargeable battery.

The American **Douglas Engelbart** invented the mouse in the 1960s; the first model had a wooden case. In 1968 he showed it to the public in a famous demonstration in San Francisco. However, the mouse only became well known in the 1980s, above all through the Apple Macintosh of 1984. Since then it has been part of almost every desktop computer.

The company **Logitech** was founded in 1981 in Apples in the canton of Vaud and became known worldwide for computer mice. The mouse also played an early role at ETH Zurich: Niklaus Wirth's Lilith computer was operated with a mouse around 1980. Today there are special mice for gamers, ergonomic mice for a healthy hand position and mice for left-handed people. On laptops a **touchpad** often replaces the mouse.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device you use to give the computer information.
The little arrow on the screen that follows the mouse.
A small menu that opens with the right mouse button.
Moving the content of a window up or down.
A touch-sensitive surface on a laptop that replaces the mouse.

gewusst: The very first computer mouse had a wooden case and only one button.
Logitech, one of the biggest mouse companies in the world, was founded in the canton of Vaud.
With left-handed settings, the left and right mouse buttons swap their jobs.

teile.einleitung: In end-to-end encryption, a message is encrypted on the sender’s device and only decrypted again on the recipient’s device. In between, nobody can read the content, not even the messenger provider. Many chat apps such as Signal, Threema or WhatsApp use this method.
wichtigste: With real end-to-end encryption, only the sender and the recipient can read the content.
Metadata such as the time and contacts often still remain visible to the provider.
Since 2016 WhatsApp has used the Signal protocol with the “Double Ratchet”.
With transport encryption (TLS), the server sees the plaintext.
In 1991 Phil Zimmermann developed the program PGP for encrypting emails.
The company behind the messenger Threema has its headquarters in the canton of Schwyz.
Proton Mail was founded in 2013 by researchers at CERN and has its headquarters in Geneva.

abschnitte.titel: What does end to end mean?
abschnitte.text: The two **ends** are the sender’s and the recipient’s devices. A message is encrypted on the sender’s mobile phone and stays an unreadable jumble of characters the whole way. Only the recipient’s phone can make it readable again with her secret key. Servers, internet providers or hackers who intercept the data on the way see only encrypted data. You can compare it with a locked letter to which only the recipient has the key.

With **transport encryption** (TLS), which you can recognise by the padlock in the browser, only the path to the server is protected. On the server the message is in **plaintext** again, and the provider could read it. With end-to-end encryption, on the other hand, the server never has access to the content. Many email services use only transport encryption. Messengers with end-to-end encryption therefore protect the content better.

The **Signal protocol** is regarded as particularly secure and uses a mechanism called the “Double Ratchet”, which creates new keys for every message. WhatsApp has used this protocol for all chats since 2016. The messenger **Threema** comes from Switzerland, and the company has its headquarters in the canton of Schwyz. For emails, **Phil Zimmermann** developed the program PGP in 1991. The encrypted email service **Proton Mail** was founded in 2013 by researchers at CERN and has its headquarters in Geneva.

Encryption protects the content, but not everything. **Metadata** such as the time, sender, recipient and size of a message often remain visible to the provider. From this you can tell who is in contact with whom and how often. Also, a message is readable again on the phone itself; anyone who gets hold of the unlocked phone can see the chats. That is why a good screen lock is part of it too.

An attacker could try to slip unnoticed between two people in a conversation; this is a **man-in-the-middle attack**. To rule this out, messengers show **safety numbers** or QR codes. When two people meet, they can compare these codes or scan each other’s. If they match, you can be sure you are talking directly to each other.

begriffe.erklaerung: Turning a message into unreadable code that only authorised people can decrypt.
The readable, unencrypted form of a message.
Data about a message, such as the time and recipient, but not the content.
Fixed rules for how devices exchange data with each other.
A code with which you check that nobody has slipped in between.

gewusst: Phil Zimmermann was investigated in the USA for years because of PGP, because strong encryption was treated like a weapon at the time.
Even the providers themselves cannot hand over end-to-end encrypted messages to authorities, because they do not know the content at all.
The name PGP stands for Pretty Good Privacy.

teile.einleitung: Logical operators such as “and”, “or” and “not” combine statements that are true or false. In programming languages such as Python they are called and, or and not and give the values True or False. With them a program makes decisions, for example whether a game carries on or whether a password is correct.
wichtigste: Logical operators combine truth values into a new truth value.
True and False gives False, because with and both sides must be true.
True or False gives True, because with or one true side is enough.
not True gives False, because not reverses the value.
With x = 8, x > 5 and x < 10 gives the value True.
In Python, and binds more strongly than or, so True or False and False gives the value True.
A truth table for two truth values has 4 rows.

abschnitte.text: A logical operator takes one or two **truth values** and calculates a new one from them. There are only two truth values: true and false, in Python **True** and **False**. The three most important operators are “and”, “or” and “not”. In Python you write them and, or and not. In languages such as Java or JavaScript you write &&, || and the exclamation mark instead.

With **and**, the result is only true if both sides are true, so True and False gives the value False. With **or**, it is enough if at least one side is true, so True or False is True. The operator **not** turns a value round: True becomes False and the other way round. A **truth table** shows all the possibilities. For two values a and b it has 4 rows, because each value can be true or false.

Logical operators are often combined with comparisons. If x = 8, then print(x > 5 and x < 10) gives the value True, because 8 lies between 5 and 10. If age = 12, then print(age < 6 or age > 65) gives the value False, because neither of the two conditions is true. With print(not (3 > 5) and 2 < 1), the left part is True but the right part is False, so the result is False. Such conditions are usually found in **if statements**.

As in arithmetic, logical operators have an **order of precedence**. In Python, not is evaluated first, then and, and or last. That is why True or False and False gives the value True. First False and False becomes False, then True or False becomes True. If you want to be sure, you use **brackets** so that everyone can see straight away what is meant.

Many programming languages only evaluate logical expressions as far as necessary. If the left side of an and is already false, the right side is not checked at all. If the left side of an or is true, the result is also already fixed. This is called **short-circuit evaluation**. It saves time and prevents some errors, such as dividing by zero.

Logical operators are also found in everyday rules. “You may go out if you have done your homework and it is not raining” is a combination using and and not. Search engines and library catalogues often understand searches with AND, OR and NOT. In electronics, the operators correspond to **logic gates**. The basis for this was laid by the English mathematician George Boole in the 19th century.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the two values true or false, in Python True or False.
A table that shows what comes out for every combination.
A statement that a program checks to decide what to do.
Stopping early when evaluating as soon as the result is fixed.

gewusst: In everyday language “or” sometimes means “either or”, but in logic or is also true if both sides are true.
In Python, True counts as 1 and False as 0, so True + True gives the value 2.
In many languages, data types for true and false are called Boolean, after the mathematician George Boole.

teile.einleitung: On a computer, a folder is a container in which you can collect and sort files. It works like a file binder or a drawer in real life. If you keep your folders well organised, you can quickly find photos, texts and homework again.
wichtigste: Folders are used to sort files on the computer.
In Windows the folder symbol is usually yellow.
In Windows a new folder is first called “New folder”.
Giving a folder a new name is called renaming.
You can drag files into a folder with the mouse.
If you delete a folder, the files in it are deleted too.
Many computers already have ready-made folders such as “Pictures” or “Documents”.

abschnitte.text: A **folder** is a place on the computer where you keep **files** together. Files are, for example, photos, texts, pieces of music or videos. A folder can also contain other folders, which are called **subfolders**. In technical language, a folder is also often called a directory.

On the screen, a folder is shown as a small picture, a **symbol** or icon. In Windows this symbol usually looks like a **yellow** file folder. On Apple computers it is usually light blue. The picture is deliberately reminiscent of real paper folders so that you understand straight away what it is for.

With a right-click and the command “New”, you can create a new folder, which in Windows is first called **“New folder”**. Then you should **rename** it, for example to “Ski camp photos”. You move files by dragging them into the folder with the mouse. If you delete a folder, you also delete everything in it, so you should look carefully first.

Folders and subfolders together form a kind of upside-down tree, called the **folder structure**. At the very top is a main folder, and below it more and more folders branch off. The route to a file is called the **path**, for example Documents, then School, then Maths. Many computers already have ready-made folders such as “Pictures”, “Music”, “Documents” and “Downloads”.

Good folder names are short and say clearly what is inside, for example “Hedgehog talk” instead of “Stuff”. You can sort by subject, by year or by project. It helps not to nest too many levels inside each other. Deleted files usually land in the **recycle bin** first, from which you can get them back if necessary.

The idea of showing files as folders on a **desktop** came about around 1980 at the company Xerox in California. In 1984 Apple brought these pictures into many people's homes with the Macintosh. Later Microsoft also took over this way of showing things in Windows. Before that, users had to create and open directories with typed commands.

begriffe.erklaerung: A stored piece of information, for example a photo or a text.
A folder that is inside another folder.
The route through the folders to a particular file.
A folder in which deleted files land first.

gewusst: On many computers there are thousands of folders, most of which the operating system created itself.
The recycle bin icon is itself a kind of special folder.
In cloud storage on the internet, too, you sort files with folders.

teile.einleitung: A public key infrastructure, PKI for short, is a system with which you can check on the internet who a digital key really belongs to. It works much like a passport issued by a trustworthy authority. Every time your browser shows a padlock symbol, a PKI is behind it.
wichtigste: A certificate authority issues digital certificates and signs them.
A registration authority checks the identity of the applicants.
Most certificates on the internet follow the X.509 standard.
The root certificate is at the very top of the chain and signs itself.
The public key is published in the certificate.
With OCSP, a browser checks online whether a certificate has been revoked.
Let's Encrypt issues certificates fully automatically with the ACME protocol.

abschnitte.text: In **public-key cryptography**, everyone has a pair of keys. Anyone may know the **public key**, but you keep the private one secret. What is encrypted with the public key can only be opened again by the private one. But the problem is: how do you know that a public key really belongs to the bank and not to a fraudster?

A **certificate** is a kind of digital ID card that links a public key to a name, for example to a website. It contains the name, the public key, a period of validity and the signature of the issuer. The format of most certificates is laid down by the **X.509** standard. Certificates are usually only valid for a few months to a year.

The **certificate authority** (CA) issues certificates and signs them. A **registration authority** first checks whether the applicant really is who they claim to be. At the very top is the **root certificate**, which signs itself and is built into browsers and operating systems. From it, a certificate chain leads down to the individual website.

If a private key is stolen, the certificate must be **revoked**. Browsers check this using revocation lists or online with the OCSP protocol. How important trust is was shown by the case of the Dutch authority **DigiNotar**, which was hacked in 2011. Afterwards the browsers removed its root certificate, and the company went bankrupt.

Since 2015 the non-profit organisation **Let's Encrypt** has offered free certificates, which are issued automatically through the ACME protocol. As a result, the vast majority of websites today are encrypted with HTTPS. In Switzerland, SwissSign, for example, issues certificates, including for electronic signatures. The program PGP uses a different model: in the **web of trust**, users vouch for each other's keys.

begriffe.erklaerung: A digital ID card that assigns a public key to an owner.
The trustworthy body that issues certificates.
The part of the key pair that anyone may know.
A digital signature that proves data is genuine.
Making a certificate invalid before its time.

gewusst: Every web browser contains a list of more than a hundred trustworthy root certificates.
By clicking on the padlock symbol in the browser, you can look at a website's certificate.

teile.einleitung: Object-oriented programming, OOP for short, is a way of building programs. You think in terms of objects which, like things in the real world, have properties and can do something. Many of today's languages, such as Java, Python or C++, work like this.
wichtigste: In OOP a program consists of objects that combine data and functions.
An object's data are called attributes, and its functions are called methods.
Simula is considered the first object-oriented programming language.
Alan Kay coined the term “object-oriented” and helped develop Smalltalk.
Important principles are abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism.
With overloading, methods have the same name but different parameters.

abschnitte.text: An **object** is a building block in the program that packs data and behaviour together. An object “Dog” could, for example, have the **attributes** name, age and coat colour. Then there are **methods** such as bark() or run(), that is, functions that belong to the object. The attributes store the state of the object, and the methods describe what it can do.

Most object-oriented languages use **classes**. A class is like a blueprint or a biscuit cutter. From a class “Dog” you can create many individual dog objects, which are called **instances**. Each instance has the same attributes but its own values, for example a different name.

With **abstraction**, you hide unimportant details and show only the essentials of an object. **Encapsulation** hides the inner data from direct access from outside; you can only get at it through methods. With **inheritance**, a class takes on properties of another, so that, for example, the class “Cat” inherits from the class “Animal”. Polymorphism means that the same method call triggers different behaviour depending on the type of object.

If you call the method makeSound() on a dog and on a cat, one barks and the other miaows. This is **polymorphism**, which means “having many forms” in Greek. With **overloading**, there are several methods with the same name but different parameters. In this way a method add() can take two numbers one time and three numbers another time.

The first object-oriented language was **Simula**, developed in Norway in the 1960s by Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard. In the 1970s the language **Smalltalk** was created at the Xerox PARC research centre in California, with Alan Kay playing a major part. In the 1980s came C++ by Bjarne Stroustrup, and Java appeared in 1995. Today OOP is one of the most widespread ways of programming.

In a computer game, every character, every enemy and every obstacle can be an object. Windows, buttons and menus on the screen are also often programmed as objects. In the learning environment **Scratch**, the characters, called sprites, are also a kind of object with their own scripts. OOP helps to break large programs down into manageable parts that can be reused.

begriffe.erklaerung: A blueprint from which objects are created.
A single object created from a blueprint.
A function that belongs to an object.
A class takes on the properties and methods of another class.
The inner data of an object are protected from direct access from outside.

gewusst: Simula was originally built to simulate processes such as queues and traffic on the computer, which is where the name comes from.
As early as around 1970, Alan Kay came up with the idea of a portable computer for children, which he called the Dynabook.
In Python even a simple number like 5 is an object with its own methods.

teile.einleitung: A large language model is an artificial intelligence computer program that has been trained on huge amounts of text and can write texts itself. Well-known examples are chatbots such as ChatGPT, which answer questions, summarise texts or help with programming.
wichtigste: In pre-training, a large language model mainly learns to predict the next token of a text.
Tokens are building blocks of text such as words or parts of words.
The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can handle at once.
A higher temperature makes the answers more random and varied.
When a model invents convincing-sounding but false information, this is called hallucination.
ChatGPT was made publicly available at the end of November 2022.
In 2025, ETH Zurich, EPFL and CSCS released the open Swiss language model Apertus.

abschnitte.text: A **language model** is a program that calculates which words are likely to come next in a text. It is called “large” because it consists of billions of numerical values, known as **parameters**, and was trained on huge amounts of text. The abbreviation is LLM. Most of today’s models are based on the **transformer** technique, which researchers presented in 2017. They run on very powerful computers in data centres.

A language model breaks every text down into small building blocks called **tokens**, for example whole words or parts of words. In **pre-training** it reads huge amounts of text from books and the internet. In doing so it practises the same task again and again: predicting the next token. From this simple exercise it learns grammar, facts and even patterns of thinking. After that it is often trained further on a smaller, specialised data set, which is called **fine-tuning**.

The **context window** shows how many tokens a model can handle at once, that is how much text it keeps in view. If a conversation is longer, the model can forget earlier parts. With the setting **temperature**, you control how random the answers are. A low temperature gives predictable texts, a higher one makes the output more varied and creative. For facts you tend to choose a low temperature, for stories a higher one.

Language models can sound very convincing and still make mistakes. If they invent information that is not true at all, this is called **hallucination**. A model does not really know what is true; it calculates with probabilities. That is why you should always check important information in reliable sources. At school the rule is also: anyone who uses AI says so and thinks for themselves too.

Large language models became well known above all through **ChatGPT**, which was made publicly available at the end of November 2022. Since then there have been many more models from different companies and research groups. In 2025, ETH Zurich, EPFL in Lausanne and the Swiss National Supercomputing Centre CSCS in Lugano released the language model **Apertus**. It is completely open, which means that its training data and design are also public. Apertus was trained on texts in a great many languages, including Swiss German and Romansh.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small building block of text, such as a word or part of a word, that a language model calculates with.
The amount of text that a language model can keep in view at once.
When a language model invents false information that sounds real.
Training a model further with special data for a task.
Numerical values in the model that are set during training.

gewusst: Shortly after its launch, ChatGPT reached many millions of users faster than almost any app before it.
The Swiss model Apertus was trained on the supercomputer Alps in Lugano.
In training, a language model reads more text than a person could read in many lifetimes.

teile.einleitung: The P versus NP problem is one of the biggest open questions in computer science and mathematics. It asks whether every task whose solution can be checked quickly can also be solved quickly. Whoever proves the answer will receive one million US dollars in prize money.
wichtigste: The class P contains problems that a computer can solve in polynomial time.
For problems in the class NP, a yes solution can be checked in polynomial time.
It has been proved that P is a subset of NP.
Nobody knows to this day whether P equals NP.
Most experts suspect that P does not equal NP.
The Clay Mathematics Institute has offered 1 million US dollars for the solution.
If P equalled NP, many of today's encryption methods would be insecure.

abschnitte.text: Imagine a difficult sudoku: you can check a finished solution quickly, but solving it takes a long time. The **P versus NP problem** asks whether there is always a quick way of solving such tasks too. The question was formulated precisely in 1971 by **Stephen Cook**. To this day nobody has been able to answer it.

The class **P** contains all decision problems that a computer can solve in **polynomial time**, that is, without the computing time exploding. The class **NP** contains problems for which a proposed yes solution can be checked in polynomial time. Every problem in P is also in NP, because what you can solve quickly you can also check quickly. The only open question is whether it is also true the other way round.

The class **co-NP** contains problems for which the no answers can be checked quickly. A famous example of progress is the **primality test**. In 2002 three Indian researchers showed with the AKS algorithm that you can tell in polynomial time whether a number is prime. This proved that the primality test belongs to P.

In 2000 the **Clay Mathematics Institute** in the USA selected seven particularly hard mathematical questions. The P versus NP problem is one of these so-called **Millennium Prize Problems**. For each correct solution there is 1 million US dollars. So far only one of the seven problems has been solved, and it was not the P versus NP problem.

If P equalled NP and a practically fast algorithm were found, it would have huge consequences. Many of today's **encryption methods**, for example in online banking, rely on certain tasks being hard to solve. These methods would then be insecure. At the same time, many planning and optimisation tasks could be solved much better.

Most experts suspect that **P does not equal NP**. In surveys of researchers, a large majority has said so. But despite decades of work, there is still no proof. Supposed proofs keep appearing, but so far they have all turned out to be flawed.

begriffe.erklaerung: The computing time only grows moderately when the task gets bigger.
Exact step-by-step instructions for solving a task.
Data is converted so that only authorised people can read it.
A number greater than 1 that can only be divided by 1 and itself.

gewusst: The only Millennium Problem solved so far is the Poincaré conjecture, which the Russian Grigori Perelman proved.
Perelman turned down the prize money of one million dollars.
The three researchers behind the AKS algorithm were a professor and two of his students in Kanpur, India.

teile.einleitung: A software bug is a mistake in a computer program that stops it doing what it is supposed to do. It is called a “bug”, the English word for a small insect. Mistakes happen to everyone, even the best programmers, and they can be found and fixed.
wichtigste: A program has a bug when it does not do what it is supposed to do.
If a robot drives into the wall instead of to the apple, there is probably a mistake in the program.
Common mistakes are one command too many, a missing command or the wrong order.
First you check the commands step by step.
Finding and fixing mistakes is called “debugging”.
Mistakes are not a bad thing, because you learn from them.
Some software bugs in history were very expensive.

abschnitte.text: A **bug** is a mistake in a program. The program then runs wrongly, crashes or does nothing at all. You notice it because the result is not what you wanted. Mistakes happen because people overlook something or think something through wrongly when programming. A computer always does exactly what is in the program, even if it is wrong.

With educational robots you see mistakes straight away. If the robot is supposed to move 3 squares and moves 4, there is one **forward command** too many in the program. If it stops after 1 square instead of 2, a forward command is missing. If it turns left instead of right, you replace “turn left” with “turn right”. The **order** is also important: “clap, hop, clap” is something different from “clap, clap, hop”.

Finding and fixing mistakes is called **debugging**. The best way is to go through the program step by step and compare each command with the plan. You can also follow the robot's route on the playing mat with your finger. Professionals use special programs, called debuggers, that let a program run slowly. After each change you test again whether everything is right now.

The word “bug” for technical faults already existed in the 19th century. A story from 1947 at Harvard University in the USA became famous. There a team around the computer pioneer **Grace Hopper** found a real moth in the Mark II computer. The moth was stuck into the logbook and described as the “first actual case of bug being found”. The logbook is now in a museum in Washington.

Some software bugs had big consequences. In 1996 the European rocket **Ariane 5** exploded shortly after launch because a number was too big for its storage space. Before the year 2000, people feared the **millennium bug**, because many programs stored years with only two digits. At that time, programs all over the world were checked and corrected. That is why today there are strict tests for important software, for example in aircraft or hospitals.

Mistakes in programming are completely normal and not a bad thing. Even at big companies, programs contain mistakes that are later fixed with **updates**. If you find and fix a mistake, you understand the program better afterwards. Many companies even pay rewards when someone reports a bug in their software. Patience and looking carefully are therefore very important in programming.

begriffe.erklaerung: English for a small insect; it means a mistake in a program.
Finding and fixing mistakes in a program.
A single instruction that a computer or robot carries out.
A new version of a program that, for example, fixes mistakes.

gewusst: Because of her achievements, Grace Hopper was called “Amazing Grace” in the USA.
Large programs often have thousands of known small bugs that are fixed bit by bit.
When debugging, it sometimes helps to explain the program out loud to a cuddly toy; while doing so, you often notice the mistake yourself.

teile.einleitung: The halting problem is one of the most famous questions in computer science: can you predict, for every program and every input, whether the program will stop at some point or run forever? The British mathematician Alan Turing proved in 1936 that this is impossible in principle. So there are questions that no computer in the world can answer, however fast it is.
wichtigste: The halting problem asks whether a program will stop at some point for a particular input.
Alan Turing showed in 1936 that the halting problem is undecidable.
The proof works by diagonalisation and leads to a contradiction.
The halting problem is semi-decidable, but its complement is not.
Rice’s theorem extends the result to all non-trivial properties of programs.
No tool can reliably detect infinite loops in all programs.
Many other problems are proved undecidable by reducing the halting problem to them.

abschnitte.text: A program receives an input and starts calculating. Either it finishes at some point, or it gets stuck, for example in an **infinite loop**. The halting problem asks whether there can be a general checking program that answers this question correctly for any program at all. Such a checking program is called a **decider**, because it would always have to answer Yes or No.

The Englishman **Alan Turing** published a paper on computable numbers in 1936. In it he described a simple thought model of a computer, the **Turing machine**. With this model he showed that the halting problem cannot be solved. At that time there were no electronic computers yet at all; Turing thought the problem through purely mathematically.

The proof is a **proof by contradiction**: you assume that there is a perfect checking program H. Then you build a nasty program that asks H about itself and does exactly the opposite: if H says “stops”, it runs forever; if H says “runs forever”, it stops at once. Whatever H answers, it is wrong. This technique is called **diagonalisation**, because it works in a similar way to Georg Cantor’s famous proof about infinite sets.

Although the halting problem is undecidable, it is **semi-decidable**. You can simply let the program run: if it stops, you know for sure that the answer is Yes. But if it keeps running, you never know whether it will still stop or run forever. For the **complement**, that is the programs that never stop, there is not even such a half method.

**Rice’s theorem** from the 1950s says even more: no non-trivial property of the function that a program calculates can be checked automatically in general. Whether a program, for example, always outputs the number 0 is therefore also undecidable. To show that a new problem cannot be solved, a **reduction** is usually used: if you could solve the new problem, you could also solve the halting problem. A closely related example is the question of whether a program halts on the empty input.

For software development this means: no tool can reliably find all infinite loops or errors in all programs. Checking programs therefore work with approximations and sometimes warn unnecessarily or miss something. A real computer with **finite memory** is different in principle: it has only finitely many states and must at some point stop or repeat a state. But this number is so huge that it cannot be tried out in practice.

begriffe.erklaerung: A problem for which there is no program that always gives the right Yes or No answer.
A simple thought model of a computer with an endless tape, invented by Alan Turing.
A part of a program that repeats again and again and never finishes.
A proof trick: you show that one problem is at least as hard as another.
In Yes cases you will surely find the answer; in No cases you may wait for ever.

gewusst: Alan Turing proved that the halting problem cannot be solved before the first electronic computer had even been built.
Even with the fastest supercomputer in the world, the halting problem cannot be solved in general.
The proof is similar to the well-known puzzle of the barber who shaves everyone who does not shave themselves.

teile.einleitung: Programming means giving a computer exact instructions about what it should do. Many commands one after another form a program, for example a game, an app or the controls of a washing machine. Because a computer does not think for itself, the commands must be clear and in the right order.
wichtigste: A command is an instruction to the computer.
Many commands one after another are called a program.
If you swap commands round, the result can be wrong, like putting on shoes before socks.
A mistake in a program is called a bug.
Finding and fixing mistakes is called debugging.
A loop repeats commands, for example “Clap!” three times.
Scratch is a programming language with colourful blocks for children.

abschnitte.text: A computer can calculate very quickly but only understands exact **commands**. When programming, you write these commands down in a **programming language**. A program is like a recipe in which every step is described exactly. The computer then carries out the steps in order.

The most important building blocks are commands, sequences, loops and conditions. A **loop** repeats commands: if you say “Clap!” three times, it claps three times. A **condition** lets the computer decide, for example “If it is raining, take the umbrella”. In variables, a program stores values such as the score in a game.

Almost every program has mistakes at first, which are called **bugs**. The programmer Grace Hopper told of a moth that was found in a computer in 1947 and had caused a fault. Finding and fixing mistakes is called **debugging**. That is why good programmers test their programs again and again.

There are hundreds of programming languages for different purposes. **Scratch** is suitable for children; in it you snap colourful blocks together. Python is popular with young people and experts because it is easy to read. JavaScript runs in every web browser and brings websites to life.

Around 1843 Ada Lovelace wrote instructions for a mechanical calculating machine by Charles Babbage, so she is considered the first programmer. In the 1940s the first electronic computers were built. In 1970 the Swiss computer scientist **Niklaus Wirth** developed the language Pascal at ETH Zurich and received the Turing Award in 1984. Today children in Switzerland take their first steps in programming in the subject media and computer science.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single instruction to the computer.
A sequence of commands that does a task.
A part of the program that repeats commands.
A mistake in a program.
Finding and fixing mistakes in a program.

gewusst: Modern programs such as operating systems consist of many millions of lines of code.
A washing machine, a car or a set of traffic lights is also controlled by programs.
The term bug for technical faults is even older than the computer.

teile.einleitung: A yes-no question is a question that can only be answered with yes or no. Such questions are particularly important in computer science, because a computer also makes its decisions step by step with exactly two possibilities.
wichtigste: There are exactly 2 answers to a yes-no question: yes or no.
“Do you have a dog?” is a yes-no question, but “What is your dog called?” is not.
A plan that leads to a solution with several yes-no questions is called a decision tree.
With clever questions, you halve the possibilities each time.
In this way you can be sure to find a number from 1 to 4 after 2 questions.
Computers work with two states, for example on and off or 1 and 0.
If-then rules such as “If it rains, I will take my umbrella” are based on a yes-no question.

abschnitte.text: A yes-no question does not need a long explanation, only a **yes** or a **no**. Questions such as “Is an apple an animal?” or “Do you have PE today?” are examples. In grammar they are also called closed questions, because the answer is limited to two possibilities. Questions with question words such as who, where or why, on the other hand, are called wh-questions (in German “W-Fragen”). They have many more possible answers.

abschnitte.titel: Two states, like a small bulb
abschnitte.text: A small bulb can only be on or off, just like the answer to a yes-no question. Computers store everything with such two-way states, which are written as 1 and 0. A single such place is called a **bit**. With 8 bits you can already tell 256 different things apart. So every photo, song and game contains a huge number of yes-no answers.

A **decision tree** is a plan made of many yes-no questions that branch like the boughs of a tree. After each answer you follow a branch further, until at the end you arrive at the solution. One example is a book for identifying animals: “Can it fly?”, then “Does it have feathers?” and so on. Computer programs and apps also use such trees, for instance to decide which advert or which video to suggest.

abschnitte.titel: Reaching the goal quickly with clever questions
abschnitte.text: Good questions split the possibilities into two halves of about the same size. If you are looking for a number from 1 to 4, you first ask “Is it greater than 2?” and know the answer after the second question. With numbers from 1 to 100, just 7 questions are enough this way. In computer science this approach is called **binary search**. In the game “Who am I?” or when guessing animals, “Can it fly?” is therefore a good first question.

Programming languages have the **if-then statement** for this, written as if. The program checks a condition that is either true or false. If it is true, a particular command is carried out, otherwise a different one. In Scratch the matching block is called “if, then, else”. This way a game reacts, for example, to whether a character is touching the edge.

begriffe.erklaerung: A question that can only be answered with yes or no.
The smallest unit of information in a computer; it can be 0 or 1.
A plan made of yes-no questions that branches like a tree and leads to the solution.
A statement in a program that can be true or false.

gewusst: With only 20 clever yes-no questions, you can tell more than a million different things apart.
The word bit is short for the English “binary digit”, meaning a digit with two possible values.
Every key on your keyboard is stored in the computer as a sequence of zeros and ones.

teile.einleitung: In computer science, an event is something that happens and that a program can react to, for example a mouse click or a key press. Many games and apps wait all the time for such events and only then do something.
wichtigste: An event is an occurrence such as a click, a key press or a touch on the screen.
Programs that react to events are called event-driven.
In Scratch, a program usually begins with “when green flag clicked”.
Event blocks in Scratch are curved at the top like a hat.
With “broadcast message”, one character can let another know something.
If two scripts start with the same event, both start running at the same time.
The red stop button stops all scripts.

abschnitte.text: In computer science, an **event** is a signal that something has just happened. This can be a mouse click, a key press, a swipe on a mobile phone or a new message. An alarm clock that rings at 7 o’clock also triggers an event. The program notices the event and then carries out the matching commands. In German an event is called an “Ereignis”.

In **event-driven programming**, the program waits until something happens. Only then is the matching part of the program started, which is called the event handler. Almost all programs with windows, buttons and menus work this way. Websites also use the language JavaScript to react to events such as a click on a button. This means the computer does not have to keep checking whether anything has happened.

In the learning language Scratch, all the event blocks are in the “Events” category. They are curved at the top like a **hat** and so always stand right at the top of a script. The best known is “when green flag clicked”, with which most programs start. If a character is to jump when you press the space bar, the script begins with “when space key pressed”. If two characters each have a script with the green flag, both start at the same time when it is clicked.

Characters in Scratch can send each other **messages**. With the “broadcast message” block, one character lets all the others know something, for example “game over”. Every character with the “when I receive message” block then starts its script. The “broadcast message and wait” block even waits until all the receiving scripts have finished. This way whole stories with several characters can be controlled.

The red **stop button** above the stage in Scratch stops all scripts at once. But there are events everywhere in technology. A light barrier at the supermarket door reports that someone is coming, and the door opens. A smartphone reacts to events such as an incoming call or a low battery. Traffic lights with a button for pedestrians also wait for the event “button pressed”.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something that happens and that a program reacts to, such as a click.
A series of commands that are carried out together.
A Scratch block with a curved top that starts a script.
A signal with which characters in Scratch let each other know something.

gewusst: Scratch was developed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in the USA and has been freely available since 2007.
A computer can process hundreds of events per second, such as every small movement of the mouse.
Games console controllers also send an event to the console every time a button is pressed.

teile.einleitung: Netiquette is a set of rules for polite and fair behaviour on the internet. The word is made up of “net” and “etiquette”, which means good manners. It applies wherever people write to each other online, for example in class chats, forums, games and comments.
wichtigste: Netiquette means rules for polite behaviour on the internet.
Anyone who writes only in CAPITAL LETTERS seems to be shouting.
A troll is someone who deliberately provokes and disrupts.
The best way to react to a troll is not to react at all.
If you are annoyed, you should wait a moment and read your reply again before sending it.
Spam is unwanted messages sent out in huge numbers.
Irony is easily misunderstood in text messages because tone of voice and facial expressions are missing.

abschnitte.text: Netiquette is an **invented word** made from the English “net” and the word “etiquette”, which means good manners. They are not laws but rules that users agree on. They are meant to make sure that everyone feels comfortable online. The basic idea is simple: you treat others on the internet the way you would like to be treated yourself. After all, behind every screen name there is a real person.

Anyone who writes only in **CAPITAL LETTERS** seems to be shouting. Ironic remarks are easily misunderstood in text messages because **tone of voice** and facial expressions are missing. A suitable emoji can help to show how something is meant. If a comment annoys you, it is best to wait a moment and read your own reply again before sending it. Once something has been sent, it often cannot be taken back.

In the class chat you only send messages that concern everyone. Private conversations are better held directly with the person concerned. You only share photos or videos of others if they agree, because in Switzerland everyone has a **right to their own image**. Nobody should be laughed at, left out or insulted. Anyone who is repeatedly picked on on the internet is experiencing **cyberbullying**, and that can be very hurtful.

A **troll** is someone who deliberately provokes, insults or disrupts in order to upset others. The best thing is not to react at all, because attention is exactly what a troll wants. Many platforms also have buttons for reporting or blocking. **Spam** is unwanted messages sent out in huge numbers, such as adverts or chain letters. You do not forward chain letters, even if they try to frighten you.

If something on the internet is weighing on you or frightening you, talk to someone you trust. That could be your parents, a teacher or friends. In Switzerland, Pro Juventute offers free and confidential advice for children and young people on the number **147**. You can call, chat or write there. You should not delete insulting messages but save them with a screenshot.

As early as the 1980s there were the first rules of behaviour on **Usenet**, an early discussion network. In 1995 the “Netiquette Guidelines” were published in an official internet document, RFC 1855. At that time they were mainly about emails and discussion forums. Today the basic ideas also apply to social networks, chats and online games. Many platforms and schools have their own rules on this.

begriffe.erklaerung: Rules for polite behaviour on the internet.
Someone who deliberately provokes and disrupts online.
Unwanted messages sent out in huge numbers.
When someone is repeatedly insulted, humiliated or left out on the internet.

gewusst: The word spam comes from a sketch by the British comedy group Monty Python in which the word is repeated over and over.
The term troll probably comes from the English fishing term “trolling”, where you pull a bait along behind a boat.
As early as 1995, when only a few people were online, there were official rules for good behaviour on the internet.

teile.einleitung: JavaScript is a programming language that makes websites lively and interactive. It runs directly in the web browser and, for example, reacts to clicks, checks forms or lets games run in the browser. Despite the similar name, JavaScript has nothing to do with the Java language.
wichtigste: JavaScript makes websites interactive.
JavaScript and Java are two different programming languages.
On normal websites, JavaScript runs in the user's browser.
You include JavaScript with the HTML element <script>.
With let you create a variable whose value may change.
console.log(2 + 3) outputs 5 in the browser console.
The comparison === checks for the same value and the same data type.
An event handler is a function that runs, for example, when something is clicked.

abschnitte.text: Websites consist of three parts: **HTML** for the content, CSS for the appearance and **JavaScript** for the behaviour. With JavaScript, menus can open, pictures can change and games can run in the browser. The code is usually included in the page with the <script> element. Every modern browser such as Firefox, Chrome or Safari can run JavaScript.

**Brendan Eich** developed the language in 1995 at the company Netscape in only about ten days. At first it was called Mocha, then LiveScript, and finally JavaScript, partly because Java was very popular at the time. Apart from the name, however, it has hardly anything in common with Java. Since 1997 the language has been internationally standardised under the name **ECMAScript**.

With **let** you create a variable whose value may change, with const one that stays the same. The command console.log(2 + 3) writes the number 5 to the **browser console**. Comments on one line begin with two slashes //, and the computer ignores them. The comparison === checks whether value and data type are the same, so 5 === "5" is false.

On websites, a lot happens through **events**, for example a click or a key press. A function that runs when such an event happens is called an **event handler**. In this way a button can show a text or increase a score when clicked. JavaScript can change every HTML element on the page through what is called the DOM.

JavaScript is one of the most widely used programming languages in the world. With **Node.js**, JavaScript has also been running on servers outside the browser since 2009. Large web applications such as online maps, email programs and learning platforms are largely made of JavaScript. Many young people learn to program with it, because all you need is a browser and a text editor.

begriffe.erklaerung: A named storage place for a value.
A named block of code that you can call again and again.
Something that happens, such as a click or a key press.
A window in the browser where you see output and errors.
The tree structure of a web page, which JavaScript can change.

gewusst: The first version of JavaScript was created in only about ten days.
In JavaScript, "2" + 3 gives the text "23", because the number is added on to the end of the text.
Almost every website you visit contains JavaScript.

teile.einleitung: Sharing photos means showing your own pictures to others, for example through chat apps or social networks. That is fun, but every shared picture can spread a long way, so it calls for care and respect.
wichtigste: Every person has the right to their own image and may have a say in whether a photo of them is shown.
You must not pass off a photo from the internet as your own.
You do not forward photos that make fun of others.
You must not post photos of teachers or classmates taken in secret.
It is best to send photos of yourself only to people you know.
The background of a photo can give away where you are.
It is better to post holiday photos only after the holidays.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who shares a photo sends it by **chat** or puts it online in a social network. Others can then look at it, save it and often send it on. Once shared, a picture can hardly ever be fully taken back. That is why people say: the internet never forgets. Before you tap “Send”, it is worth taking a short moment to think.

abschnitte.titel: The right to your own image
abschnitte.text: In Switzerland every person has the **right to their own image**. It is part of the protection of personality, which is set out in the Civil Code. So as a rule you may not publish photos of others in which they can easily be recognised without their permission. Posting a funny photo of your teacher taken in secret is therefore not allowed. It is best always to ask first: “May I share this photo?”

Whoever takes a photo is its **author** and has rights to it. That is why you may not simply pass off a picture from the internet as your own or use it again. In Switzerland, since 2020, even quite everyday photos have been protected by the Copyright Act. Some photographers allow their pictures to be used under certain conditions, for example if their name is given. For school work, you always say where a picture comes from.

A photo often shows more than you think. In the **background** you may see a street sign, the school building or the house number. Many mobile phones also store, invisibly, where and when a picture was taken. Anyone who posts holiday photos straight away gives away that nobody is at home at the moment. That is why it is better to share holiday pictures only after the holidays and to check who can see the photos.

If someone sends you a photo to make fun of another child, you do not send it on. Forwarding like this can turn into **cyberbullying** and hurts the people affected very much. If someone shows an embarrassing photo of you, talk to an adult you trust. In Switzerland the Pro Juventute helpline on **147** also helps, around the clock. In social networks you can also report unsuitable pictures.

begriffe.erklaerung: The right to decide for yourself whether photos of you are shown.
The person who created a work such as a photo.
When someone is repeatedly shown up or picked on over the internet or by mobile phone.
The personal area that is nobody else’s business.

gewusst: Many smartphones invisibly store the exact place where each photo was taken, if location services are switched on.
The Pro Juventute helpline 147 is free for children and young people in Switzerland.
Even a photo in a private chat can be saved with a screenshot and passed on.

teile.einleitung: A unit test checks a small part of a program, for example a single function, completely on its own. In German it is called “Modultest”. Such tests run automatically and show straight away whether a part of the program still works correctly after you have changed something.
wichtigste: In German a unit test is called “Modultest”.
It checks a small part of a program separately from the rest.
With an assertion, a test checks an expected value.
A mock object is a stand-in object that simulates a real dependency.
A good unit test is independent of other tests.
The Swiss computer scientist Erich Gamma wrote the test framework JUnit for Java together with Kent Beck.
Test-driven development has the three phases red, green and refactor.

abschnitte.text: A program consists of many small building blocks, the **modules** or units, such as individual functions. A unit test calls such a building block with particular inputs. Then it checks whether the result matches the expected value. This check is called an **assertion**. If the value is wrong, the test fails and reports the error.

Suppose a function is meant to add two numbers. A unit test then checks, for example, whether add(2, 3) really gives 5. In Python you write such tests with the **unittest** module from the standard library or with the popular tool pytest. Many tests follow the pattern “arrange, act, assert”. A program often has hundreds or thousands of such tests, which run through in a few seconds.
