A good unit test is fast, small and **independent** of other tests. It should always give the same result, whatever order the tests run in. If a part of the program depends on something else, such as a database or the internet, this is replaced by a **mock object**. A mock only pretends to be the real object and also checks how it is called. In this way you really only test the one building block.

In **test-driven development** you even write the test before the actual code. In the red phase, the new test fails at first because the function is still missing. In the green phase you write just enough code for the test to pass. In the refactor phase you tidy up the code without any test failing. The American Kent Beck made this approach well known around the year 2000.

With **SUnit**, Kent Beck wrote the first test framework of this kind for the programming language Smalltalk. Later, together with the Swiss computer scientist **Erich Gamma**, he developed the JUnit framework for Java. Gamma comes from Zurich and is also known as a co-author of a famous book about design patterns. Modelled on JUnit, similar frameworks were created for many languages, which together are called xUnit. Today unit tests are part of everyday work in most software companies.

Unit tests find errors early, when they are still easy to fix. If you later change something in the code, the tests show immediately whether anything has broken. Such new errors in code that already worked are called **regressions**. Many companies have all the tests run automatically with every change. However, unit tests do not replace testing the whole program together.

begriffe.erklaerung: A test for a small part of a program, called “Modultest” in German.
A check in a test whether a result matches the expected value.
A stand-in object that imitates a real component in a test.
A ready-made basic structure of program code that you can build on.
A new error in a part of a program that worked before.

gewusst: According to a well-known story, Kent Beck and Erich Gamma wrote the first version of JUnit during a flight they took together.
In test-driven development, the test is written before the code for it exists.
Large software projects often have more lines of test code than actual program code.

teile.einleitung: A programming language is an artificial language with which people give a computer exact instructions. Computers really only understand zeros and ones, which is why we need languages that people can read. Today there are hundreds of them, from Python to Java to the children's language Scratch.
wichtigste: With a programming language you write programs, that is, step-by-step instructions for the computer.
Ada Lovelace is considered the first programmer because of her program for the Analytical Engine.
With the Plankalkül, Konrad Zuse designed the first high-level programming language.
Around 1970 Niklaus Wirth developed the language Pascal at ETH Zurich.
A compiler translates the whole source code into machine code before it runs.
Haskell is a functional programming language.
Well-known languages today are Python, Java, JavaScript and C.

abschnitte.text: Inside, a computer only works with **machine code**, long rows of zeros and ones. Programming languages make it possible to write commands with words and symbols that people understand. The text a programmer writes is called **source code**. Like a real language, every programming language has fixed rules for words and sentence structure, which are called syntax. Even one forgotten character can stop a program from running.

So that the computer can run the source code, it has to be translated. A **compiler** translates the whole program into machine code at once, before it starts. An **interpreter**, on the other hand, reads the program line by line and carries out each instruction straight away. Languages such as C are usually compiled, Python is usually interpreted. Compiled programs often run faster, while interpreted ones are more convenient for trying things out.

As early as 1843 the Englishwoman **Ada Lovelace** wrote a program for the Analytical Engine, a calculating machine by Charles Babbage that was never completed. In the 1940s the German engineer **Konrad Zuse** designed the Plankalkül, the first high-level programming language. In the 1950s the language Fortran was created at IBM for scientific calculations. Many other languages followed, such as Cobol, Basic and C.

Around 1970 the Swiss computer scientist **Niklaus Wirth** developed the language **Pascal** at ETH Zurich. He named it after the French mathematician Blaise Pascal. Pascal had a particularly clear structure and was therefore used in schools and universities all over the world for learning to program. Later Wirth also designed the languages Modula-2 and Oberon. In 1984 he received the Turing Award for his work, a kind of Nobel Prize for computer science.

Programming languages follow different ways of thinking, which are called **paradigms**. In imperative languages such as C, you give the computer one command after another. In object-oriented languages such as Java, you organise the program into objects, for example a game character with properties and abilities. Functional languages such as **Haskell** build programs out of mathematical functions. Many modern languages such as Python combine several of these ideas.

Programs are found in mobile phones, games consoles, cars, washing machines and ticket machines. Websites are often brought to life with JavaScript, and apps are written in languages such as Kotlin or Swift. For children there are languages such as **Scratch**, in which you put coloured blocks together like puzzle pieces. In many Swiss schools, programming is now part of lessons in the subject media and computer science.

begriffe.erklaerung: The text of a program as a person writes it.
A program that translates the whole source code into machine code before it starts.
A program that translates the source code line by line and runs it straight away.
The writing rules of a programming language, similar to the grammar of a language.
A mistake in a program.

gewusst: The Python language is not named after the snake but after the British comedy group Monty Python.
Zuse's Plankalkül was only published decades after he invented it and for a long time was never run on a computer at all.
Ada Lovelace was the daughter of the famous English poet Lord Byron.

teile.einleitung: A cryptographic hash function turns any data, such as a text or a whole file, into a short code of fixed length, the hash value. This value is like a digital fingerprint: even the smallest change gives a completely different code. You cannot work back from the hash value to the original data.
wichtigste: A cryptographic hash function turns any data into a value of fixed length.
SHA-256 produces a hash value with 256 bits.
Collision resistance means that two inputs with the same hash can hardly be found.
The avalanche effect makes sure that small changes alter the hash completely.
SHA-1 was broken in practice in 2017 in the “SHAttered” project.
MD5 is considered insecure because collisions can easily be produced.
Passwords are stored with a salt and methods such as Argon2.
SHA-3 is based on the Keccak algorithm.

abschnitte.text: A **hash function** takes data of any size and calculates a string of characters of fixed length from it. With SHA-256 the result is always 256 bits long, whether you put in a word or a whole film. A **cryptographic** hash function must also be especially secure. It is a **one-way function**: it is easy to calculate but cannot be reversed.

**Collision resistance** is important: it should be practically impossible to find two different inputs with the same hash value. There is also the **avalanche effect**: if only one letter changes, the hash value looks completely different. With an n-bit hash, a birthday attack needs about 2 to the power of n/2 attempts to find a collision. That is why long hash values are needed; with 256 bits that is still an unimaginable number of attempts.

Good websites do not store your password, only its hash value. When you log in, the password you enter is hashed and compared. A random addition, the **salt**, protects against precomputed tables with which attackers could crack many hash values at once. Special, deliberately slow methods such as **Argon2**, winner of the Password Hashing Competition in 2015, make trying out passwords even harder.

**MD5** was presented in 1991; today collisions can be produced with it in a short time. With **SHA-1**, researchers from Google and the Dutch research institute CWI achieved a practical collision in 2017 in the “SHAttered” project. For security-critical purposes, SHA-2, for example SHA-256, or SHA-3 is used today. SHA-3 is based on the **Keccak** algorithm, which won a public competition in 2012.

abschnitte.titel: Where hashes are found in everyday life
abschnitte.text: When downloading programs, you can use the hash value to check whether the file has arrived unchanged. **Digital signatures**, for example on secure websites, are based on hash functions. The cryptocurrency Bitcoin uses SHA-256 for its blockchain. Version control systems such as Git also recognise files by their hash values.

begriffe.erklaerung: The short result of a hash function, like a fingerprint of the data.
Two different inputs give the same hash value.
Easy to calculate but practically impossible to reverse.
A random addition to the password before hashing.
A tiny change to the input changes the hash completely.

gewusst: A SHA-256 value is usually written as 64 hexadecimal digits, because each digit represents 4 bits.
For the SHAttered attack on SHA-1, the researchers needed enormous computing power that would have taken a single processor thousands of years of work.
If a website can send you your old password by email, it is probably not storing it as a hash.

teile.einleitung: A presentation program is software you use to design slides for a talk. The slides contain keywords, pictures, diagrams or videos. When giving the talk, you usually show them with a projector on the wall or on a big screen.
wichtigste: A single page in a screen presentation is called a slide.
The slide master sets the appearance of all the slides.
A slide transition is the effect when changing from one slide to the next.
Presenter view shows notes that only the speaker can see.
Slides should have a few keywords instead of long paragraphs.
In many programs you start the presentation from the beginning with the F5 key.
Dark writing on a light background is usually easiest to read.

abschnitte.text: With a **presentation program** you create a series of pages called **slides**. Well-known programs are Microsoft PowerPoint, Apple Keynote, Google Slides and the free LibreOffice Impress. You can insert text, pictures, tables, diagrams, sounds and videos. During the talk you then click through slide by slide.

The **slide master** sets how all the slides look, such as the background, font and colours. If you change it, all the slides change at once. A **slide transition** is the effect when changing to the next slide, for example a fade. With animations you can make individual elements appear one after another.

In the classroom, the presentation is often projected onto the wall with a **projector**. In many programs you start the screen presentation from the beginning with the **F5** key. **Presenter view** shows notes and the next slide on your own screen, which the audience cannot see. With a small wireless clicker you can move on to the next slide without standing at the computer.

A slide should have **a few keywords** instead of long paragraphs, because the audience should listen and not read. The writing should be big enough to read even at the back of the room. Dark writing on a light background is usually easiest to read. Pictures often say more than many words, and too many colourful effects tend to distract.

In the past, talks were shown with an **overhead projector**, on which you laid transparent sheets; this is where the German word “Folie” for slide comes from. There were slide projectors for photos. In 1987 the program PowerPoint appeared; it was first intended for Apple computers and was bought by Microsoft in the same year. Since then it has been hard to imagine schools, companies and universities without screen presentations.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single page of a presentation.
A device that projects a picture from the computer large onto the wall.
A template that sets the appearance of all the slides.
Movement or appearance of elements on a slide.

gewusst: In German, a projector is called a “Beamer”, which sounds English but is used in this sense almost only in German-speaking countries.
In Switzerland the overhead projector is often called a “Hellraumprojektor”.
In some presentation competitions, the slides change automatically after a few seconds and the speakers have to keep up.

teile.einleitung: A register is a very small and very fast storage place directly in a computer's processor. This is where the numbers and addresses the processor is currently working with are kept. Registers are like a cook's hands: what he is working on right now he holds directly in his hand, not in the store cupboard.
wichtigste: A register is a very fast storage place directly in the processor.
The program counter stores the address of the next instruction.
The instruction register contains the instruction being carried out right now.
In simple processors, the results of the arithmetic unit end up in the accumulator.
The stack pointer points to the current end of the stack.
In the status register, flags show properties of a result, for example whether it was zero.
The x86-64 architecture has 16 general-purpose registers.

abschnitte.text: A **register** is a storage place inside the **processor**. It is much smaller than the main memory, but also much faster. A register usually holds only a single number, often with 64 bits in today's processors. The processor can access it in a single clock cycle. That is why it first fetches data from main memory into registers before calculating with it.

The **program counter** remembers the address of the next instruction in memory. The processor fetches this instruction and puts it into the **instruction register**. There it is decoded and carried out. Then the program counter counts on, and the whole thing starts again. When a program jumps, the program counter is simply set to a different address.

In simple processors, the results of the arithmetic unit end up in a special register, the **accumulator**. The word means “collector”, because results collect there. Modern processors have several **general-purpose registers** for this, which can be used for many things. The x86-64 architecture, which is in most of today's PCs, has 16 of them. Many smartphone processors with ARM architecture even have 31 general-purpose registers.

The **stack pointer** points to the current end of the stack in memory. The stack works like a pile of plates: whatever was put on last is taken off first. The processor stores return addresses there, for example, when a subroutine is called. When the subroutine is finished, it fetches the address back and carries on from there. In this way subroutines can even call themselves.

The **status register** consists of individual bits, the **flags**. Each flag describes a property of the last result. The zero flag is set if the result is zero. The carry flag shows, after an addition, a carry out of the most significant bit, similar to written arithmetic. With flags, a program decides, for example, whether to jump or carry on.

Registers are at the top of the **memory hierarchy**. Below them come the cache, the main memory and finally the hard drive or SSD. The further down, the bigger but also the slower the memory becomes. A computer has only a few dozen registers but billions of bytes of main memory. Good compilers therefore try to keep frequently used values in registers as much as possible.

begriffe.erklaerung: The calculating centre of the computer, also called the CPU.
A register with the address of the next instruction.
A register in which calculation results end up in simple processors.
A single bit that shows something like a little flag.
An area of memory where the last thing put in is the first to come out.

gewusst: The flag is called that because it is raised like a little flag when something is true.
Accessing a register is many times faster than accessing main memory.
The x86-64 standard was originally developed by the company AMD and is therefore also called AMD64.

teile.einleitung: A hash table is a data structure in which a computer can store data and find it again at lightning speed. A calculation rule, the hash function, works out directly from each key the number of the place where the entry is stored. So the computer does not have to search the whole list, rather like a cloakroom with numbered hooks.
wichtigste: A hash table stores pairs of keys and values.
The hash function works out the place in the table from the key.
On average a search takes only O(1), that is roughly the same time however big the table is.
If two keys get the same place, this is called a collision.
Collisions are resolved with chaining or with open addressing such as linear probing.
In the worst case a search can take O(n).
In Python, the data type dict is a hash table inside.

abschnitte.text: A hash table is a row of numbered places, also called **buckets**. Each entry consists of a **key**, for example a name, and a value, for example a telephone number. Instead of looking at all the entries in turn, the computer works out at once where the entry it is looking for must be. That is why a search is possible in constant time on average, which is written as O(1).

The **hash function** turns a key into a place number. A simple example is h(k) = k mod 7, that is the remainder when dividing by 7. The key 23 then lands in place 2, because 23 divided by 7 is 3 remainder 2. A good hash function spreads the entries as evenly as possible over all the places.

Sometimes two different keys get the same place; this is called a **collision**. In **chaining**, each place keeps a small list of all the entries that have landed there. In open addressing you look for another free place, and in **linear probing** simply the next one. If very many keys land in the same place, you have to check them all, and in the worst case a search takes O(n).

The **load factor** tells you how full the table is: the number of entries divided by the number of places. With 75 entries and 100 places it is therefore 0.75. If the table gets too full, collisions pile up and everything slows down. Then you do a **rehash**: the table is made bigger and all the entries are shared out again.

Programming languages have hash tables built in; in Python the type is called **dict**, in Java, for example, HashMap. Databases use them to find entries quickly. Spellcheckers, caches in the browser and contact lists on the mobile phone also often work with hash tables. The IBM researcher Hans Peter Luhn described the idea of hashing as early as the 1950s.

begriffe.erklaerung: The feature by which you search for an entry, for example a name.
The number that the hash function works out from a key.
Two different keys land in the same place.
Each place keeps a list of all the entries that have landed there.
How full the table is, worked out as entries divided by places.

gewusst: A cloakroom with numbered tickets works much like a hash table: the number tells you at once where your jacket is hanging.
Even with a huge hash table with millions of entries, a search usually takes hardly any longer than with a small one.
Hans Peter Luhn, who helped to found hashing, also invented a check digit formula that is still used for credit card numbers today.

teile.einleitung: Artificial intelligence, AI for short, refers to computer programs that solve tasks for which people normally need their minds. These include recognising pictures, understanding language, translating texts or answering questions. AI usually learns from a huge number of examples, but it does not think or feel like a person.
wichtigste: In German, artificial intelligence is called “Künstliche Intelligenz”, KI for short; in English it is AI.
An AI learns to recognise cats in photos, for example, with a huge number of example pictures.
Mobile phones with AI can recognise their owner by their face.
AI is good at translating texts and processing language.
A chatbot is a program you can write to as if it were a person.
An AI has no real feelings like a person.
You should always check important answers from an AI.
You do not tell an AI in a chat your address or your password.

abschnitte.text: **Artificial intelligence** is a branch of computer science that aims to make computers act intelligently. In English it is called **AI** for short. Today's AI is usually specialised in particular tasks, such as playing chess, translating languages or recognising faces. An AI that can do everything as well as a person does not exist so far.

Most modern AI systems use **machine learning**. Instead of programming every rule one by one, you show the computer a huge number of examples, such as thousands of photos with and without cats. The program finds patterns by itself that let it recognise cats. For this, **artificial neural networks** are often used, which are loosely inspired by the brain.

AI is in many devices: the mobile phone uses **face recognition** to decide who may unlock it. Translation programs translate texts into other languages in seconds. Voice assistants understand spoken commands, and streaming services suggest suitable films. A **chatbot** like ChatGPT, which appeared at the end of 2022, can answer questions in full sentences.

The term artificial intelligence was created in 1956 at a conference in Dartmouth in the USA. In 1997 the IBM computer **Deep Blue** beat the world chess champion Garry Kasparov. In 2016 the program AlphaGo beat one of the best players of the difficult board game Go. Switzerland also does a lot of research on AI, for example at ETH Zurich, at EPFL in Lausanne and at the IDSIA institute in Ticino.

An AI has no consciousness and no real feelings, even if it sounds friendly. It can be wrong and sometimes convincingly make things up, so you should **check** important answers. You do not give an AI in a chat personal details such as your address and password. You should also be careful with pictures and voices created by an AI, so-called **deepfakes**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Computers learn from examples instead of being programmed with fixed rules.
A program you can write to as if it were a person.
The many examples an AI learns from.
Exact step-by-step instructions for the computer.
A picture, video or sound recording faked with AI.

gewusst: As early as 1950, Alan Turing proposed a test to check whether a machine can write like a person.
An AI does not know whether its answer is correct; it only calculates what is most likely to fit.
Training large AI models needs huge data centres with thousands of special chips.

teile.einleitung: The GNU General Public License, GPL for short, is one of the best-known licences for free software. It allows everyone to use, change and pass on a program, but requires that changed versions also stay free. It was written by Richard Stallman, the founder of the free software movement.
wichtigste: The GPL is a licence for free software.
It was written by Richard Stallman and is published by the Free Software Foundation.
The first version appeared in 1989, version 2 in 1991 and version 3 in 2007.
Under the principle of copyleft, derived works must be passed on under the same conditions.
Anyone who passes on a GPL program in compiled form must also make the source code available.
The Linux kernel is under version 2 of the GPL.
The Affero GPL also applies when software is only used as a service over a network.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who writes a program holds the **copyright** in it, as with a book or a song. With a **licence** you set out what others may do with the program. With many commercial programs you may only use them, but not change them or pass them on. The GPL takes a different path and gives all users wide freedoms. It is the best-known licence for **free software**.

The **Free Software Foundation** defines four basic freedoms. You may run the program for any purpose. You may study how it works and change it. You may pass on copies, and you may also pass on the improved versions. For this to be possible, you need access to the **source code**, that is the program text that people can read.

The heart of the GPL is **copyleft**, a play on the word copyright. It means: anyone who changes a GPL program and passes it on must also publish the new version under the GPL. If you pass on a program in compiled form, you must also make the source code available. In this way nobody can take a free program and turn it into a closed one. The **Affero GPL** extends this rule to programs that are only used as a service over a network.

**Richard Stallman** worked at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and in 1983 started the GNU project, a free operating system. GNU is a recursive abbreviation and stands for “GNU’s Not Unix”. In 1985 he founded the Free Software Foundation. The first version of the GPL appeared in 1989, and the very widespread version 2 in 1991. Version 3 of 2007 contains, among other things, rules against devices that technically block changed software.

The most famous example is the **Linux kernel**, which is under version 2 of the GPL. Linux today runs on many servers, in Android smartphones and in supercomputers. Other well-known GPL programs are the image editing program GIMP, the media player VLC and the blogging software WordPress. There are also more permissive licences such as the MIT licence, which do not require copyleft.

begriffe.erklaerung: A permission that sets out what you may do with a work.
The text of a program that people can read.
The rule that changed versions must stay under the same free conditions.
Software that you may use, study, change and pass on.
To translate source code into a program that the computer can run directly.

gewusst: The mascot of the GNU project is a gnu, an African antelope.
In free software, “free” mainly means freedom and not necessarily free of charge; you may also sell GPL software.
The abbreviation GNU contains itself, which is why it is called recursive.

teile.einleitung: The hexadecimal system is a number system with base 16. For this it needs 16 digits: 0 to 9 and the letters A to F. Computer scientists love it because it lets them write long rows of zeros and ones briefly and clearly.
wichtigste: The hexadecimal system has base 16.
The digits are 0 to 9 and A to F, where F has the value 15.
The hexadecimal number 10 is equal to the decimal number 16.
One hexadecimal digit stands for exactly 4 bits.
The decimal number 255 is written as FF in hexadecimal.
Web colours such as #FF0000 for red are written in hexadecimal.
In hexadecimal, 9F is followed by the number A0.

abschnitte.text: In the familiar **decimal system** we count with ten digits from 0 to 9. The **hexadecimal system** has sixteen digits, so after 9 come the letters A, B, C, D, E and F. A means 10, B means 11 and so on up to F with the value 15. After F comes 10, which in the hexadecimal system stands for sixteen.

Each place is worth 16 times as much as the place to its right. In **1F**, the 1 stands for 1 times 16 and the F for 15, so together 31. In **2A** that gives 2 times 16 plus 10, so 42. The largest two-digit hexadecimal number is FF, which is 15 times 16 plus 15, so 255.

Computers calculate in the **binary system** with only 0 and 1. Because 16 is exactly 2 to the power of 4, one hexadecimal digit fits exactly 4 bits. A **byte** of 8 bits can therefore always be written with exactly two hexadecimal digits. Instead of 11111111 you simply write FF, which is much shorter and less likely to lead to mistakes.

On websites, colours are often given as a **colour code** such as #FF0000. The first two digits stand for red, the middle ones for green and the last ones for blue, each from 00 to FF. #FF0000 is therefore pure red, #00FF00 green and #0000FF blue. #FFFFFF is white and #000000 is black.

abschnitte.titel: Where else you meet hex numbers
abschnitte.text: Programmers often write hexadecimal numbers with the prefix **0x**, for example 0xFF. Memory addresses, error codes and the MAC addresses of network devices are shown in hexadecimal. IPv6 addresses also consist of hexadecimal digits. With a hex editor you can look at the contents of any file as hexadecimal numbers.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number of different digits in a number system.
The smallest unit of information; it is 0 or 1.
A group of 8 bits, which can be shown with two hexadecimal digits.
A number system with only two digits, 0 and 1.
A hexadecimal number such as #FF0000 that describes a colour.

gewusst: With only six places in the hexadecimal system, over 16 million different colours can be described.
Programmers sometimes write words such as CAFE or BEEF as hex numbers, because they consist only of the letters A to F.
The number 42 is 2A in hexadecimal.

teile.einleitung: A firewall is a protective program or device that controls which data may go into and out of a network. It works like a doorman who only lets in guests who are on the list.
wichtigste: A firewall controls the data traffic between networks.
The English word firewall literally means a wall that stops fire from spreading.
At home there is often a firewall in the router, which protects the whole home network.
A firewall directly on your own computer is called a personal firewall.
It decides according to fixed rules, for example about addresses and ports.
A port is a number that marks a particular service on a device.
A firewall alone does not protect against all the dangers on the internet.

abschnitte.text: A **firewall** sits between a network and the internet and checks all the data that wants to get through. It lets permitted data pass and blocks suspicious data. The name comes from the fire wall in buildings, which stops a fire from spreading. In the same way, the firewall is meant to stop attacks from the internet from spreading into your own network. The first firewalls for computer networks appeared at the end of the 1980s.

A firewall works with fixed **rules**. A rule can say, for example, that connections from a particular address are forbidden. Other rules concern **ports**, which are numbers for particular services on a device. Websites mostly use port 443, emails use other ports. In this way a firewall can, for instance, allow websites but block other kinds of access.

abschnitte.titel: Firewalls at home and on the computer
abschnitte.text: In most households there is a firewall in the **router**, the device that connects the home network to the internet. It protects all the devices in the house at the same time. In addition, operating systems such as Windows or macOS have a built-in firewall that runs directly on the computer. This is called a **personal firewall**. You should not simply switch it off, because otherwise the computer can be attacked more easily.

Big companies, banks and schools often have their own powerful firewall devices. They protect thousands of computers and important data. Some firewalls even look inside the data to recognise malicious programs. In schools, a firewall can also block certain websites. Experts in **IT security** keep adapting the rules to new dangers.

A firewall does not protect against all the dangers on the internet. If you click on a dangerous link yourself or open a suspicious attachment, it often does not help. That is why further protective measures are needed, such as **updates**, an antivirus program and secure passwords. Most important of all, though, is to be careful yourself. Experts compare security to an onion made of several layers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A protective system that controls which data may enter a network.
A number that marks a particular service on a device.
A device that connects the home network to the internet.
Several computers and devices that are connected to each other.

gewusst: Real fire walls have existed in houses for centuries, long before there were computers.
A firewall can check many thousands of data packets per second.
There are 65,535 different port numbers that a device can use.

teile.einleitung: An Ozobot is a small robot about the size of a walnut. It moves over paper or tablets and follows drawn lines as it goes. You can give it commands with colour codes and on the computer, which is why it is often used in schools for learning to program.
wichtigste: An Ozobot is a small robot for learning to program.
It follows a line drawn on paper.
Its sensors for recognising the lines are on its underside.
For the colour codes you need pens in black, red, green and blue.
A colour code is a sequence of coloured patches on the line that gives a command.
At a junction without a colour code, the Ozobot chooses a route at random.
You can also program it with blocks on the computer.

abschnitte.text: The **Ozobot** is a small educational robot developed by the American company Evollve. It came on the market from 2014 and is only a few centimetres in size. Inside there is a rechargeable battery, two small motors with wheels and several **sensors**. A coloured light on top shows what the robot is doing at the moment.

On its underside, the Ozobot has sensors that recognise colours and lines. If you draw a line on paper with a thick felt-tip pen, it follows it. The line should be about as wide as a felt-tip nib and may have curves. If it comes to a **junction** without a command, it decides at random where to go.

A **colour code** is a short sequence of coloured patches directly on the line. For this you need the four colours black, red, green and blue. Each combination means a different command, for example go faster, go slower, turn round or turn left at the next junction. In this way you can draw a whole program on a sheet of paper.

With the **OzoBlockly** software you can also control the Ozobot without lines. You put together colourful **programming blocks** on a computer or tablet, similar to Scratch. The program is then transferred to the robot through light signals from the screen or through a connection. In this way you learn about loops, conditions and sequences.

In many Swiss schools the Ozobot is used in the subject **media and computer science**, which is part of the Lehrplan 21 curriculum. Even children in the lower primary years can solve simple tasks with pens. Older pupils use it to program small races, mazes or dances. The robot shows clearly that a computer does exactly what you tell it to do.

begriffe.erklaerung: A machine that carries out tasks by itself following a program.
A component that measures something in the surroundings, for example light or colour.
A sequence of coloured patches that gives the Ozobot a command.
A sequence of commands that a machine carries out.

gewusst: An Ozobot can also move along lines drawn on a tablet screen.
With colour codes you can even tell an Ozobot to dance in a circle for a while.
Because the robot is so small, several Ozobots fit together on a single A4 sheet.

teile.einleitung: A program window is a rectangular area on the screen in which a program is displayed. You can open, move, enlarge, shrink and close windows. Thanks to windows, you can work with several programs at the same time.
wichtigste: The top bar of a window is called the title bar.
In Windows you close a window with the X at the top right.
The button with the small line shrinks the window down into the taskbar.
A maximised window fills the whole screen.
You move a window by dragging its title bar.
The active window is the one you clicked on last.
With the scroll bar you move through long content.

abschnitte.text: A **window** is an area on the screen in which a program shows its content. This can be a text document, a website or a game. Many windows can be open at the same time and can also overlap. An operating system such as Windows even gets its name from the English word for these windows.

At the top is the **title bar** with the name of the program or document. In Windows there are three buttons on the right of the title bar: a line to minimise, a square to maximise and an X to close. At the edge there is often a **scroll bar**, which you use to move through long texts. Below the title bar there is usually a menu bar and the actual work area.

If you drag the title bar with the mouse, you move the window to another place. At the edges and corners you can change its size. Minimised windows disappear into the **taskbar** at the bottom of the screen and can be opened again from there. On a Mac the buttons are three coloured dots at the top left.

If several windows are open, only one is ever **active**, namely the one clicked on last. It lies on top and reacts to input from the keyboard. With the key combination Alt and Tab you can switch quickly between open windows in Windows. The Windows key and D shows the desktop by clearing all the windows away.

The idea of windows came about in the 1970s at Xerox's research centre, among other things with the **Xerox Alto** computer of 1973. Windows became well known in 1984 with the Apple Macintosh. Microsoft brought out the first version of Windows in 1985. Today there are windows on almost all computers, and even mobile phones show apps in a similar way.

begriffe.erklaerung: The top bar of a window with the name of the program.
The bar at the bottom of the Windows screen with the open programs.
Make a window so big that it fills the whole screen.
Shrink a window down into the taskbar without closing it.
A bar at the edge with which you move through long content.

gewusst: Windows together with a mouse and icons are called a graphical user interface.
You can have dozens of windows open at the same time on a computer, as long as there is enough memory.

teile.einleitung: The Hypertext Transfer Protocol, HTTP for short, is the agreement by which your browser and a web server talk to each other. Every time you open a web page, your browser sends an HTTP request, and the server answers. Without HTTP there would be no World Wide Web.
wichtigste: HTTP sets out how browsers and web servers exchange data.
Tim Berners-Lee developed HTTP from 1989 onwards at CERN.
The status code 404 means that the requested page was not found.
Status codes in the 5xx class show an error on the server.
With the method POST you send form data to the server.
HTTP is stateless, which is why websites remember sign-ins with cookies.
HTTP/3 is built on the transport protocol QUIC.

abschnitte.text: HTTP works on the principle of **request and response**. The browser, the **client**, sends a request to a **server**, for example “Give me the home page”. The server answers with a status code and the content, such as an HTML file or a picture. For a single web page, dozens of such requests often take place.

Every request has a **method**, which says what the browser wants. With **GET** you fetch data, for example a web page. With **POST** you send data in the body of the request to the server, such as a completed form. Other methods are PUT for storing and DELETE for deleting data.

The server begins every response with a three-digit **status code**. 200 means “everything is fine”, and 301 is a permanent **redirect** to a new address. 404 means that the page you were looking for was not found, and it is probably the best-known code. Codes beginning with 4 are errors on the browser’s side, codes beginning with 5 errors on the server.

The physicist **Tim Berners-Lee** developed HTTP from 1989 onwards at **CERN** near Geneva, together with HTML and the first web browser. The version HTTP/1.1 was the most widely used for decades. **HTTP/2** made it possible to send several requests in parallel over a single connection. **HTTP/3** uses the faster transport protocol QUIC.

HTTP is **stateless**, which means that each request stands on its own and the server forgets everything afterwards. So that a sign-in nevertheless lasts over many clicks, websites use **cookies**. Normal HTTP sends everything unencrypted, which is why there is **HTTPS**. There the connection is encrypted, which many browsers show with a small padlock.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fixed agreement on how two computers communicate with each other.
A three-digit number with which the server says whether a request worked.
The encrypted, secure form of HTTP.
The device or program that asks a server for something, for example your browser.

gewusst: There is even a joke status code 418, which means “I’m a teapot”.
Every web address actually begins with “http://” or “https://”, even if modern browsers often hide it.
Many websites make their 404 error page funny, for example with games or drawings.

teile.einleitung: Personal data is any information that reveals something about you and with which someone can recognise or find you. This includes your name, your address, your telephone number or photos of you. On the internet it is especially important to take good care of this data.
wichtigste: Your address is personal data.
You do not give your phone number to strangers on the internet.
In games, a made-up name is safer than your real name.
You do not post the name of your school publicly, because otherwise people could find you.
If a website asks for your name and address, you ask your parents first.
Your password is a secret that you do not pass on to anyone.
General knowledge such as the capital of Switzerland is not personal data.

abschnitte.text: Personal data, called **“Personendaten”** in Swiss law, is information about a particular person. Examples are name, birthday, address, phone number, email address and photos. Even the name of your school or your sports club can reveal where you often are. The capital of Switzerland or today's weather, on the other hand, are not personal data, because they say nothing about you.

A photo in front of your house with the **house number** visible shows strangers where you live. School uniforms, street signs or number plates in the background can also give clues. Many mobile phones also store the place where a picture was taken. That is why it is worth looking at photos carefully before posting them.

Many **apps and websites** collect data about you, such as what you click on, how long you play or where you are. Companies use this information to show you suitable advertising or to improve what they offer. Some data is also sold on to other companies. That is why you should only give the details that are really necessary.

In games and chats, use a **made-up name** instead of your real name. Never give your address, phone number or password to strangers, even if they seem friendly. If a website asks for personal details, talk to your parents first. Set the **privacy settings** in apps so that only friends can see your posts.

In Switzerland the **Data Protection Act** regulates how personal data is handled; a revised version has applied since 1 September 2023. Companies must explain which data they collect and what they need it for. You have the right to find out which data a company has stored about you. If you have questions, the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner, FDPIC for short, can help.

begriffe.erklaerung: Any information relating to a particular person.
Rules and measures that protect your personal data from misuse.
The personal sphere that concerns only you and the people you trust.
A secret word with which you log in to an account.

gewusst: Once something is on the internet, it is often almost impossible to delete it completely.
Many phone photos contain hidden details about where they were taken, which you can switch off in the settings.

teile.einleitung: An emoji is a small picture symbol that is used in messages, emails or posts. There are emojis for faces, animals, food, flags and much more. With them you can show feelings without writing many words.
wichtigste: An emoji is a small picture symbol.
The word “emoji” comes from Japanese.
Emojis are often used to show feelings.
The thumbs up usually means “good” or “agreed”.
World Emoji Day is on 17 July.
An emoji looks a little different depending on the device.
The forerunners of emojis are emoticons made of punctuation marks, such as :-).

abschnitte.text: The word **emoji** comes from Japanese: “e” means picture and “moji” means written character. So it has nothing to do with the English word “emotion”, even though it sounds similar. The first well-known emojis were designed in 1999 by the Japanese **Shigetaka Kurita** for a mobile phone internet service. His set of 176 small pictures is now part of the collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

Even before emojis there were **emoticons**, faces made of punctuation marks. The sequence :-) shows a laughing face if you tilt your head to the side. In 1982 the computer scientist Scott Fahlman suggested using :-) for messages that were meant as a joke. Many programs now automatically turn such sequences into an emoji.

In written messages there is no voice, face or gesture. Emojis help to show **feelings**, such as joy, surprise or sadness. An emoji with a tear and a sad mouth shows that you are sad, and a thumbs up usually means “good” or “agreed”. But emojis can also be misunderstood, because people interpret them differently. For important messages it is therefore better to write in words as well what you mean.

So that emojis work on all devices, they are set in **Unicode**, a worldwide standard for written characters. Each emoji has its own number there, just like each letter. But what it looks like exactly is decided by each manufacturer. That is why an emoji often looks a little different on an iPhone, an Android phone or in an app. New emojis are added every year, and today there are several thousand.

abschnitte.titel: Emojis in culture and everyday life
abschnitte.text: **World Emoji Day** is celebrated every year on 17 July. The date comes from the calendar emoji, which shows 17 July on many devices. In 2015 the Oxford Dictionaries chose the emoji “face with tears of joy” as word of the year. There are also emojis for national flags, including the Swiss flag, and for many skin colours. This is meant to let as many people as possible see themselves in them.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small picture symbol in digital texts.
A face made of punctuation marks, for example :-).
A worldwide standard that gives every written character a number.
A company that makes and designs a device or software.

gewusst: The word emoji has nothing to do with the English “emotion”, even though it sounds similar.
The emoji “face with tears of joy” was chosen as word of the year in 2015, even though it is not a word at all.
Anyone can suggest new emojis to the Unicode Consortium, but only a few are accepted.

teile.einleitung: NoSQL is an umbrella term for databases that do not store data in classic tables with rows and columns. Today the name usually stands for “Not only SQL”. Such databases are often built for huge amounts of data and many servers, as needed by large web services and social networks.
wichtigste: Today NoSQL usually stands for “Not only SQL”.
There are different kinds: document, key-value, column-oriented and graph databases.
MongoDB is a document-oriented database.
Redis is a key-value database and is often used as a fast cache.
Graph databases such as Neo4j are suitable for highly connected data.
With sharding, data is distributed across many servers according to a key.
In the event of a network partition, the CAP theorem requires a choice between consistency and availability.
Many NoSQL systems follow the BASE principle instead of ACID.

abschnitte.text: Classic **relational databases** store data in tables and are queried with the language **SQL**. NoSQL databases take other routes and store data, for example, as documents or as a network. The term became well known from 2009, when many new databases were created for large web services. Today NoSQL is usually understood as “Not only SQL”, because these systems complement classic databases rather than replace them.

A **document database** such as MongoDB stores records as flexible documents, similar to index cards with different fields. A **key-value database** such as Redis works like a huge dictionary and is often used as a fast cache. Column-oriented databases such as Apache Cassandra were originally developed at Facebook and released as open source in 2008. **Graph databases** such as Neo4j store connections, such as friendships in social networks.

Large services have so much data that a single server is not enough. With **sharding**, the data is divided up according to a key, for example all user names from A to M on one server and the rest on another. In addition, several copies are often kept so that nothing is lost if a computer fails. This distribution is called horizontal scaling.

The **CAP theorem** of the computer scientist Eric Brewer describes a dilemma of distributed databases. If the connection between the servers fails, a so-called network partition, you have to choose: either all servers always answer immediately, or all of them always show the same state. Both at once are then not possible. Many NoSQL systems choose availability and accept that copies may differ for a short time.

Classic databases guarantee **ACID**, which means, among other things, that every change is valid everywhere immediately and stored safely. Many NoSQL systems instead follow the **BASE** principle, which stands for “Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency”. **Eventual consistency** means that all copies agree again after a certain time. For a like counter this is no problem, but for a bank account it would be risky.

begriffe.erklaerung: An organised system for storing and querying data.
A query language for databases with tables.
Dividing data across several servers according to a key.
Everyone sees the same, correct state of the data at the same time.
Expanding a system so that it can cope with more data or users.

gewusst: Originally, “NoSQL” was the name of a hashtag for a developers' meeting in 2009.
In social networks, a like counter may show different numbers for a short time without anything bad happening.
Many websites combine a classic SQL database with a NoSQL database used as a cache.

teile.einleitung: A comment is a piece of text in program code that is meant only for people. The computer simply skips it when running the program. With comments, programmers explain what their code does and why.
wichtigste: A comment explains the code for people.
In Python a comment begins with the character #.
Python ignores comments when running a program.
The line print("Hi")  # greeting only outputs Hi.
Making a line of code temporarily inactive with # is called commenting out.
In JavaScript a one-line comment begins with //.
In Python, explanatory texts over several lines are often written between three quotation marks.
If # is inside quotation marks it is not a comment, so print("#Tag") outputs #Tag.

abschnitte.text: Programs are not only read by the computer but also by **people**. A **comment** is a note in the source code that explains what a part does. When the program runs, the computer simply **ignores** the comment. So it never changes what the program does.

Every programming language has its own characters for comments. In **Python** a comment begins with #, and everything after it up to the end of the line is skipped. In **JavaScript**, Java and C a one-line comment begins with //. Longer comments over several lines go between /* and */ there, and in HTML between <!-- and -->.

In Python, longer explanatory texts are often written between **three quotation marks** at the beginning and the end. If such a text is right at the start of a function or class, it is called a **docstring**. It describes what the function does and which values it expects. Programs and development environments can display docstrings when you look for help on a function.

Sometimes you want to switch off a line of code briefly without deleting it. Then you put a # in front of it, and the line becomes a comment. This is called **commenting out**. It helps when **looking for errors**, because you can test whether a particular line is causing a problem.

Good comments mainly explain **why** something was done in a certain way, not just what happens. A comment like “adds 1” above a line that adds 1 is not much help. Comments should be short, clear and always up to date. If you comment your code well, you will still understand it months later, and others in the **team** find their way around more quickly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A note in program code that the computer skips.
The text of a program written by people.
Temporarily turning a line of code into a comment and so making it inactive.
An explanatory text in three quotation marks at the beginning of a Python function or class.

gewusst: In the source code of large programs, experts sometimes find funny or annoyed comments left by earlier programmers.
The character # is called “Raute” in German and often hash in English.
Comments do not make a program slower, because the computer skips them when running it.

teile.einleitung: A pixel is the smallest dot of a digital picture. Every photo on a mobile phone and every picture on a screen consists of thousands or millions of these tiny dots. Only together do they make up the whole picture.
wichtigste: A picture on the screen consists of many pixels.
The word pixel is short for the English “picture element”.
If you enlarge a picture a lot, you see small squares.
A screen mixes all colours from the three light colours red, green and blue.
A pixel that does not light up at all appears black.
The more pixels a picture has, the sharper it looks.
Art made of a few, clearly visible pixels is called pixel art.

abschnitte.text: A **pixel** is a tiny coloured square, similar to a little stone in a mosaic. A digital picture is built like a grid of rows and columns of pixels. You work out the number of pixels like this: pixels per row times the number of rows. So a picture with 3 rows of 4 pixels each has 12 pixels.

Each pixel on a screen consists of three even smaller lights in **red, green and blue**. This is called **RGB**. If all three shine brightly, you see white; if none shines, the pixel is black. Different brightnesses of the three colours produce millions of shades, for example yellow from red and green.

The number of pixels in a picture is called its **resolution**. A Full HD screen has 1,920 by 1,080 pixels, which is over two million dots. A 4K screen even has about eight million pixels. The more pixels, the finer and sharper the picture looks, because you can no longer see the individual dots.

Digital cameras and phone cameras also work with pixels. Their image sensor has millions of tiny light-sensitive points. One million pixels is called a **megapixel**. Many phone cameras today have 12 megapixels or more.

Early video games only had a few pixels available, which is why characters looked blocky. Famous examples are the aliens from “Space Invaders” or the first Super Mario. This way of building pictures from clearly visible pixels is called **pixel art**. It is still popular today, for example in the game “Minecraft”, whose world consists of blocks with pixel patterns.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest dot of a digital picture.
The number of pixels in a picture or screen.
The three light colours red, green and blue, from which a screen mixes all colours.
One million pixels.
Art made of a few, clearly visible pixels.

gewusst: With a magnifying glass you can see the red, green and blue lights on some screens.
A Full HD picture has exactly 2,073,600 pixels.
Many cross-stitch patterns and fuse bead pictures are really pixel art made of fabric or plastic.

teile.einleitung: IPv6 is the newer version of the Internet Protocol, the rules by which devices on the internet get addresses. An IPv6 address is 128 bits long and so offers so many addresses that they will practically never run out. IPv6 was developed because the addresses of the older IPv4 were running out.
wichtigste: IPv6 is the successor of IPv4.
An IPv6 address has 128 bits and 32 hexadecimal digits.
Addresses are written in eight blocks with colons.
The abbreviation “::” for zero blocks may appear at most once.
The loopback address is ::1.
With SLAAC, devices form their own address without a central server.
Broadcast no longer exists in IPv6.

abschnitte.text: The older **IPv4** has 32-bit addresses, which is only about 4.3 billion of them. With smartphones, computers and connected devices all over the world, that is no longer enough. **IPv6** uses 128 bits and offers about 340 undecillion addresses, a number with 39 digits. With that you could give every grain of sand on Earth lots of its own addresses.

An IPv6 address consists of 32 **hexadecimal digits**, divided into eight blocks of four digits each. An example is 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001. Leading zeros in a block may be left out, and a run of blocks containing only zeros is replaced by **“::”**. This turns the address into 2001:db8::1, where “::” may appear at most once, otherwise the address would not be unambiguous.

The **loopback address** ::1 means “this computer itself”. Addresses beginning with fe80::/10 are **link-local** and only apply in your own local network. Instead of broadcast to all devices, IPv6 has multicast to selected groups. With **SLAAC**, a device can form a global address for itself from information provided by the router.

The **header**, the front part of every packet, is simpler in IPv6. The header checksum of IPv4 was removed without replacement, because other layers already check for errors. Routers no longer have to split packets up; the sender does that. The Time to Live field is called Hop Limit in IPv6.

The basics of IPv6 were laid down in the 1990s. On 6 June 2012, large companies switched IPv6 on permanently at the “World IPv6 Launch”. Today IPv4 and IPv6 often run side by side at the same time, which is called **dual stack**. Switzerland is one of the countries where IPv6 is already widely used.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number by which a device can be reached on the internet.
A number system with the digits 0 to 9 and A to F.
An address a computer uses to address itself.
A device speaks IPv4 and IPv6 at the same time.
A method by which devices form their own IPv6 address.

gewusst: A version 5 of the Internet Protocol was never generally introduced, so people jumped straight from IPv4 to IPv6.
The address 2001:db8:: is reserved only for examples and documentation.
IPv6 has about 79 octillion times more addresses than IPv4.

teile.einleitung: Hardware is everything on a computer that you can touch: the case, keyboard, screen, processor and cables. The counterpart is software, that is the programs that run on the hardware. Only when the two work together can a computer play games, calculate or write texts.
wichtigste: Hardware is the physical parts of a computer.
With the keyboard you type in letters, with the mouse you move the pointer.
On the screen you see pictures and texts, and the loudspeaker gives out sounds.
The processor is the part that calculates in the computer.
A printer puts texts on paper, and a microphone records your voice.
Every computer needs electricity to run at all.
A laptop is a computer that you can fold shut and take with you.

abschnitte.text: With **input devices** you give the computer information. The **keyboard** is used to type letters and numbers, and the **mouse** to move the pointer and click. With the microphone the computer records your voice, and with a camera pictures. A tablet’s touchscreen is also an input device, because it senses your fingers.

**Output devices** show you what the computer has done. Pictures, texts and videos appear on the **screen**. The loudspeaker or headphones give out sounds and music. The **printer** puts a text or a photo from the computer onto paper.

The most important part is the **processor**, also called the CPU, which manages billions of calculation steps per second. The **working memory** briefly remembers what the computer is working on at that moment. On the hard disk or SSD, photos, games and documents stay stored even after switching off. All the parts sit on a large circuit board, the motherboard, and are supplied with electricity by the power supply.

A **desktop PC** stands in one place on the desk and has a separate screen. A **laptop** has the screen, keyboard and battery in one device and can be folded shut. Smartphones, tablets, games consoles and even modern cars also contain computer hardware. Large data centres consist of thousands of servers, which, for example, provide websites.

In 1941 the German Konrad Zuse built the Z3, one of the first working programmable computers. Early computers filled whole rooms and weighed many tonnes. In 1950 **ETH Zurich** rented Zuse’s Z4 computer and later built a Swiss computer of its own, the ERMETH. Today every mobile phone has more computing power than these huge machines.

The company **Logitech**, known for mice, keyboards and webcams, was founded in 1981 in Apples in the canton of Vaud. In Switzerland old devices are taken back free of charge, thanks to the advance recycling fee. Electronic waste never belongs in the household rubbish, but goes back to the shop or to a collection point. In this way valuable metals such as copper and gold can be used again.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the parts of a computer that you can touch.
Programs and apps that run on the hardware.
The calculating centre of the computer, also called the CPU.
A fast short-term memory that is cleared when you switch off.
A device that you connect to the computer, for example a printer.

gewusst: A modern processor contains billions of tiny switches called transistors.
In English, the word “hardware” originally meant something like ironmongery.
The first computer mouse, from the 1960s, had a case made of wood.

teile.einleitung: In computer science, a list is a data structure in which several values are stored in order. Like a shopping list, each element has its fixed place. Lists are among the most important tools in programming, for example in the Python language.
wichtigste: A list stores several values in a fixed order.
In Python lists are written with square brackets, for example [4, 8, 15].
The places are counted starting from 0, not 1.
With append you add an element at the end, with pop you remove the last one.
If you access a place that does not exist, an error occurs.
In a linked list, each element points to the next one.
Lists are the basis for many other data structures.

abschnitte.text: A **list** is an ordered collection of values, such as numbers, words or names. Each value is called an **element** and has a particular place. In Python you write a list with square brackets: numbers = [4, 8, 15]. Lists can be made longer or shorter, sorted and changed.

The places in a list are addressed with an **index**, and counting starts at 0. With numbers = [4, 8, 15], numbers[1] therefore gives 8, not 4. If a list has three elements, the places are 0, 1 and 2. If you ask for l[3], you get an error called IndexError.

With l.append(5) you add 5 at the end, so [1, 2] becomes [1, 2, 5]. With l.pop() you remove the last element, so [4, 5, 6] becomes [4, 5]. With l[0] = 9 you replace the first element, so [1, 2, 3] becomes [9, 2, 3]. Other useful commands are sum([2, 4, 6]) with the result 12, max([4, 9, 2]) with the result 9 and sorted([5, 2, 8]), which gives [2, 5, 8].

There are also **linked lists**, in which the elements are not next to each other in memory. Each **node** contains the data and a pointer to its successor, like the carriages of a train that are coupled together. In the last node this reference points to null, that is, to no element. In a doubly linked list, each node also refers to its predecessor.

In a linked list you have to work your way along node by node from the front to find the k-th element. In the worst case this takes as long as the list has elements, which computer scientists write as O(n). On the other hand, inserting directly after a known node is very fast, namely O(1), regardless of the length. So depending on the task, you choose the right kind of list.

Lists are in almost every program: in the playlist of a music app, in the contacts list of a mobile phone or in the leaderboard of a game. Other data structures are also built from lists, such as the **stack**, where you always take the top element, or the queue. The programming language Lisp from 1958 was even built entirely on lists. Its name comes from “List Processing”.

begriffe.erklaerung: A way of storing data in the computer in an orderly manner.
The number of a place in a list; it starts at 0.
A building block of a linked list with data and a reference.
A reference to where another element is stored in memory.

gewusst: In Python a list can contain numbers, words and even other lists at the same time.
In Python, l[-1] gives you the last element of a list without knowing its length.

teile.einleitung: Machine learning is a field of artificial intelligence in which computers learn from examples instead of having every rule programmed into them exactly. A program sees lots of data, finds patterns in it and can then make predictions for new cases. This is how computers today recognise faces, translate texts or suggest videos.
wichtigste: In machine learning, computers learn patterns from data.
In supervised learning, a model is trained with data together with the correct answers.
In reinforcement learning, an agent learns through rewards and penalties.
The k-means method divides data without labels into a given number of groups.
Overfitting means that a model learns the training data by heart and does badly with new data.
In 1959 Arthur Samuel coined the term “machine learning”.
In 2016 the program AlphaGo beat the Go professional Lee Sedol 4 to 1.

abschnitte.text: In machine learning you do not write every rule yourself. Instead, you show the computer lots of **training data**, for example thousands of photos of cats and dogs. A learning method adjusts a **model** so that it gets better and better at telling the pictures apart. After that, the model can also judge photos it has never seen before. Machine learning is an important part of artificial intelligence.

In **supervised learning**, the model is given examples with the correct answer, the so-called label, such as “spam” or “not spam” for emails. In unsupervised learning there are no labels; the model looks for groups by itself. One example is the **k-means** method, which divides data points into a given number of groups. In **reinforcement learning**, an agent tries something out and receives rewards or penalties. This is how programs learn, for example, to play games better and better.

Many modern methods use **artificial neural networks**, which are loosely reminiscent of nerve cells in the brain. As early as 1958, Frank Rosenblatt presented the perceptron, an early artificial neuron. A network consists of many layers of such neurons, which are connected by weights. With the **backpropagation** method, you calculate how each weight affects the error and improve it step by step. Networks with very many layers are called deep learning.

A common problem is **overfitting**. The model learns the training data almost by heart instead of understanding the general pattern. With new data it then makes lots of mistakes, much like a child who has only learned the answers to an exercise by heart. That is why models are always checked with test data that was not used in training. Another problem is one-sided data, because then the model also takes on its **prejudices**.

The American **Arthur Samuel** coined the term “machine learning” in 1959 when he developed a program that learned to play draughts. For a long time, however, there were no fast computers and no large amounts of data. From about 2012, powerful graphics processors and the internet made big advances possible. In 2016 the program **AlphaGo** from the company DeepMind beat the Go professional Lee Sedol 4 to 1. Since 2022, chatbots such as ChatGPT, which are based on machine learning, have been known worldwide.

abschnitte.titel: In everyday life and in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: Machine learning is found in spam filters, translation programs, voice assistants and the suggestions of streaming services. In medicine it helps to evaluate X-ray images, and in farming to recognise weeds. In Switzerland, research on it is carried out at ETH Zurich, EPFL in Lausanne and the **IDSIA** institute in Lugano, among others. In 2025 ETH, EPFL and the national supercomputing centre CSCS released the open language model Apertus. It remains important for people to check the results critically.

begriffe.erklaerung: Examples from which a computer program learns.
The result of learning, which makes predictions for new cases.
The correct answer that belongs to a training example.
When a model learns examples by heart instead of understanding the pattern.
A computing model made of many connected artificial neurons.

gewusst: Arthur Samuel's draughts program from the 1950s learned so well that it eventually played better than its inventor.
Go has so many possible positions that people believed for a long time that computers would only beat humans at it very late.
Image recognition programs often learn from millions of photos that people have labelled beforehand.

teile.einleitung: A label is a small sign or sticker that says what something is or what is inside it. Labels help us to recognise things quickly and keep things tidy, and computers also work with such labels.
wichtigste: A label says what is in a box, a jar or a crate.
The label on an exercise book often shows your name and the subject.
On food, the label shows the use-by date and the ingredients.
A label in a T-shirt often shows the size.
A small picture helps children who cannot read yet.
A wrong label leads to mistakes, for example if the salt jar says “Sugar”.
Computers also organise data with names and keywords that work like labels.

abschnitte.text: A **label** is a sign made of paper, fabric or plastic that is stuck to or hangs from an object. It marks the object so that you know what it is or what is inside it. The German word for label, “Etikett”, comes from the French étiquette. In Switzerland people sometimes also say “Kleber” or “Anschrift”. Labels come in all sizes, from a tiny price tag to a big sign on a crate.

In the classroom, boxes often have labels such as “Pencils”, “Scissors” or “Glue”. A pair of scissors then belongs in the “Scissors” box, so that every child can find it again. A small **picture** on the label helps children who cannot read yet. Your exercise book also has a label with your name and the subject. At the airport, the label on a suitcase shows where it is to travel to.

On food in the shop, the label is especially important. It shows the **ingredients**, the use-by date and often the price. In Switzerland, **allergens** such as nuts or milk must also be clearly stated. This can be very important for people with allergies. A label must therefore always be correct, because a wrong label can mislead people.

In almost every piece of clothing there is a small sewn-in label. It shows the **size**, for example 140 or M. You can often also see what material the item is made of, such as cotton. Small symbols show how it may be washed, ironed or dried. These symbols are called care symbols.

Computers also work with labels. A **file name** such as “Holidays_2026.jpg” is a kind of label for a file. Many programs let you give photos or emails keywords, which are called **tags**. In the shop, tills read the **barcode** on the label to find the price. As in the classroom, the same applies here: only if the labelling is correct can you find everything again.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sign or sticker that says what something is or what is inside it.
A substance that causes an allergy in some people, such as nuts.
A pattern of bars that a till can read with light.
A keyword with which you label and organise data on a computer.

gewusst: Some labels contain a tiny radio chip, with which devices can read them without seeing them.
Wine bottles have long carried artistically designed labels, which some people collect.
The French word étiquette also means good manners, which is where the word etiquette comes from.

teile.einleitung: Downloading means fetching a file from the internet onto your own device and saving it there. This can be pictures, music, games, apps or documents. The German word is “Herunterladen”, which means loading down.
wichtigste: The German word for downloading is “Herunterladen”.
When downloading, a file is saved onto your device.
The opposite of downloading is uploading.
An arrow pointing down often stands for downloading.
On a computer, downloaded files often end up in the “Downloads” folder.
Big files such as a long film take the longest.
Files from unknown sites can contain a computer virus.

abschnitte.text: On the internet, files are kept on big computers called **servers**. When downloading, the server sends a copy of the file over the network to your device. Your device then saves this copy, so that you can open it even without the internet. The opposite, sending a file from you to the internet, is called **uploading**.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the file end up?
abschnitte.text: On a computer, downloaded files usually end up in the **Downloads** folder. In the browser, an **arrow pointing down** shows which files are being loaded at the moment. Apps on the mobile phone are installed automatically after downloading. If you like things tidy, clear out the download folder from time to time.

How quickly something loads depends on the **file size** and on the speed of the internet connection. A short text arrives in an instant. A photo takes a little longer, and a long film in high quality takes the longest. The speed is measured in **megabits per second**.

Not all files on the internet are harmless. Files from unknown sites can contain a **computer virus** or other malicious programs. So only download apps from official stores and ask an adult first. You should also not open email attachments from strangers.

Music, films and games are protected by **copyright**. In Switzerland it is allowed to download music and films for private use, as long as you do not pass them on. Software and games, on the other hand, may not simply be downloaded illegally. The safest way is to use official services such as streaming services and app stores.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fetching a file from the internet; in German “Herunterladen”.
Sending a file to the internet; in German “Hochladen”.
A computer on the internet that provides files and websites for others.
A program meant to harm a computer or its users, for example a virus.

gewusst: With streaming, a film is only loaded bit by bit and played straight away, instead of being saved in full.
An arrow pointing down onto a line is the sign for downloading on almost every device in the world.
A whole feature film in high quality can be several gigabytes in size.

teile.einleitung: Home computers were cheap computers for use at home, which moved into many children’s bedrooms and living rooms in the late 1970s and the 1980s. With them you could play, learn and even program yourself. Famous models such as the Commodore 64 are cult objects today.
wichtigste: Home computers were affordable computers for private people.
The Apple II of 1977 was one of the first successful home computers.
The Commodore 64 of 1982 is regarded as the best-selling home computer model of all time.
The ZX Spectrum of 1982 came from Great Britain.
Many home computers had the programming language BASIC built in.
The television was often used as the screen.
Programs were often stored on music cassettes.

abschnitte.text: Before home computers, computers were huge and expensive machines for companies, banks and universities. At the end of the 1970s, **microprocessors** became so cheap that small computers for families became possible. A typical home computer consisted of a keyboard in which all the electronics were housed. You connected it to the **television** and so did not need a monitor of your own.

The **Apple II** came out in 1977 and made the company Apple well known. In 1982 the **Commodore 64** from the USA and the **ZX Spectrum** from the British company Sinclair appeared. Other well-known devices were the Atari computers and the Amstrad CPC, which was sold in German-speaking countries under the Schneider name. In 1985 Commodore brought out the **Amiga**, which was famous for its graphics and sound.

Hard disks were far too expensive for private people back then. That is why programs and games were often stored on ordinary **music cassettes**, recorded as whistling and hissing sounds. Loading a game could take several minutes. Later **floppy disks** became more popular, because they were faster and more reliable.

On many devices, the programming language **BASIC** appeared on the screen straight after switching on. You could type in commands directly, for example to display text or do small calculations. Magazines printed whole programs, which people typed in line by line. In this way many young people took their first steps in **programming**.

Many people used home computers above all for **video games**. Besides that, people wrote letters, kept address lists or learnt vocabulary. In the 1990s, **personal computers** with Windows largely replaced home computers. Today fans collect the old devices, and with what are called **emulators** you can play the games again on modern computers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A cheap computer for the family, widespread above all in the 1980s.
A simple programming language for beginners.
A flat, magnetic storage disc in a plastic case.
A program that imitates an old computer on a new device.

gewusst: The Commodore 64 had a working memory of 64 kilobytes, which is less memory than a single small mobile phone photo needs today.
Back then some games were even broadcast on the radio and could be recorded with a cassette recorder.
Many of today’s well-known game developers learnt to program on home computers as children.

teile.einleitung: A password is a secret word or a secret string of characters with which you prove that you are allowed to use something. It protects, for example, your email account, your games or your mobile phone from access by others. How good this protection is depends a lot on how you choose and keep your password.
wichtigste: A password is used to protect accounts, devices and data.
Short or simple passwords like “1234” are easy to guess.
A long sentence as a password is much more secure than a short word.
A short number password for a mobile phone or bank card is called a PIN.
You should use a separate password for every account.
If someone knows your password who shouldn't, you change it immediately.
