A note stuck on the screen is a bad place for a password.

abschnitte.text: A password works like a **key** for the digital world. Only someone who knows it can get into an account, an app or a device. Together with the user name, it is used for **logging in**. The word originally comes from guards who only let through people with the right watchword.

Fraudsters often simply try out the most common passwords, such as “123456”, “password” or the name of the pet. Computer programs can test a huge number of combinations in a short time; this is called a **brute-force attack**. The shorter and simpler a password, the faster it is cracked. Another trick is **phishing**: fake emails or websites ask you to enter your password.

Long passwords are the most secure, because the number of possible combinations grows enormously. A good option is a **passphrase**, a sentence of several words that don't go together, such as “Blue cow dances on Mount Pilatus”. You can also add numbers and special characters. Names, birthdays and dictionary words on their own, on the other hand, are weak.

For mobile phones and bank cards, people often use a **PIN**, a short secret number. Because it is so short, a device is locked after several wrong attempts. Many services also offer **two-factor authentication**. Then, as well as the password, you need a code that is sent to your phone, for example.

Don't tell anyone your password, not even your best friend; only your parents may know it. Don't stick it on a note on the screen, and don't type it in when someone is looking over your shoulder. Don't use the same password everywhere, otherwise all your accounts are at risk if there is a data leak. A **password manager** can store many passwords safely. In Switzerland, the Federal Office for Cybersecurity gives tips on handling passwords safely.

begriffe.erklaerung: Personal identification number, a short secret number.
A password made of several words or a whole sentence.
An attempt at fraud in which fake messages are used to steal passwords.
Logging in with two proofs, for example a password and a code on your phone.
A program that keeps many passwords in encrypted form.

gewusst: Even soldiers in ancient Rome used secret watchwords to tell friend from foe.
Every extra character makes a password much harder to guess, because the number of possibilities multiplies.
A four-digit PIN has only 10,000 possible combinations, which is why a phone locks itself after a few wrong attempts.

teile.einleitung: An icon is a small picture on the screen that stands for a program, a file or a command. In German it is also called a “Symbol”. Icons help you to find your way around computers and mobile phones quickly, even without much reading.
wichtigste: An icon is a small picture on the computer.
In German, an icon is also called a “Symbol”.
A magnifying glass often stands for searching.
A cogwheel often stands for settings.
A small house often stands for the home page.
A floppy disk often stands for saving.
Icons became well known with graphical user interfaces in the 1980s.

abschnitte.text: An icon is a small, simple **picture sign** on a screen. It can stand for a program, a file, a folder or a command. If you click or tap on it, something happens; for example, an app opens. The word comes from the Greek word for image.

Many icons look similar on almost all devices. A **magnifying glass** stands for searching, a **cogwheel** for settings and a small **house** for the home page. A printer stands for printing, a loudspeaker for the volume and a waste bin for deleting. So you usually understand the meaning at first glance.

abschnitte.titel: The floppy disk as the save icon
abschnitte.text: The icon for saving still often shows a **floppy disk**. Floppy disks used to be the usual storage media, but they have hardly been used for many years. That is why many children have never seen a real floppy disk and only know it as a symbol. Icons like this, which imitate an object that has disappeared, are sometimes linked with **skeuomorphism**.

Icons became well known with **graphical user interfaces**, in which you click on pictures with the mouse instead of typing commands. The first ideas for this came about in the 1970s at the company Xerox in California. Icons became famous in 1984 with Apple’s **Macintosh**, whose icons were designed by the designer Susan Kare. Later Windows also took over this way of working.

A good icon is simple, clear and easy to recognise even at a small size. It should be understandable for people from different countries. Icons are often accompanied by a short text so that there are no misunderstandings. This is especially important for **accessibility**, so that everyone can use a device well.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small picture sign on the screen that stands for something.
Everything you see on the screen and use to operate a device.
A flat storage medium in a plastic case that used to be common.
Design that makes it possible for everyone to use something, including people with a disability.

gewusst: The first Macintosh icons were designed square by square on squared paper.
A smartphone home screen consists almost entirely of app icons.
The save icon still shows a floppy disk, even though floppy disks are hardly used any more.

teile.einleitung: An HTTP cookie is a small text file that a website stores in your browser. In this way the site can remember who you are or what is in your shopping basket. Cookies are handy, but they are also used to track your behaviour on the internet.
wichtigste: A cookie is a small text file that a website stores in the browser.
In online shops, cookies make sure that the shopping basket stays the same as you click on.
The company Netscape developed cookies in 1994 for its web browser.
Session cookies are deleted when you close the browser.
Third-party cookies come from another company, often for advertising.
You can delete cookies in the browser settings.
Cookies cannot run programs; they only contain text data.

abschnitte.text: The word cookie means biscuit in American English, but it has nothing to do with food. A cookie is a small piece of **text data** that a website places in your **browser**. It contains, for example, an identification number or the language you chose. On your next visit, the browser sends the cookie back to the site, and the site recognises you again.

Websites are loaded using the protocol **HTTP**, and HTTP forgets everything after each request. Without cookies, an online shop would no longer know at the next click what is in your **shopping basket**. The cookie therefore works like a cloakroom ticket that you show on every visit. This idea was invented in 1994 at the company **Netscape**.

**Session cookies** only apply while the browser is open and disappear afterwards. **Persistent cookies** stay stored until an expiry date is reached, for example so that you stay signed in. **Third-party cookies** do not come from the site you are visiting but from other companies, for example advertising networks. With them it is possible to track which sites someone visits one after another.

Because cookies can be used to collect data, there are rules on **data protection**. That is why many websites show a **cookie banner** and ask whether you agree to certain cookies. In Switzerland, the Data Protection Act requires websites to say openly which data they process. You can usually refuse advertising cookies without the site no longer working because of it.

Read the cookie banner carefully before you click on “Accept all”. There is often a button such as “Necessary only” or “Reject”. In the **browser settings** you can delete stored cookies at any time. A **private window** deletes cookies automatically as soon as you close it.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small text file that a website stores in the browser.
A cookie that is deleted when the browser is closed.
A cookie from another company, usually for advertising or statistics.
A notice window that asks whether you agree to cookies.

gewusst: Unlike a virus, cookies cannot run anything on your computer, because they only contain text.
In most browsers, a single cookie may only be about 4 kilobytes in size.
The name probably comes from the programming term “magic cookie” for a small packet of data.

teile.einleitung: Pascal is a programming language that the Swiss computer scientist Niklaus Wirth published in 1970. It was made above all for learning to program cleanly and readably. For decades, many pupils and students all over the world wrote their first programs with it.
wichtigste: Pascal was developed by Niklaus Wirth at ETH Zurich.
The language appeared in 1970.
It is named after the French mathematician Blaise Pascal.
Pascal was especially popular for teaching structured programming.
In Pascal an assignment is written with the pair of characters :=.
Blocks of statements begin with begin and end with end.
Turbo Pascal was a very popular development environment in the 1980s.

abschnitte.text: **Niklaus Wirth** developed Pascal at the end of the 1960s at ETH Zurich and published the language in **1970**. He wanted a language that is clearly structured and encourages good programming habits. He named it after **Blaise Pascal**, who built one of the first calculating machines in the 17th century. Pascal built on older languages such as Algol but was simpler.

A Pascal program begins with the word program and a name. Statements are grouped between **begin** and **end**, and there is a full stop at the end. You assign a value to a variable with **:=**, for example x := 5. With writeln you output a text and then move to the next line.

In Pascal you have to declare every variable with its **data type** beforehand, for example integer for whole numbers or char for characters. This lets the computer find many errors before the program even runs. The language supports **structured programming** with clear loops and branches such as if, while and for. Wild jumps right across the program should be avoided.

At the beginning of the 1980s, home computers and PCs became popular. In 1983 the company Borland brought out **Turbo Pascal**, a fast and inexpensive development environment. With it you could write, compile and test programs all in one program. Early programs for the Apple Macintosh were also largely written in Pascal.

Wirth himself developed the successor languages **Modula-2** and **Oberon**. In 1995 Turbo Pascal led to **Delphi**, with which you could build programs with windows and buttons. Today there are free tools such as Free Pascal and Lazarus. In schools Pascal has now mostly been replaced by languages such as Python, but many of Pascal's ideas live on.

begriffe.erklaerung: A named storage place for a value, for example a number.
The kind of value, such as whole number, decimal number or text.
A program that translates source code into machine code.
A program in which you write, compile and test code.

gewusst: The Dane Anders Hejlsberg, who developed Turbo Pascal, later also created the languages C# and TypeScript.
A Hello World program in Pascal is only a few lines long.
Not only this language is named after Blaise Pascal, but also the unit of measurement for pressure.

teile.einleitung: Headphones are small loudspeakers that you wear directly on or in your ears. This lets you listen to music, films or games on your own without disturbing others. They come with or without a cable, big over the ears or tiny in the ear.
wichtigste: With headphones you hear sounds on your own without others having to listen too.
Listening too loudly can damage your ears permanently.
Headphones with a built-in microphone are called a headset.
Very small headphones that you put straight into your ear are called earphones.
Many wireless headphones connect via Bluetooth.
The letters L and R stand for the left and the right side.
In traffic you should not wear loud headphones, because then you cannot hear cars and bikes.

abschnitte.text: Each side of a pair of headphones contains a tiny **loudspeaker**, also called a driver. It turns electrical signals into sound by making a thin membrane vibrate back and forth. Because the loudspeaker sits so close to the ear, very little energy is enough for a good sound. The sides are marked **L** for left and **R** for right. That way you can hear in music and games which direction a sound is coming from.

**Over-ear** headphones are big and enclose the whole ear. On-ear models only rest on the ear and are a little lighter. **Earphones** are very small and are put straight into the ear, some with soft silicone tips. A **headset** also has a microphone so that you can make phone calls, play online or take part in video calls. There are also bone-conduction headphones, which carry the sound through the bones of the skull to the inner ear.

You plug wired headphones into the **headphone socket** on the computer, which usually has a diameter of 3.5 millimetres. Some devices use a USB connection instead. Wireless headphones usually connect via **Bluetooth**, a radio technology for short distances. They have a battery that you need to charge regularly. Many modern models also have active **noise cancelling**, which makes noise such as engine sounds on the train or plane almost disappear.

If you listen to music very loudly for a long time, you can damage your **hearing** permanently. In the inner ear there are fine hair cells that break when there is too much noise and do not grow back. A warning sign is a whistling or rushing sound in the ear, called **tinnitus**. A simple rule of thumb is: at most about 60 percent of the volume and a break after an hour. Many mobile phones now warn you themselves if you are listening too loudly.

In **traffic** you must be able to hear cars, bikes, trams and warning signals clearly. With loud headphones or strong noise cancelling you often notice them too late. So it is better to take your headphones off when cycling and crossing the road. Some headphones have a **transparency mode** that lets surrounding sounds through. But it does not completely replace paying attention.

As early as around 1910, the American Nathaniel Baldwin built headphones that were used by the navy. For a long time, it was mainly radio operators, telephone operators and pilots who used headphones. From 1979 Sony's portable cassette player, the **Walkman**, made light headphones popular with many people. Later came MP3 players and smartphones with earphones. Today wireless earphones are a completely everyday accessory.

begriffe.erklaerung: Headphones with a built-in microphone for speaking and listening.
A radio technology that connects devices over short distances without cables.
A technology that measures surrounding noise and almost cancels it out with counter-sound.
A constant whistling or rushing sound in the ear, often after too much noise.

gewusst: Active noise cancelling produces a counter-sound that cancels out the noise like a mirror image.
Some headphones pass the sound on through the bones, so your ears stay free.
Headphones can also work the other way round as a very simple microphone, because the membrane can turn sound into electric current.

teile.einleitung: Online advertising is advertising on the internet, for example on websites, in apps, in games or before videos. Companies pay to have their products shown to as many people as possible. If you can recognise online advertising, you are less likely to fall for tricks.
wichtigste: Many free apps and websites earn their money from advertising.
You can often recognise advertising by the word “Ad” or “Advert”.
A short advertising film, for example before a video, is called a commercial.
An influencer who is paid for praising something is also advertising.
You should not click on a flashing window saying “You've won!”.
The safest way to close an advert window is with the small X.
Not everything an advert promises is really true.

abschnitte.text: **Online advertising** is any kind of advertising you see on the internet. This includes pictures at the edge of a website, called **banners**, and windows that suddenly open, called **pop-ups**. Short advertising films before videos and paid posts on social networks also count. Even in search engines, paid results are often right at the top.

abschnitte.titel: Why is there so much of it?
abschnitte.text: Many apps, games and websites are free, but making them still costs money. That is why they show **advertising**, because companies pay for every advert or every click. This is how video platforms and search engines, for example, earn a lot of money. That is why people say: if something is free, you often pay with your attention.

Websites use small files, the **cookies**, to remember what you look at. From this they build up a picture of what you are interested in. Then you get **personalised advertising**, that is, adverts that match your own interests exactly. If you search a lot for football boots, you will often see adverts for football boots afterwards.

Some advertising is not honest or is even dangerous. Messages like “You've won! Click here!” are almost always a trick to steal data or sell something. There are also fake close buttons that actually open a new page. The safest way to close a window is with the small **X**, or you ask an adult.

Reputable websites label advertising with words like **Ad**, “Advert” or “Sponsored”. In games, advertising often appears as a video that you have to watch to get a reward. Programs that hide advertising are called ad blockers. It is important to stay calm, not to buy anything hastily and not to enter any personal details.

One of the first advertising banners appeared on an American website in 1994. Back then, many people still clicked on it out of curiosity. Today online advertising is one of the biggest advertising markets in the world. Large internet companies such as Google and Meta earn most of their money from **advertising**.

begriffe.erklaerung: An advertising picture on a website, often at the top or at the edge.
A window that suddenly opens by itself.
A short advertising film.
A small file that a website uses to remember what you have done.
A program that hides advertising on websites.

gewusst: In some games you can watch advertising videos to get extra lives or coins.
Companies often only pay when someone really clicks on their advert.
In many apps, advertising is designed so that you can easily tap it by mistake.
